One: «ما» is interrogative in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ, «ذا» means «الذي», «أراد الله» is the ṣila, and the referring pronoun is omitted since its conditions are fulfilled, its implied form being «أرادَه اللهُ»; the relative is the khabar of the interrogative «ما». The second: «ماذا» is like one noun in the position of the accusative by the verb after it, its implied form being "what thing did Allah intend?". The position of this clause is accusative by the saying [as its object].
[«الإرادة» (will) linguistically is seeking a thing with inclination toward it; it may be stripped down to [mere] seeking, and that is what is attributed to Allah the Exalted. Its middle radical is wāw, from «رادَ يرودُ», i.e. to seek. So the underlying form of «أراد» is «أَرْوَدَ», like «أَقام», and the maṣdar is «الإِرادة», like «الإِقامة»; its underlying form is «إرْوَاد», which underwent weakening, and the feminine tāʾ was given as compensation for what was omitted.]
His saying «مَثَلاً» is accusative as a tamyīz (specification). It was said: it comes in the sense of emphasis, because from the fact that it was pointed to with «هذا» it was known to be a parable, so the tamyīz came after it emphasising the noun pointed to. It was also said: accusative as a ḥāl. There is disagreement about the one it describes: it was said, the demonstrative, the governing element being the sense of pointing; and it was said, the name of Allah the Exalted, i.e. "using it as a parable". It was also said: [accusative] by cutting off (al-qaṭʿ), which is the view of the Kufans; its meaning according to them is that it was originally meant to follow what precedes it, the underlying form being «بهذا المثلِ» (by this parable), and when it was cut off from following it became accusative. On this is the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
312 - سَوامِقُ جَبَّارٍ أثيثٍ فُروعُهُ ... وعَاليْنَ قِنْواناً من البُسْرِ أَحْمَرَا
(Lofty, tall palms with dense branches, which have raised up clusters of red unripe dates.)
Its underlying form is «من البسر الأحمر».
His saying: {يُضِلُّ بِهِ كَثِيراً}: the bāʾ is causal, and likewise in {يَهْدِي بِهِ}. These two clauses have no grammatical position, because they are like an explanation of the two clauses headed by «أمَّا», and they are from the speech of Allah the Exalted. It was also said: they are in the position of the accusative because they are two adjectives of «مَثَلاً», i.e. a parable by which people are divided into those astray and those guided; on this view they are from the speech of the disbelievers. Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed it to be a ḥāl from the name of Allah, i.e. "leading many astray by it and guiding many by it".
Ibn ʿAṭiyya allowed the clause {يُضِلُّ بِهِ كَثِيراً} to be from the speech of the disbelievers, and the clause {وَيَهْدِي بِهِ كَثِيراً} from the speech of the Creator, Exalted is He. This is not evident, because it creates confusion in the construction. The pronoun in «به» refers to «ضَرْب» (striking), implicitly put in genitive construct with «المثل», i.e. "by the striking of the parable". It was also said: the first pronoun is for denial and the second for affirmation, the force of the speech indicating that.
It was read: {يُضَلُّ به كثيرٌ ويُهدى به كثيرٌ، وما يُضَلُّ به إلا الفاسقُون}, in the passive; and it was also read: {يَضِلُّ به كثيرٌ ويَهْدي به كثيرٌ، وما يَضِلُّ بِه إلا الفاسقون}, in the active. Some said: "It is the reading of the Qadariyya." I say: Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted from Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī that it is the reading of the Muʿtazila, then said: "And Ibn Abī ʿAbla is among the trustworthy Syrians" — meaning its reader. In any case it contradicts the script (sawād) of the muṣḥaf.
[Translator's note: the source text prints «يُضِلُّ» and «ويهدى» in the first reading; they are rendered as passive here in keeping with the stated description "in the passive".]
If it is asked: how did He describe the guided here as many, when they are few, according to His saying {وَقَلِيلٌ مَّا هُمْ} [Ṣād: 24] and {وَقَلِيلٌ مِّنْ عِبَادِيَ الشكور} [Sabaʾ: 13]? The answer is that even if they are few in outward form, they are many in reality, as in his saying:
313 - إنَّ الكرامَ كثيرٌ في البلادِ وإنْ ... قَلُّوا كما غيرهُم قَلَّ وإنْ كَثُروا
(The noble are many in the lands even if they are few, just as others are few even if they are many.)
So that is in two respects.
His saying: {وَمَا يُضِلُّ بِهِ إِلاَّ الفاسقين}: «الفاسقين» is the object of «يُضِلُّ», and it is an emptied exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh); its meaning has preceded. According to al-Farrāʾ it may be accusative as the excepted (mustathnā), with what it is excepted from omitted, the implied form being: "and He does not lead anyone astray by it except the transgressors", as in his saying:
314 - نَجا سالمٌ والنَّفْسُ منه بشِدْقِه ... ولِمَ يَنْجُ إلا جَفْنَ سيفٍ ومِئْزَرا
(Sālim escaped with his soul at the corner of his mouth, and he escaped with nothing but a sword-sheath and a waist-wrapper.)
i.e. "he did not escape with anything". Abū al-Baqāʾ disallowed its accusative as an exception, as though he took into account the doctrine of the majority of the Basrans.
«الفِسْق» linguistically is going out. One says «فَسَقَتِ الرُّطَبَةُ عن قِشْرِها», i.e. the ripe date came out of its skin. The «فاسق» is one who goes out of obedience to Allah the Exalted. One says «فَسَق يفسُقُ ويفسِقُ», with ḍamma and kasra in the imperfect, «فِسْقاً وفُسوقاً», so he is «فاسقٌ». Ibn al-Anbārī claimed that «فاسق» was not heard in the speech of the Jāhiliyya nor in its poetry — and this is astonishing. Ruʾba said:
315 - يَهْوِينَ في نَجْدٍ وغَوْراً غائراً ... فواسِقاً عن قَصْدِها جَوائِزاً
(They [the she-camels] plunge on in highland and in deep lowland, straying from their course, veering aside.)

semin-durr:19-19.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {أَوْ كَصَيِّبٍ مِّنَ السمآء}: about «أو» there are five views. The most evident: that it is for detailing (tafṣīl), meaning that among those who consider the state of these people, some liken them to the state of the kindler described thus, and some liken them to the people of a downpour described thus. Second: that it is for vagueness (ibhām), i.e. Allah left it vague to His servants whether they are likened to these or to those. Third: that it is for doubt, meaning that the observer doubts how to liken them. Fourth: that it is for permission (ibāḥa). Fifth: that it is for choice (takhyīr), i.e. people were permitted to liken them to this or to that, and were given the choice in that. The Kufans added two other meanings for it. One: its meaning «و» ("and"); they recited:
225 - جاء الخلافةَ أو كانَتْ له قَدَراً ... كما أتى ربَّه موسى على قَدَرِ
(He came to the caliphate, and it was decreed for him, as Moses came to his Lord according to a decree.)
The other: its meaning «بل» ("rather"); they recited:
226 - بَدَتْ مثلَ قَرْن الشمسِ في رَوْنَقِ الضُّحَى ... وصورتِها أَوْ أَنْتَ في العينِ أَمْلَحُ
(She appeared like the rim of the sun in the brightness of forenoon and in its form — nay, you are lovelier to the eye.)
i.e. "rather, you".
«كصيّب» is conjoined to «كمثل», so it is in the position of nominative. Two muḍāfs must be omitted for the meaning to be sound, the implied form being "or like the likeness of the people of a downpour"; that is why the plural pronoun refers to it in His saying {يَجْعَلُونَ أَصْابِعَهُمْ في آذَانِهِم}, because the meaning is their being likened to the people of the downpour, not to the downpour itself. Al-ṣayyib is rain, so called because of its descending; one says «صاب يصوب» when it descends. [The poet] said:
227 - فلسْتُ لإِنسِيٍّ ولكن لِمَلأَكٍ ... تَنَزَّلَ من جوِّ السماءِ يَصُوبُ
(You are not [the child] of a human, but of an angel who came down from the expanse of the sky, descending.)
Another said:
228 - فلا تَعْدِلي بيني وبينَ مُغَمَّرٍ ... سَقَتْكِ رَوايا المُزْنِ حيثُ تَصُوبُ
(Do not put me on a level with an untried man — may the laden rain-clouds water you wherever they pour down.)
There is disagreement about the pattern of «صيّب». The doctrine of the Basrans is that it is «فَيْعِل», the origin being «صَيْوِب», then assimilated, like «ميّت» and «هيّن», whose origins are «مَيْوِت» and «هَيْوِن». Some of the Kufans said its pattern is «فَعِيل», the origin being «صَوِيب» on the pattern of «طويل». Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is a mistake, because it should then have remained sound and not been modified, like «طويل»." Abū al-Baqāʾ said the same. It has also been said its pattern is «فَعْيِل», then metathesised and assimilated.
Know that if it is said that the clause {ذَهَبَ الله بِنُورِهِمْ} is resumptive, and of {صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ} that it is a description of the hypocrites, they would be two parenthetical clauses between the two conjoined elements, I mean «كمثل» and «كصيّب». This is a disputed question; al-Fārisī disallowed it, and he was refuted with the poet's saying:
229 - لَعَمْرُكَ والخُطوبُ مُغَيِّراتٌ ... وفي طولِ المُعَاشَرَةِ التَّقالي
لقد بالَيْتُ مَظْعَنَ أمِّ أَوْفَى ... ولكنْ أمُّ أَوفَى لا تُبالي
(By your life — and misfortunes change things, and in long companionship there is mutual aversion — I did care about Umm Awfā's departure, but Umm Awfā does not care.)
He separated between the oath, his saying «لعمرك», and its answer, his saying «لقد باليت», with two clauses: one «والخطوب مغيّرات», the second «وفي طول المعاشرة التقالي».
[His saying] «من السماء» admits two aspects. First: that it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «صيّب», because it governs as a verb does, the implied form being "like rain descending from the sky", «من» being for the beginning of the extent. Second: that it is in the position of genitive as an adjective of «صيّب», so it is attached to something omitted, and «من» is partitive; in that case a muḍāf must be omitted, the implied form being "like a downpour being from the rains of the sky".
Al-samāʾ is everything above you, a roof and the like; it is derived from al-sumuww, which is height. The origin is «سَماو»; the wāw was changed into hamza only because it occurred final after an additional alif, which is a regular substitution, as in «كِساء» and «رِداء», unlike «سِقاية» and «شَقاوة», because the weak letter is not final; for that reason, when the feminine tāʾ enters it, it remains sound, as in «سَماوة». The poet said:
230 - طيَّ الليالي زُلَفاً فَزُلَفَا ... سَماوَةَ الهلالِ حتى احْقَوْقَفَا
(As the nights fold, stage after stage, the body of the new moon until it becomes bent.)
Al-samāʾ is feminine and may be masculine; they recited:
231 - فلو رَفَعَ السماءُ إليه قوماً ... لَحِقْنَا بالسماءِ مَعَ السحابِ
(Had the sky raised a people up to it, we would have reached the sky with the clouds.)
So he referred the pronoun in his saying «إليه» to the sky as masculine. Its plurals are «سماوات», «أسْمِيَة» and «سُمِيّ». The origin [of the last] is «فُعول», but it was modified as «عُصِيّ» was, by changing the two wāws into two yāʾs; this change is regular in the plural and rare in the singular, as in «عتا عُتِيّاً», just as leaving it sound in the plural is anomalous: they said «إنكم تنظرون في نُحُوٍّ كثيرة» ("you are looking into many grammars"). It is also pluralised as «سَماء», but its singular is «سَماوة», so it is of the class of «تمرة» and «تمر». His saying indicates that:
232 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . فوق سَبْعِ سَمَائِيا
(…above seven skies.)
The point of proof is that «سبع» is specified by it, and it and its sisters are specified only by a genitive plural.
His saying, Exalted is He: «فيه ظلماتٌ ورعدٌ وبرقٌ» admits four aspects. First: that it is an adjective of «صيّب». Second: that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from it, even though it is indefinite, because it is specified either by governing the preposition after it or by an adjective consisting of the preposition after it. Third: that it is a ḥāl of the pronoun latent in «من السماء», if that is said to be an adjective of «صيّب». On all three assumptions it is attached to something omitted, except that on the first view it is in the position of genitive as an adjective of a genitive noun, and on the latter two in the position of accusative as a ḥāl. On all these views «ظلمات» is its fāʿil (agent), because the preposition-and-genitive and the adverb, when they rest upon a qualified noun, the possessor of a ḥāl, the possessor of a predicate, or upon a negation or interrogative, govern as the verb does; al-Akhfash makes them govern without restriction, like the adjective; the exact treatment of this will come. Fourth: that it is a fronted khabar (predicate) and «ظلمات» a mubtadaʾ (subject); the clause then admits two aspects: genitive as an adjective of «صيّب»; and second, accusative as a ḥāl, the possessor of the ḥāl possibly being «كصيّب» — even though it is indefinite, because it is specified by what precedes — or the pronoun latent in «من السماء» if that is made an adjective of «صيّب». The pronoun in «فيه» is the pronoun of the downpour.
Know that making the preposition an adjective or ḥāl and putting «ظلمات» in the nominative as its agent is preferable to making «فيه ظلمات» a clause on its own in the position of an adjective or ḥāl, because the preposition is closer to the single word than the clause is, and the basic form of the adjective and the ḥāl is to be single words.
«ورعدٌ وبرقٌ» are conjoined to «ظلمات» under the two considerations mentioned. They are originally maṣdars (verbal nouns): you say «رعدت السماء ترعُد رعداً» and «برقت برقاً». Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "On that basis they are [singular] here", meaning as maṣdars. They may mean «الراعد» and «البارق» ("the thundering", "the flashing"), as in «رجلٌ عدلٌ». The apparent view is that in the verse the maṣdar is not what is meant by them; rather they were made names for the rumbling and the flashing, which is what the verse intends, and there is then no need to make them mean the active participle.
His saying, Exalted is He: {يَجْعَلُونَ أَصْابِعَهُمْ في آذَانِهِم}: the apparent view is that this clause has no grammatical position because it is resumptive, as if it were asked: "What is their state?" and it was said: "They put…". It has also been said: rather it has a position, and then there is disagreement about it. It has been said: genitive, because it is an adjective of the genitive noun, i.e. "people of a downpour putting…", the [resumptive] pronoun being omitted or the alif-lām standing in its place, the implied form being: "they put their fingers in their ears from the thunderbolts from it", or "from its thunderbolts". It has been said: its position is accusative as a ḥāl of the pronoun in «فيه». The discussion of the resumptive is as before. Al-jaʿl here means "placing". It also means "creating", taking one object; it means "making into" or "naming", taking two objects; and it is for commencing, governing as «عسى» does.
«أصابعهم» is the plural of «إصبع», in which there are ten dialect forms: with the three vowels on the hamza combined with the three vowels on the bāʾ, and the tenth «أُصْبوع» with ḍamma on the hamza. The wāw in «يجعلون» refers to the omitted muḍāf, as explained above. Know that when the muḍāf is omitted, two considerations are allowed: to take account of it or not to take account of it. Both are combined in His saying, Exalted is He: {وَكَم مِّن قَرْيَةٍ أَهْلَكْنَاهَا فَجَآءَهَا بَأْسُنَا بَيَاتاً أَوْ هُمْ قَآئِلُونَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 4], the implied form being "how many people of a town": He did not take account of it in His saying {أَهْلَكْنَاهَا فَجَآءَهَا}, and took account of it in His saying {أَوْ هُمْ قَآئِلُونَ}. {في آذَانِهِم} and {مِّنَ الصواعق} are both attached to the putting, and «من» means causation. «الصواعق» is the plural of «صاعقة», which is the violent crash of the thunder's sound accompanied by a piece of fire. One also says «ساعقة» with sīn, and «صاقعة» with the qāf put first; he recited:
233 - ألم تَرَ أنَّ المجرمين أصابَهُمْ ... صواقِعُ، لا بل هُنَّ فوق الصواقِعِ
(Do you not see that thunderbolts struck the criminals — no, rather [strikes] above thunderbolts?)
Like it is another's saying:
234 - يَحْكُمُونَ بالمَصْقُولَةِ القواطِعِ ... تَشَقُّقَ اليدَيْنِ بِالصَّواقِعِ
(They judge with the polished cutting [swords], [splitting] like hands splitting from thunderbolts.)
It is the reading of al-Ḥasan. Al-Naḥḥās said: "It is the dialect of Tamīm and some of Banū Rabīʿa." So «صاقعة» may be metathesised from «صاعقة», or may not — which is more evident, since it is established as an independent dialect form, as said. One also says «صَعْقة», and al-Kisāʾī read it so in al-Dhāriyāt. One says «صُعِقَ زيدٌ» and «أصعقه غيرُه»; [the poet] said:
235 - تَرى النُّعَراتِ الزُرْقَ تَحْتَ لَبَانِهِ ... أُحادَ وَمَثْنَى أصْعَقَتْهَا صواهِلُهْ
(You see the blue gadflies under his chest, singly and in pairs, struck dead by his neighing.)
His saying, Exalted is He: «حَذَرَ الموت» has two aspects. The more evident: that it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose) governed by «يجعلون»; multiple objects of purpose do no harm, because a verb may be explained by several causes. Second: that it is accusative as a maṣdar, its governor being omitted, the implied form being "they beware with a wariness like the wariness of death". Al-ḥadhar and al-ḥidhār are two maṣdars of «حذِر», i.e. he feared intensely.
Know that the object of purpose, with respect to its being accusative or made genitive by a preposition, is of three kinds. A kind usually accusative: what is not made definite by «أل» nor annexed, as in «جئت إكراماً لك». A kind the reverse of it: what is made definite by «أل»; of its coming in the accusative is the poet's saying:
236 - لا أَقْعُدُ الجُبْنَ عن الهَيْجَاءِ ... ولو توالَتْ زُمَرُ الأعداءِ
(I do not hold back from battle out of cowardice, even if throngs of enemies follow one after another.)
And a kind in which both are equal: the annexed one, as in the noble verse, whether definite or indefinite. Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī combined both in his saying:
237 - وَأَغْفِرُ عوراءَ الكريمِ ادِّخَارَهُ ... وأُعْرِضُ عن شَتْمِ اللئيمِ تَكَرُّمَا
(I forgive the noble man's ugly word, to keep him in store, and I turn away from the base man's insult, out of nobility.)
«حذر الموت» is a maṣdar annexed to its object, its agent being omitted. This is one of the places where omitting the agent alone is allowed; [the second is the verb whose agent is not named (the passive); the third is the agent of «أفعل» in exclamation according to the correct view; outside these, omitting the agent alone is not allowed], contrary to the Kufans. Al-mawt is the opposite of life; one says «مات يموت» and «يَمات»; the poet said:
238 - بُنَيَّتي سَيِّدَةَ البناتِ ... عِيشي ولا يُؤْمَنُ أن تَماتي
(My little daughter, mistress of daughters, live — though there is no safety from your dying.)
In this dialect «مِتْنا» and «مِتُّ» were read with kasra on the mīm, like «خِفْنا» and «خِفْتُ». So the pattern of «مات» in the first dialect is «فَعَل» with fatḥa on the middle radical, and in the second «فَعِل» with kasra. «المُوات» with ḍamma is also death, and with fatḥa it is what has no spirit in it. «المَوَتان», with the middle voweled, is the opposite of «الحَيَوان»; from it is their saying «اشترِ المَوَتانَ ولا تشترِ الحَيَوان», i.e. buy lands and do not buy slaves, for they are exposed to perishing. «المُوتان» with ḍamma on the mīm is death striking livestock. «مُوِّت فلان», with doubling, is for intensity; [the poet] said:
239 - فَعُرْوَةُ مات موتاً مستريحاً ... فها أنا ذا أُمَوَّتُ كلَّ يومِ
(ʿUrwa died a restful death, while here I am, dying every day.)
«المستميت» is what is continuous [Translator's note: printed «الأمر المسترسل», "the continuous matter"]; Ruʾba said:
240 - وزَبَدُ البَحْرِ له كَتِيتُ ... والليلُ فوق الماء مُسْتَمِيتُ
(The sea's foam has a seething sound, and the night lies over the water, unbroken.)
His saying, Exalted is He: «والله محيطٌ بالكافرين» is a clause of mubtadaʾ and khabar. The origin of «مُحيط» is «مُحْوِط», since it is from «حاط يحوط»; it was modified as «نستعين» was. Al-iḥāṭa is enclosing a thing from all its sides; here it expresses their being under His dominance and not escaping Him. It has also been said: there is an omitted muḍāf, i.e. His punishment encompasses them. Al-Zamakhsharī said of this clause: "It is parenthetical, with no grammatical position", as if he meant by that that the clause «يجعلون أصابعهم» and the clause «يكاد البرق» are one thing, because they belong to one story, so what is between them occurred as a parenthesis.

semin-durr:27-27.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {الذين يَنقُضُونَ}: there are four aspects in it. The first: that it is a naʿt (adjective) of «الفاسِقين». The second: that it is accusative (manṣūb) by way of censure (ʿalā al-dhamm). The third: that it is nominative (marfūʿ) as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is the clause in His saying {أولئك هُمُ الخاسرون}. The fourth: that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "they are the transgressors."
Al-naqḍ (breaking) is the undoing of the composition of a thing and returning it to its first state. Al-ʿahd (covenant) in their speech has several meanings, among them: bequest (waṣiyya), guarantee (ḍamān), sufficing (iktifāʾ) and command (amr). Al-khasār is diminution, in a balance or otherwise; Jarīr said:
316 - إنَّ سَليطاً في الخسار إنَّهْ ... أولادُ قومٍ خُلِقوا أَقِنَّهْ
(Indeed Salīṭ are in loss; indeed they are the sons of a people created as slaves.)
And «خَسَرْتُ الشيء», with fatḥa, and «أَخْسَرْتُه» mean: I diminished it; and al-khusrān, al-khasār and al-khaysarā all mean perdition.
And «مِنْ بعد» is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «يَنْقُضُون», and «مِنْ» is for the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya); it has also been said that it is redundant (zāʾida), but that is nothing. As for «ميثاقَه», the pronoun in it may refer back to «العهد», or it may refer back to the name of Allah the Exalted. On the first, it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) annexed to its object; on the second, annexed to its agent. Al-mīthāq is a maṣdar like al-mīlād and al-mīʿād in the sense of al-wilāda (birth) and al-waʿd (promise). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is a noun in the place of the maṣdar, as in his saying:
317 - أكُفْراً بعدَ رَدِّ الموتِ عني ... وبعد عطائِك المئةَ الرِّتاعا
(Ingratitude, after death was warded off from me, and after your giving the hundred grazing camels?)
i.e. your giving (iʿṭāʾika)." But there is no need calling for that. The root denotes binding and tying. Its plural is mawāthīq and mayāthiq, and Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited:
318 - حِمىً لا يَحُلُّ الدهرُ إلا بإذنِنا ... ولا نَسْأَل الأقوامَ عهدَ المَيَاثِقِ
(A protected domain that time does not enter except by our leave, and we do not ask other peoples for the pledge of covenants.)
And «يقطعونَ» is conjoined to «ينقضون» [Translator's note: the printed text reads «ينقصون», evidently a misprint for «ينقضون»], so it too is part of the ṣila (relative clause). And «ما» is a relative noun, and {أَمَرَ الله بِهِ} is its ṣila and [contains] its referent (ʿāʾid). Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be an indefinite qualified noun (nakira mawṣūfa). It cannot be maṣdariyya, because the pronoun refers back to it — except according to Abū al-Ḥasan [al-Akhfash] and Ibn al-Sarrāj. It is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of «يَقْطَعون».
His saying: {أَن يُوصَلَ}: there are three aspects in it. The first: the genitive, as a badal (substitute) for the pronoun in «به», i.e. "what Allah commanded the joining of," as in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
319 - أمِنْ ذِكْرِ ليلى أَنْ نَأَتْكَ تَنُوصُ ... فَتَقْصُرُ عنها خَطْوَةً وتَبُوصُ
(Is it from the memory of Laylā — her having gone far from you — that you shrink back, falling short of her by a step, and lag behind?)
i.e. "from her going far." [The second is] the accusative, in which there are two aspects. One of them: that it is a badal of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from «ما أمر الله». The second: that it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose); al-Mahdawī construed it as "out of dislike that it be joined," and others construed it as "that it not be joined." [The third is] the nominative, as the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, i.e. "it is that it be joined"; this is very far-fetched, even though Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned it.
And {يُفْسِدُونَ} is also conjoined to the ṣila, and {فِي الأرض} is attached to it. His saying {أولئك هُمُ الخاسرون} is like His saying {وأولئك هُمُ المفلحون} [al-Baqara: 5]. It has already been stated that this clause may be the khabar of {الذين يَنقُضُونَ} if that is made a mubtadaʾ; and if it is not made a mubtadaʾ, then it is resumptive, and so has no grammatical position in that case. The meaning of al-khasār has preceded. And al-amr (command) is a demand from the higher to the lower.

semin-durr:84-84.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَكُمْ لاَ تَسْفِكُونَ}: this is like His saying: {وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَ بني إِسْرَائِيلَ: لاَ تَعْبُدُونَ إِلاَّ الله} [al-Baqara: 83].
His saying: {مِّن دِيَارِكُمْ} is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «تُخْرِجُون», and «مِنْ» is for the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya). «دِيار» is the plural of «دَار», whose root form is «دَوَر», because it is from «دَار يدُور دَوَراناً» (to turn, revolve). The root form of «دِيار» is «دِوار»; the wāw was changed into a yāʾ only because of the kasra before it and because it is weak (muʿtall) in the singular. This is a regular rule in every plural on the pattern «فِعال» whose final radical is sound, when the middle radical of its singular is weakened or is a quiescent weak letter, such as: «دار» and «دِيار», and «ثِياب». For that reason «رِواء» remained sound, because its final radical is weak, and «طِوال» because the middle radical of its singular, «طويل», is vowelled; as for «طِيال» for «طِوال», it is anomalous (shādhdh). The ruling for the maṣdar (verbal noun) is the same as this, for example: «قامَ قِياماً» and «صامَ صِياماً»; and for that reason «لِواذ» remained sound, because its verb is sound in their saying «لاوَذ». As for «دَيَّار», it is from the word «الدَّار», and its root form is «دَيْوار»; the yāʾ and the wāw came together and were made weak according to the well-known rule, so its pattern is «فَيْعال», not «فَعَّال», since if it were «فَعَّال» it would have been said «دَوَّار», like «صَوَّام» and «قَوَّام». «الدار» is the place where a people gather, consisting of buildings. Al-Khalīl said: "Every place where people settle, even if there are no buildings."
It was also read: «تَسْفُكُون» with a ḍamma on the fāʾ, «تُسَفِّكون» from the doubled form «سَفَّك», and «تُسْفِكون» from the quadriliteral «أَسْفك».
His saying: {دِمَآءَكُمْ} may be taken literally, for there have been those who killed themselves; and it may be taken figuratively, and that in several ways. The first: putting the cause in place of the effect, i.e. if you shed the blood of others, then your own blood has been shed; this is close to their saying: "Killing is the best preventer of killing." [The poet] said:
583 - سَقَيْناهُمُ كأساً سَقَوْنا بمثلِها ... ولكنهم كانُوا على الموتِ أَصْبَرَا
(We gave them a cup to drink, and they gave us the like of it to drink, but they were more steadfast in the face of death.)
It was also said: "The meaning is: let not some of you shed the blood of others," and al-Zamakhsharī chose this. And it was said: "Do not shed it by committing what necessitates its being shed, such as apostasy and the like."
His saying: {ثُمَّ أَقْرَرْتُمْ}: Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "There are two views on it. The first is that «ثُمَّ» has its normal function of conveying conjunction and delay, and what it is conjoined to is omitted, its implied form being: 'so you accepted, then you affirmed.' The second is that «ثُمَّ» came for ordering the report, not for ordering what is reported about, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {ثُمَّ الله شَهِيدٌ} [Yūnus: 46]."
His saying: {وَأَنْتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ} is like His saying: {وَأَنْتُمْ مُّعْرِضُونَ} [al-Baqara: 83].

semin-durr:86-86.t:
The parallels of {أولئك الذين اشتروا} ... and what follows it have already been discussed. However, one of the grammarians (muʿribīn) mentioned some rejected views which must be pointed out. He allowed «أولئك» to be a mubtadaʾ (subject), {الذين اشتروا} its khabar (predicate), and {فَلاَ يُخَفَّفُ عَنْهُمُ العذاب} a second khabar of «أولئك». He said: "The fāʾ entered the khabar because of the relative noun, which resembles a condition." This is a mistake, for he did not make His saying {فَلاَ يُخَفَّفُ} a khabar of the relative noun, so that the fāʾ could enter its khabar; rather he made it a khabar of «أولئك» — and how far is this from that! He also allowed «الذين» to be a second mubtadaʾ and {فَلاَ يُخَفَّفُ} its khabar, [the fāʾ] having entered because it is the khabar of a relative noun, and the clause being a khabar of «أولئك». He said: "No returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) is needed here, because «الذين» are «أولئك», just as you say: «هذا زيدٌ منطلقٌ»." This too is a mistake, for three reasons. The first: the clause lacks a link (rābiṭ). His saying "because «الذين» are «أولئك»" is of no use, because a clause that dispenses [with a link] must itself be the very mubtadaʾ. As for his comparison with «هذا زيدٌ منطلقٌ», it is not correct, for «هذا» is a mubtadaʾ, «زيدٌ» a khabar and «منطلقٌ» a second khabar; it is not permissible for «زيدٌ» to be a second mubtadaʾ and «منطلقٌ» its khabar, with the clause as a khabar of the first, because it lacks a link. The second: the relative noun here refers to specific people and is not general, so it does not resemble a condition, and the fāʾ does not enter its khabar. The third: its ṣila (relative clause) is past in form and meaning, so it does not resemble the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ) in referring to the future, and the fāʾ may not enter the khabar. So it is determined that «أولئك» is a mubtadaʾ and the relative noun with its ṣila is its khabar, and {فَلاَ يُخَفَّفُ} is conjoined to the ṣila. The difference of the two verbs in tense does no harm, for ṣilas are of the category of clauses, and in conjoining clauses agreement of tense is not a condition: you may say «جاء الذي قَتَلَ زيداً أمسٍ وسيقتُل عمراً غداً» ("the one who killed Zayd yesterday and will kill ʿAmr tomorrow came"). That is only a condition where the verbs are treated as single words.
His saying: {وَلاَ هُمْ يُنصَرُونَ}: two views are permissible regarding «هم». The first: that it is in the position of nominative (marfūʿ) as a mubtadaʾ and what follows it is its khabar, so that a nominal clause has been conjoined to a verbal clause, namely {فلا يُخَفَّفَ}. The second: that it is nominative by an omitted verb which this overt one explains, the case being one of ishtighāl (preoccupation of the verb); when the verb was omitted the pronoun became detached, and it is like his saying:
600 - وإنْ هُو لم يَحْمِلْ على النفسِ ضَيْمَها ... فليسَ إلى حُسْنِ الثَّنَاءِ سَبيلُ
(And if he does not make the soul bear its hardship, there is no way to fine praise.)
This [second view] has a factor preferring it over the first, namely that you will then have conjoined a verbal clause to one like it, and this is one of the places in which construing with a verb is preferred in the chapter of ishtighāl. The preferring factor is not that the negating «لا» precedes it, for it is not one of the particles specific to the verb nor more appropriate to it — contrary to Ibn al-Sīd, who claimed that the negating «لا» is one of the factors preferring an implied verb; that is a view which is shunned, though it is strong in terms of argument. So His saying «يُنْصَرون» has no grammatical position on this [second] view, because it is explicative (mufassir), and its position is nominative on the first view because it occupies the place of the khabar.

semin-durr:8-8.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {وَمِنَ الناس مَن يَقُولُ} . . . the verse. {مِنَ الناس} is a fronted khabar (predicate), and «من يقول» is a postponed mubtadaʾ (subject). «مَنْ» may be a relative noun or an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, i.e. "the one who says" or "a party who says". On the first view the clause has no grammatical position, since it is a ṣila (relative clause); on the second its position is the nominative, since it is a naʿt (adjective) of the mubtadaʾ. Abū al-Baqāʾ considered it weak that it be a relative noun; he said: "because «الذي» refers to specific people, whereas the meaning here is indefinite" — end of quote. This claim of his is not conceded, because what has been transmitted is that the verse was revealed concerning specific people, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and his band. The master al-Zamakhsharī said: "If the al is for the genus, then «مَنْ» is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, as in His saying: {مِّنَ المؤمنين رِجَالٌ صَدَقُواْ} [al-Aḥzāb: 23]; and if it is for prior reference (al-ʿahd), it is a relative noun." It is as though he intended matching genus with genus and prior reference with prior reference; however, what he said is not binding. Rather, it is permissible for the al to be for the genus while «مَنْ» is a relative noun, and for it to be for prior reference while «مَنْ» is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective. Al-Kisāʾī claimed that it [i.e. indefinite qualified «مَنْ»] occurs only in a position specific to indefinite nouns, as in the poet's saying:
158 - رُبَّ مَنْ أنْضَجْتُ غيظاً قلبَه ... قد تَمَنَّى لِيَ مَوْتاً لَمْ يُطَعْ
(Many a one whose heart I have cooked with rage has wished me death, but was not granted it.)
What he said is the more common usage; however, it has come in a position not specific to indefinite nouns; the poet said:
159 - فكفى بنا فضلاً على مَنْ غيرُنا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(It suffices us as excellence over one who is other than us …)
«مَنْ» may be a relative noun, an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, as has preceded, conditional, and interrogative. Does it occur as an indefinite noun not qualified by an adjective, or as redundant (zāʾida)? There is a disagreement. Al-Kisāʾī adduced as evidence for its being redundant the saying of ʿAntara:
160 - يا شاةَ مَنْ قَنَصٍ لِمَنْ حَلَّتْ له ... حَرُمَتْ عليَّ ولَيْتَها لم تَحْرُمِ
(O what a doe of the hunt for one to whom she is lawful! She has been made unlawful to me — would that she had not been made unlawful.)
But there is no proof in it, since it is possible that it is qualified by «قَنَص», either by way of hyperbole or by the omission of a muḍāf.
The «مِنْ» in «مِنَ الناس» is partitive (li-l-tabʿīḍ). Some claimed that it is explicative (li-l-bayān), and that is a mistake, since nothing precedes that it could explain. «الناس» is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) that has no singular from its own root; synonymous with it is «أناسِيٌّ», the plural of «إنسان» or «إِنْسِيّ». It is literal (ḥaqīqa) for human beings and is applied to the jinn figuratively (majāzan). The grammarians disagreed about its derivation. The doctrine of Sībawayh and al-Farrāʾ is that its root is hamza, nūn and sīn, and the original form is «أناس», derived from «الأنس» (familiarity, companionship); the poet said:
161 - وما سُمِّي الإِنسانُ إلا لأُِنْسِه ... ولا القلبُ إلا أنه يَتَقَلَّبُ
(Man [insān] was named only for his companionship [uns], and the heart [qalb] only because it turns about [yataqallab].)
— because he became familiar with Ḥawwāʾ (Eve); and it was said: rather, he became familiar with his Lord. Then the hamza was dropped for lightening. Evidence for that is the poet's saying:
162 - إنَّ المَنايا يَطَّلِعْ ... نَ على الأُناس الآمنينا
(The fates come upon people [al-unās] who feel secure.)
Another said:
163 - وكلُّ أُناسٍ قاربوا قَيْدَ فَحْلِهِمْ ... ونحنُ خَلَعْنا قيدَه فهو سارِبُ
(Every people [unās] has shortened the hobble of its stallion, while we have removed its hobble, so it roams free.)
Another said:
164 - وكلُّ أُناسٍ سوف تَدْخُل بينهم ... دُوَيْهِيَّةٌ تَصْفَرُّ منها الأنامِلُ
(Among every people [unās] a little calamity will enter from which the fingertips turn yellow.)
Al-Kisāʾī held that it is from nūn, wāw and sīn, the original being «نَوَسَ»; the wāw was changed to alif because it is vowelled and what precedes it has fatḥa. And «النَّوْس» is motion. [Translator's note: the text reads «والنَّوْس والحركةُ» ("al-naws and motion"); the sense is "al-naws is motion".] Some held that it is from nūn, sīn and yāʾ, the original being «نَسِي»; then the lām [of the root] was shifted to the position of the ʿayn, so it became «نَيَس», then the yāʾ was changed to alif for the reason given for «نوس». He said: they were so named because of their forgetfulness (nisyān), and from it comes «الإِنسان», because of his forgetfulness; the poet said:
165 - فإنْ نَسِيْتَ عُهوداً منك سالفةً ... فاغفرٍ فأولُ ناسٍ أولُ الناس
(If you have forgotten past pledges of yours, then forgive, for the first forgetter [nāsin] was the first of people [al-nās].)
And similar to it:
166 - لا تَنْسَيَنْ تلك العهودَ فإنما ... سُمِّيتَ إنساناً لأنك ناسِي
(Do not ever forget those pledges, for you were named insān only because you are forgetful [nāsī].)
So its pattern on the first view is «عال», on the second «فَعَل», and on the third «فَلَع», by metathesis (al-qalb).
«يقول»: an imperfect verb, and its fāʿil (agent) is a pronoun referring back to «مَنْ». Al-qawl literally is the utterance coined for a meaning; it is also applied to the utterance indicating a predicative relation (al-nisba al-isnādiyya), and to inner speech (al-kalām al-nafsānī) as well; the Exalted said: {وَيَقُولُونَ في أَنفُسِهِمْ لَوْلاَ يُعَذِّبُنَا الله بِمَا نَقُولُ} [al-Mujādala: 8]. Its six permutations — namely q-w-l, l-w-q, w-q-l, q-l-w, l-q-w and w-l-q — indicate lightness and quickness, even though some of these roots are specific to other meanings. The basic rule of al-qawl is that it is transitive to one object, as in «قُلْتُ خطبةً» ("I delivered a sermon"); clauses are quoted after it, and they are in the position of the accusative as mafʿūl bihi (direct object), unless it is made to carry the meaning of supposition (al-ẓann), in which case it governs as that verb governs — under conditions, among those other than Banū Sulaym, mentioned in the books of grammar — as in the poet's saying:
167 - متى تقولُ القُلُصَ الرواسِما ... يُدْنِيْنَ أمَّ قاسمٍ وقاسما
(When do you think the swift young she-camels will bring Umm Qāsim and Qāsim near?)
— and without a condition among them [i.e. Banū Sulaym], as in the poet's saying:
168 - قالتْ وكنتُ رجلاً فطيناً ... هذا لَعَمْرُ اللهِ إسرائينا
(She thought — and I was a sharp man — "By the life of Allah, this is Isrāʾīn.")
«آمَنَّا»: a verb and its fāʿil, and «بالله» is attached (mutaʿalliq) to it; the clause is in the position of the accusative by «القول». The bāʾ is repeated in His saying «وباليومِ» for the meaning given earlier on His saying: {وعلى سَمْعِهِمْ وعلى أَبْصَارِهِمْ} [al-Baqara: 7]. Someone asked: the khabar must convey something other than what the mubtadaʾ conveyed, and it is known that the one who says such-and-such is from among people, not from others. The answer given to that is: this is a division in meaning, because mention of the believers preceded, then mention of the disbelievers, then He followed it with mention of the hypocrites, so it became analogous to a division in wording, as in His saying: {وَمِنَ الناس مَن يُعْجِبُكَ} [al-Baqara: 204], {وَمِنَ الناس مَن يَشْتَرِي} [Luqmān: 6]; thus it has the force of dividing people into believer, disbeliever and hypocrite. Better than this is to say: the khabar conveyed the intended partition, because not all people said that while being non-believers, so the implied sense became: "and some people are thus and thus."
Know that «مَنْ» and its sisters have a wording (lafẓ) and a meaning (maʿnā). Their wording is singular and masculine; if something other than that is meant by them, you may observe their wording at one time and their meaning at another, so you say: «جاء مَنْ قام وقعدوا» ("there came the one who stood up, and they sat down"). The noble verse is likewise: the wording was observed first, so it was said «مَنْ يقول», and the meaning second, in «آمَنَّا». Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "That is good because the singular precedes the plural in rank, and it is not permitted for a speaker to go back from a plural wording to the singular; were you to say: «ومن الناس مَنْ يقومون ويتكلم» it would not be permitted." In the phrasing of the judge Ibn ʿAṭiyya there is something to consider, because he prohibited observing [the wording after observing] the meaning, and that is permitted, though observing the wording first is preferable. Among what refutes him is the poet's saying:
169 - لستُ مِمَّنْ يَكُعُّ أو يَسْتَكينو ... ن إذا كافَحَتْهُ خيلُ الأعادي
(I am not of those who shrink back or submit when the cavalry of the enemies confronts him.)
And the Exalted said: {وَمَن يُؤْمِن بالله وَيَعْمَلْ} [al-Taghābun: 9] until He said «خالدين», so He observed the meaning; then He said: {قَدْ أَحْسَنَ الله لَهُ رِزْقاً}, so He observed the wording after observing the meaning. [Translator's note: the passage containing «خالدين» followed by {قَدْ أَحْسَنَ الله لَهُ رِزْقاً} is al-Ṭalāq: 11, not al-Taghābun: 9, as the source has it.] Likewise he [the poet] observed the meaning in his saying «أو يَستكينون», then observed the wording in «إذا كافحته». This treatment applies to it in all its states, I mean its being relative, conditional and interrogative. As for when it is qualified by an adjective, the Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "Observing the meaning is not among what I have memorized of the speech of the Arabs" — meaning that you say: «مررت بمَنْ محسنون لك» ("I passed by someones doing good to you").
«الآخِر» is a naʿt of «اليوم», and it is the counterpart of «الأول» (the first); the meaning of "the Last Day" is, i.e., [that which comes after] the limited times. [Translator's note: the source reads «أي عن الأوقات المحدودة», which seems corrupted; the bracketed words are a conjectural rendering.]
{مَا هُم بِمُؤْمِنِينَ}: «ما» is negating. It may be the Ḥijāzī «ما», which puts the noun in the nominative and the khabar in the accusative, so «هم» is its noun and «بمؤمنين» its khabar, with the bāʾ redundant for emphasis; or it may be the Tamīmī «ما», which governs nothing, so «هم» is a mubtadaʾ and «بمؤمنين» the khabar, the bāʾ also being redundant. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī claimed, and al-Zamakhsharī followed him, that the bāʾ is not added in the khabar of «ما» unless it is governing; this is refuted by the saying of al-Farazdaq, who was a Tamīmī:
170 - لَعَمْرُكَ ما مَعْنٌ بتاركِ حَقِّه ... ولا مُنْسِئٌ مَعْنٌ ولا مُتَيَسِّرُ
(By your life, Maʿn is not one to forgo his due, nor is Maʿn one to defer payment or to be lenient.)
However, the preferred view regarding «ما» [here] is that it is Ḥijāzī, because when the bāʾ is dropped the accusative is made explicit; Allah the Exalted said: {مَّا هُنَّ أُمَّهَاتِهِمْ} [al-Mujādala: 2], {مَا هذا بَشَراً} [Yūsuf: 31]. Most of the usage of the Ḥijāz is adding the bāʾ in its khabar, so much so that some claimed he had not preserved the accusative outside the Qur'an except in the poet's saying:
171 - وأنا النذيرُ بحَرَّةٍ مُسْوَدَّةٍ ... تَصِل الجيوشُ إليكمُ أَقْوادَها
أبناؤُها متكنِّفَون أباهُمُ ... حَنِقُو الصدورِ وما هُمُ أولادَها
(I am the warner of a blackened lava-field [i.e. an army] whose troops lead their columns to you; its sons surround their father, their breasts full of rage — and they are not its children.)
He brought the pronoun in His saying {وَمَا هُم بِمُؤْمِنِينَ} in the plural in consideration of the meaning of «مَنْ», as preceded in His saying «آمنَّا». If it is asked: why did He bring the khabar of «ما» as an active participle not restricted to a time, and not bring after it a verbal clause so as to correspond with their saying «آمنَّا», so that it would be said: «وما آمنوا»? The answer is: He turned away from that in order to convey that faith is negated of them at all times; had it been brought corresponding to their saying «آمنَّا», saying «وما آمنوا», it would have been a negation of faith in past time only, whereas what is intended is negation absolutely, i.e. they are not engaged in anything of faith at any time whatsoever.

semin-durr:28-28.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {كَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ بالله}: «كيف» is an interrogative noun by which one asks about states. It is indeclinable (mabnī) because it contains the meaning of the hamza [of interrogation], and it was made indeclinable on the lightest of the vowels [the fatḥa]. The entry of a preposition upon it is anomalous; they said: «على كيف تبيعُ الأَحْمَرَيْنِ» (At how much do you sell the two red things?). Its being conditional is rare, and it does not make [verbs] jussive, contrary to the Kufans. When a noun is substituted for it or occurs as an answer to it, it is accusative if there is after it a verb that governs it, e.g. «كيف قمت؟ أصحيحاً أم سقيماً» (How did you rise — healthy or ill?), and «كيف سِرْت؟» to which you say «راشداً» (rightly guided); otherwise both are nominative, e.g. «كيف زيدٌ؟ أصحيحٌ أم سقيمٌ» (How is Zayd — healthy or ill?). If after it there occurs a noun asked about by it, then [that noun] is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and it [«كيف»] is a fronted khabar (predicate), e.g. «كيف زيدٌ؟». The verb after it is sometimes omitted; Allah the Exalted said: {كَيْفَ وَإِن يَظْهَرُوا عَلَيْكُمْ} [al-Tawba: 8], i.e. "how do you befriend them?" «كيفَ» in this verse is accusative by resemblance to the adverb (ẓarf) according to Sībawayh, i.e. "in what state do you disbelieve?", and as a ḥāl (circumstantial) according to al-Akhfash, i.e. "upon what state do you disbelieve?" What governs it on both views is «تكفرون», and the owner of the ḥāl is the pronoun in «تكفرون». Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned only the view of al-Akhfash, then said: "The implied form is: 'Obstinately do you disbelieve.'" There is an objection to this implied form, since with it the meaning of the interrogative — intended for wonder, rebuke or disavowal — disappears. Al-Zamakhsharī said, after making the interrogative one of disavowal (inkār): "Its precise formulation is that when He disavows that their disbelief should have any state in which it is found — and it is known that every existent must have a state, and it is impossible for it to exist without any attribute at all — that is a disavowal of its very existence by way of demonstrative proof (al-ṭarīq al-burhānī)."
In the speech there is an iltifāt (shift of address) from the third person in His saying «وأمَّا الذين كفروا» and what follows, to the second-person address in His saying «تَكْفُرون، وكُنْتُم». Its benefit is that disavowal, when directed at the one addressed, is more forceful. «تكفرونَ» came as an imperfect, not a past, because what is disavowed is persistence in disbelief, and it is the imperfect that conveys that; and also lest it be a rebuke of one who believed after disbelief.
«كَفَرَ» is made transitive by a preposition, e.g. {تَكْفُرُونَ بالله}, {تَكْفُرُونَ بِآيَاتِ الله} [Āl ʿImrān: 70], {كَفَرُواْ بالذكر} [Fuṣṣilat: 41]; and it has been made transitive by itself in His saying, Exalted is He: {أَلاَ إِنَّ ثَمُودَ كَفرُواْ رَبَّهُمْ أَلاَ بُعْداً لِّثَمُودَ} [Hūd: 68], and that is because it was made to include (ḍummina) the meaning of «جَحَدوا» (they denied).
His saying: {وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً فَأَحْيَاكُمْ}: the wāw is the wāw of the ḥāl, and its sign is that «إذ» can fit in its place. The clause {كُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً} is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl, and «قد» must be implied so that the past verb can properly occur as a ḥāl. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: how is it valid for it to be a ḥāl when it is past? I say: the wāw did not enter upon {كُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً} alone, but upon the whole of His saying from {كُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً} to {تُرْجَعُونَ}, as though it were said: How do you disbelieve in Allah, when this is your story and your state: that you were dead — sperm-drops in the loins of your fathers — and He made you living, then He will cause you to die after this life, then He will give you life after death, then He will call you to account?"
Then he said: "If you ask: part of the story is past and part of it is future, and neither the past nor the future can properly occur as a ḥāl unless it is an action present at the time of the existence of that of which it is a ḥāl — so what is the present thing that occurred as a ḥāl? I say: it is the knowledge of the story, as though it were said: How do you disbelieve when you know this story, its beginning and its end?" The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said, in substance: this is forced — meaning his interpreting this clause as a nominal clause. He said: "What led him to that is his belief that the clauses are included under the ruling of the first clause." He said: "But that is not necessary; rather, His saying, Exalted is He, {ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكُمْ} and what follows are resumptive clauses by which He, Exalted is He, gives information, not included under the ḥāl. For that reason He differentiated between them and the clauses before them by the conjunction and by the verb form that preceded them in His saying {وَكُنْتُمْ أَمْوَاتاً فَأَحْيَاكُمْ}."
The fāʾ in His saying «فَأَحْيَاكُمْ» has its usual sense of immediate sequence (taʿqīb), and «ثم» has its usual sense of delay (tarākhī), because what is meant by the first death is the prior non-existence, by the first life the creation, by the second death the familiar death, and by the second life the life of the resurrection. So the fāʾ and «ثم» came in their usual senses of immediate sequence and delay according to this interpretation, and it is the best of the views; it is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid. The return to the recompense is also delayed after the resurrection. The pronoun in «إليه» refers to Allah the Exalted; this is the apparent [view] because it is like the pronouns before it, and there is an omitted muḍāf, i.e. "to His reward and His punishment." It has also been said [that it refers] to the recompense for deeds; and it has been said: to the place in which Allah undertakes judgement between you; and it has been said: to the giving of life indicated by «أَحْياكم», meaning that you will be returned to the first state you were in at the beginning of the first life, in that you possess nothing for yourselves.
The majority read «تُرْجَعُون» as passive, and it has been read as active wherever it occurs. The justification of the two readings is that «رَجَع» is both intransitive and transitive. The reading of the majority is from the transitive, and it is preferable, because its underlying form is «ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ يُرْجِعُكُمْ» (then to Him He will return you), since the attribution in the preceding verbs is to Allah the Exalted, so it is fitting that this one be likewise; but it was made passive for the sake of the verse-endings (fawāṣil) and pauses (qawāṭiʿ).
«أَمْوات» is the plural of «مَيِّت», and its regular pattern would be faʿāʾil, like sayyid and sayāʾid. It is preferable that «أموات» be the plural of «مَيْت» in the lightened form, like aqwāl as the plural of qayl. This root has been discussed previously.

semin-durr:35-35.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَقُلْنَا يَاآدَمُ اسكن أَنْتَ وَزَوْجُكَ الجنة}: this clause is conjoined to the clause «إذْ قلنا», not to «قُلْنا» alone, because their times differ. «أنت» is a tawkīd (emphasis) of the latent (mustatir) pronoun in «اسكُن», so that conjoining to it becomes sound, and «زوجُك» is conjoined to it. This is the doctrine of the Basrans, I mean: the requirement of a separation between the two conjoined items when the one conjoined to is an attached nominative pronoun; and it is not required that the separator be a tawkīd — rather any separation whatsoever, as in: {مَآ أَشْرَكْنَا وَلاَ آبَاؤُنَا} [al-Anʿām: 148]. As for the Kufans, they permit that without a separator, and they cited:
365 - قُلْتُ إذا أقبلَتْ وزهرٌ تَهادى ... كنعاجِ الفَلا تَعَسَّفْنَ رَمْلا
(I said, when she approached, and Zahr [with her] swaying along like the wild cows of the desert treading across sand…)
To the Basrans this is poetic licence (ḍarūra), on which no analogy is built. Some have forbidden «زوجُك» from being conjoined to the latent pronoun in «اسكُنْ», and made it a conjoining of clauses, in the sense that «زوجُك» is nominative by an omitted verb, i.e. "and let your wife dwell" (وَلْتَسْكُنْ زوجك), omitted because «اسكنْ» indicates it; and he compared it with His saying, Exalted is He: {لاَّ نُخْلِفُهُ نَحْنُ وَلاَ أَنتَ} [Ṭā Hā: 58], and claimed that this is the doctrine of Sībawayh. It seems his doubt in that is that the conjoined item ought properly to be able to occupy the place of the item conjoined to, and here «زوجُك» cannot occupy the place of the pronoun, because the agent of a singular masculine imperative verb, such as قُمْ and اسكُنْ, can only be a latent pronoun, and likewise the agent of نفعلُ; so how could an overt noun stand in the place of the pronoun before it? What he claimed amounts to nothing, because Sībawayh's doctrine, by his explicit text, contradicts it, and because there is no disagreement over the soundness of «تقوم هندٌ وزيدٌ» (Hind and Zayd stand), although Zayd cannot directly follow «تقوم» because of its feminine form.
Sukūn and suknā mean: settling (istiqrār). From it comes al-miskīn (the destitute), because of his lack of settledness, movement and freedom of action; al-sikkīn (the knife), because it cuts off the movement of the slaughtered animal; and al-sakīna (tranquillity), because through it anxiety departs.
«الجَنَّةَ» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), not an adverb (ẓarf), as in: سَكَنْتُ الدارَ (I inhabited the house). It has also been said: it is an adverb by extension (ʿalā al-ittisāʿ), the original being that the verb is made transitive to it by «في», since it is a specific adverb of place. What comes after the verb "to say" is in the accusative by it.
His saying: {وَكُلاَ مِنْهَا رَغَداً}: this clause is conjoined to «اسكُنْ», so it is in the position of the accusative by the verb "to say". The origin of كُلْ is أُأْكُلْ with two hamzas: the first is the connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl), and the second is the first radical (fāʾ) of the word. Had this word come according to this origin, one would say اُوكُلْ, changing the second into a letter consonant with the vowel before it; however, the Arabs dropped its first radical in the imperative for lightness, and thereupon dispensed with the connecting hamza, so its pattern is عُلْ. Like it are خُذْ and مُرْ, and no other verbs are measured by analogy on these verbs: you do not say جُرْ from أَجَر. The Arabs do not restore this first radical after a conjunction; rather they say: قم وخذ وكُلْ — except «مُرْ», for most commonly its first radical is restored after wāw and fāʾ. Allah the Exalted said: {وَأْمُرْ قَوْمَكَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 145] and {وَأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ} [Ṭā Hā: 132]; not restoring it is rare. Sībawayh reported «اؤْكُلْ» according to the origin, and it is anomalous (shādhdh).
Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The nūn has been dropped from «كُلا» [for the imperative]". This expression gives the false impression of the doctrine of the Kufans, that the imperative is, in their view, declinable (muʿrab) by gradual derivation, as has preceded; whereas to the Basrans it is treated like the jussive: if the jussive is made quiescent, the imperative from it is made quiescent, and if a letter is dropped from it, it is dropped from the imperative.
«منها» is attached to it, and «مِنْ» is partitive, and an omitted muḍāf must be supposed, i.e. "of its fruits". «مِنْ» may also be for the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), and that is better. «رَغَداً» is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun). It has preceded that Sībawayh's doctrine in this and the like is that it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial). It has also been said: it is a maṣdar in the position of a ḥāl, i.e. "eat, the two of you, in goodness and ease".
It has been read «رَغْداً» with a quiescent ghayn, and this is the dialect of Tamīm. Some said: every word of the pattern with a guttural middle radical and a sound final radical may have its middle radical vowelled with fatḥa or made quiescent, as in nahr and baḥr. This is questionable; rather, what is transmitted is that faʿl with a quiescent middle radical, when its middle radical is guttural, may not be given fatḥa according to the Basrans unless it is heard, in which case one restricts oneself to it, and that is then on the basis of two dialects, not that one of them is taken from the other. As for the Kufans, some of this is in their view a word with two dialectal forms, and some of it originally has sukūn and may be given fatḥa by analogy. As for the claim that faʿal, with an open, guttural middle radical, may be made quiescent, so that al-saḥr is permitted for al-saḥar — this no one permits. Al-raghad: ample and pleasant. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
366 - بينما المرءُ تراهُ ناعماً ... يَأْمَنُ الأحداثَ في عيشٍ رَغَدْ
(While you see a man living in comfort, feeling safe from misfortunes in an ample life…)
One says: رَغُِدَ عيشُهم (their life became ample) with ḍamma and kasra on the ghayn, and أَرْغَدَ القومُ: the people came into ampleness.
His saying: {حَيْثُ شِئْتُمَا}: حيث is an adverb of place. The well-known view is that it is indeclinable (mabnī) on ḍamma, because it resembles a particle in needing a clause; and its vowel is ḍamma by assimilation to «قبل» and «بعد». Al-Kisāʾī transmitted its declension from the tribe of Faqʿas. It has dialectal forms: حيث with all three vowels on the thāʾ, and حَوْث likewise with all three; حاث with alif has also been transmitted. It is restricted [to adverbial use and is not freely inflected, though it may be put in the genitive by مِنْ, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {مِنْ حَيْثُ أَمَرَكُمُ} [al-Baqara: 222], {مِّنْ حَيْثُ لاَ يَعْلَمُونَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 182]; and it is restricted] to annexation to a clause absolutely, and is not annexed to a single word except rarely. He said:
367 - أَمَا تَرى حيثُ سهيلٍ طالِعا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Do you not see where Canopus is, rising…)
And another said:
368 - وَنَطْعَنُهم تحت الحُبَى بعد ضَرْبهم ... ببيضِ المواضي حيثُ لَيِّ العَمائم
(We pierce them beneath the waist-wraps after striking them with gleaming, sharp blades where the turbans are wound.)
«ما» may be added to it, and it then puts two verbs in the jussive, as protasis and apodosis, like إنْ; it does not put them in the jussive without «ما», contrary to some people. It may also be imbued with the sense of causation. Al-Akhfash claimed that it can be an adverb of time and cited:
369 - للفتى عَقْلٌ يَعيشُ به ... حيث تَهْدي ساقَهُ قَدَمُهْ
(The young man has a mind by which he lives, wherever his foot guides his leg.)
There is no proof in it, because it is in its normal sense there.
What governs it here is «كُلا», i.e. "eat, the two of you, in whatever place you wish", as a granting of latitude to them. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted it to be a badal (substitute) of «الجنَّة»; he said: "because al-janna is a direct object, so «حيث» would be a direct object". This is questionable, because it is not freely inflected, as has preceded, except for being put in the genitive by «مِنْ».
His saying: «شِئْتُمَا»: the clause is in the position of the genitive by annexation of the adverb to it. Is the kasra on the shīn original, as in your saying جِئْتُما and خِفْتُما, or transformed from a fatḥa to indicate that the root has yāʾ, as in بِعْتما? Two views, built on what the pattern of شَاءَ is: al-Mubarrad's doctrine is that it is faʿala with a fatḥa on the middle radical, and Sībawayh's doctrine is that it is faʿila with a kasra on it; the morphology of both is evident.
His saying: {وَلاَ تَقْرَبَا هذه الشجرة}: lā is prohibitive, and «تَقْرَبا» is jussive by it, its nūn having been dropped. It has been read «تِقْرَبا» with a kasra on the imperfect prefix. The alif is the fāʿil (agent), and «هذه» is a mafʿūl bihi, the demonstrative for the feminine. It has dialectal forms: هذي, هذهِ [and هذهِ] with a kasra on the hāʾ, with lengthening and without it, هذهْ with the hāʾ quiescent, and ذِهْ with a kasra on the dhāl alone. The hāʾ is a substitute for the yāʾ, because of its closeness to it in faintness. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said — and it has also been transmitted from al-Naḥḥās —: "There is in the language no feminine hāʾ preceded by a kasra other than «هذه»." This is questionable, because that hāʾ which indicates the feminine is not this one, since that one is a substitute for the feminine tāʾ in pause; whereas this hāʾ has no indication of the feminine; rather what indicates it is the word as a whole, just as you say: the yāʾ in «هذي» is for the feminine. Its rule as regards nearness, distance and the intermediate, and the entry of the hāʾ of alerting and the kāf of address, is the rule of «ذا», which has preceded. One also says for it: تَيْك, تَيْلَكَ, تِلْكَ and تالِك. The poet said:
370 - تعلَّمْ أنَّ بعدَ الغَيِّ رُشْدا ... وأنَّ لتالِكَ الغُمَرِ انْحِسَاراً
(Know that after error comes right guidance, and that those floods of trouble have a receding.)
Hishām said: "One also says: تافَعَلَتْ", and they cited:
371 - خَليليَّ لولا ساكنُ الدارِ لم أُقِمْ ... بتا الدارِ إلاَّ عابرَ ابنِ سبيلٍ
(My two friends, were it not for the one who dwells in the house, I would not have stayed at this house except as a passing wayfarer.)
«الشجرةِ» is a badal of «هذه»; it has also been said: a naʿt of it, being interpreted as a derived word, i.e. "this one present among the trees". The well-known view is that when a derived word comes after a demonstrative, it is its naʿt, and if it is a non-derived (jāmid) noun, it is a badal of it. Al-shajara is the singular of al-shajar, a generic noun, and it is what stands on a trunk, unlike al-najm (stemless plants); their precise treatment will come in Sūrat al-Raḥmān, if Allah the Exalted wills. It has been read «الشجرة» with kasra on the shīn and the jīm, and with the jīm quiescent, and with the jīm replaced by yāʾ, with fatḥa or kasra on the shīn, because of its closeness to it in point of articulation, just as jīm was substituted for yāʾ in his saying:
372 - يا رَبِّ إنْ كنْتَ قَبِلْتَ حَجَّتِجْ ... فلا يَزالُ شاحِجٌ يأتيكَ بِجْ
(O Lord, if You have accepted my pilgrimage, then may a braying [mount] keep coming to You with me.)
By that he means حَجَّتي and بي. Another said:
373 - إذا لم يكُنْ فِيكُنَّ ظِلٌّ وَلاَ جَنًى ... فَأَبْعَدَكُنَّ اللهُ من شِيَرَاتِ
(If there is in you neither shade nor fruit, then may Allah banish you, O trees.)
Abū ʿAmr said: "Only the Berbers of Mecca and its Blacks read it so." Al-shajar has also been pluralized as shajrāʾ, and no plural has come on this pattern except qaṣaba / qaṣbāʾ, ṭarafa / ṭarfāʾ and ḥalafa / ḥalfāʾ; al-Aṣmaʿī used to say: "ḥalifa, with a kasra on the lām". According to Sībawayh these words are both singular and plural.
You say: قَرِبْتُ الأمرَ أقرَبه, with a kasra on the middle radical in the past and a fatḥa in the imperfect, i.e. "I became involved in it". Al-Jawharī said: "قَرُب with ḍamma, يقرُبُ, قُرْباً, i.e. he drew near; and قَرِبْتُهُ with kasra, قُرْبَاناً: I drew near [to it]; and قَرَبْتُ أقرُبُ قِرابَةً, like كَتَبْتُ أكتُبُ كِتابة, when you journey towards water and there is one night between you and it.
It has been said: when one says لا تَقْرَبْ with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, its meaning is 'do not become involved in the act', and when one says لا تَقْرُب with ḍamma, its meaning is 'do not draw near to it'."
His saying: {فَتَكُونَا مِنَ الظالمين}: there are two aspects in it. The first: that it is jussive, conjoined to «تَقْرَبَا», as in his saying:
374 - فقلت له: صَوِّبْ ولا تَجْهَدَنَّهُ ... فَيُذْرِكَ من أُخرى القَطَاةِ فَتَزْلَقِ
(So I said to him: "Keep low, and do not overtax it, lest it toss you from the back of its rump and you slip off.")
The second: that it is accusative as the answer to the prohibition, like His saying, Exalted is He: {لاَ تَطْغَوْاْ فِيهِ فَيَحِلَّ} [Ṭā Hā: 81]. The accusative is by an implied «أَنْ» according to the Basrans, by the fāʾ itself according to al-Jarmī, and by divergence (al-khilāf) according to the Kufans; and so it is with everything that comes like this.
{مِنَ الظالمين} is the khabar (predicate) of kāna. Al-ẓulm: putting a thing in other than its place; hence land that did not deserve digging and was dug is called maẓlūma ("wronged"). Al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī said:
375 - إِلاَّ أَوارِيَّ لأَيَاً ما أُبَيِّنُهَا ... والنُّؤْيُ كالحوضِ بالمظلومةِ الجَلَدِ
(Except tethering-posts, which I can make out only with difficulty, and the trench [around the tent] like a trough in the "wronged", hard ground.)
It has also been said: it was called maẓlūma because rain does not come to it. ʿAmr ibn Qamīʾa said:
376 - ظَلَمَ البطاحَ له انهِلاَلُ حَرِيصةٍ ... فصفَا النِّطافُ له بُعَيْدَ المُقْلَعِ
(The pouring of a scouring rain "wronged" the valley-beds for it, so the pools cleared for it shortly after it ceased.)
And they said: "Whoever resembles his father has not done wrong." He said:
377 - بأبِهِ اقتدى عَدِيٌّ في الكَرَمْ ... ومَنْ يشابِهْ أَبَه فما ظَلَمْ
(ʿAdī followed his father's example in generosity, and whoever resembles his father has done no wrong.)

semin-durr:20-20.t:
The words of the Exalted: {يَكَادُ البرق يَخْطَفُ أَبْصَارَهُمْ}: «يكادُ» is the imperfect of كَادَ, which denotes nearness to the action (muqāraba). It operates as «كانَ» operates (i.e. it is one of kāna and its sisters in function), except that its khabar (predicate) can only be an imperfect verb; its coming as an explicit noun is anomalous (shādhdh). The poet said:
241 - فَأُبْتُ إلى فَهْمٍ وما كِدْتُ آيباً ... وكم مثلِها فارَقْتُها وهي تَصْفِرُ
(I returned to Fahm, though I was scarcely returning; and how many a one like it have I left while it whistled [empty].)
Most commonly its khabar is free of «أنْ», the reverse of «عسى»; its being joined to it is anomalous. Ruʾba said:
242 - قد كادَ مِنْ طولِ البلى أن يَمْحَصا ...
(From long decay it had nearly worn away.)
[It is anomalous] because «كاد» is for nearness to the action, while «أَنْ» confines [the verb] to the future, so the two are incompatible.
Know that when «كاد» itself is affirmative, its khabar is negative in meaning, because it denotes nearness: if you say «كاد زيدٌ يفعلُ», the meaning is that he came near to the action, but did not do it. When it is negated, its khabar is negated a fortiori, because if nearness to the action is negated, the action itself is negated all the more. For this reason the words of the Exalted {لَمْ يَكَدْ يَرَاهَا} [al-Nūr: 40] are more eloquent than if it had been said «لم يَرَها», because he did not even come near to seeing it, so how could he see it?
A group, among them Ibn Jinnī, Abū al-Baqāʾ and Ibn ʿAṭiyya, claimed that its negation is affirmation and its affirmation is negation, so much so that someone composed a riddle on it, saying:
243 - أَنَحْوِيَّ هذا العصرِ ما هي لفظةٌ ... جَرَتْ في لِسانَيْ جُرْهُمٍ وَثَمُودِ
إذا نُفِيَتْ - والله أعلمُ - أُثْبِتَتْ ... وإِنْ أُثْبِتَتْ قامَتْ مَقَامَ جُحُودِ
(O grammarian of this age, what is a word that ran on the tongues of Jurhum and Thamūd which, when negated — and Allah knows best — is affirmed, and when affirmed stands in the place of denial?)
They related of Dhū al-Rumma that when he recited his line:
244 - إذا غَيَّر النأيُ المحِبِّينَ لم يَكَدْ ... رسيسُ الهوى من حُبِّ مَيَّةَ يَبْرَحُ
(When distance changes lovers, the lingering touch of passion for Mayya scarcely departs.)
he was faulted for it, because he said «لَمْ يَكَدْ يَبْرَحُ», so that it would mean it had departed; so he changed it to «لم يَزَلْ» (it has not ceased), or something with its meaning.
What misled these people is the word of the Exalted: {فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُواْ يَفْعَلُونَ} [al-Baqara: 71]. They said: here it is negated and its khabar is affirmed in meaning, because the slaughter took place, given His words «فَذَبَحُوها». The answer concerning this verse is from two angles. First: it is understood as referring to two different times, i.e. they slaughtered it at one time, and they were not near to doing it at another time. Second: He expressed, by negating nearness to the action, how extreme their obstinacy and their difficulty in doing it were.
As for what they related of Dhū al-Rumma, the majority held Dhū al-Rumma to be mistaken in retracting his wording, and said: it is more eloquent and better than what he changed it to.
Know that the khabar of «كاد» and its sisters other than «عسى» can only have as its fāʿil (agent) a pronoun referring back to its ism (subject), because they are for nearness or for commencement — unlike «عسى», which is for hope: you say «عسى زيدٌ أن يقومَ أبوه» (perhaps Zayd's father will stand), and that is not permitted with the others. As for the poet's words:
245 - وَقَفْتُ على رَبْعٍ لِميَّةَ ناقتي ... فما زِلْتُ أبكي عندَهُ وأُخَاطِبُهْ
وَأَسْقِيهِ حتى كَادَ مِمَّا أَبُثُّه ... تُكَلِّمُنِي أَحْجَارُه ومَلاعِبُهْ
(I halted my she-camel at an abode of Mayya's, and kept weeping there and addressing it, and watering it [with tears], until, from the grief I poured out, its stones and playgrounds nearly spoke to me.)
where he brought the fāʿil overt: some took it as anomalous. But it ought to be said: this was permitted only because the stones and playgrounds are an expression for the abode itself, so they are it; it is as if it were said «حتى كاد يكلِّمني» (until it nearly spoke to me), but he expressed it by the sum of its parts. And the words of the other poet:
246 - وقد جَعَلْتُ إذا ما قُمْتُ يُثْقِلُني ... ثَوْبي فَأَنْهَضُ نَهْضَ الشاربِ السَّكِرِ
وكنتُ أمشي على رِجْلَيْنِ مُعْتَدِلاً ... فَصِرْتُ أمشي على أخرى من الشجر
(I have come to the point that whenever I stand, my garment weighs me down, and I rise as a drunken drinker rises; I used to walk upright on two legs, and now I walk on a third made of wood.)
where he brought the fāʿil of the [khabar of] «جعل» overt: two answers have been given. First: it is on the omission of a muḍāf, its implied form being «وقد جَعَل ثوبي إذا ما قمت يُثْقلني» (my garment has come to weigh me down whenever I stand). Second: it is of the type of putting the cause in place of the effect, for his rising in such a manner is caused by his garment's weighing him down; the meaning is: I have come to rise as the intoxicated drinker rises, because my garment weighs me down.
The pattern of «كاد» is كَوِدَ, with kasra on the middle radical; it is one of the wāw-verbs, like خاف يَخاف. There is another dialect in it: fatḥa on its middle radical; in this dialect its first radical takes ḍamma when it is attached to the tāʾ of the speaker and its sisters, so you say كُدْت and كُدْنا, like قُلْت and قُلْنا. Sometimes the kasra of its middle radical is transferred to its first radical when attached to an overt noun, as in the poet's words:
247 - وكِيدَ ضِباعُ القُفِّ يأكُلْنَ جُثَّتي ... وكِيدِ خِراشٌ عند ذلك يَيْتَمُ
(The hyenas of the rugged ground nearly devoured my corpse, and Khirāsh was nearly orphaned at that.)
It may not be redundant (zāʾida), contrary to al-Akhfash. All of this will come under the incomplete (nāqiṣa) «كاد». As for the complete (tāmma) «كاد» meaning «مَكَر» (to plot), it is on the pattern فَعَل with fatḥa on the middle radical, one of the yāʾ-verbs, as shown by His words: {إِنَّهُمْ يَكِيدُونَ كَيْداً * وَأَكِيدُ كَيْداً} [al-Ṭāriq: 15–16].
«البرق» is its ism, and «يخَطف» its khabar. One says خَطِف يَخْطَفُ, with kasra on the middle radical of the past and fatḥa in the imperfect, and خَطَف يخطِف, the reverse of the first dialect. There are many readings in it; the well-known one is the first. The second: يَخْطِف, with kasra on the ṭāʾ.
The third: يَخَطَّفُ, with fatḥa on the yāʾ, the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ, and the ṭāʾ doubled; the origin is يَخْتَطِفُ, and the tāʾ of the iftiʿāl form was changed to ṭāʾ for assimilation. The fourth: likewise, except that it has kasra on the khāʾ, following the kasra of the ṭāʾ. The sixth: likewise, except that it has kasra on the yāʾ as well, following the khāʾ. [Translator's note: the source passes from the fourth to the sixth; no fifth reading is listed.] The seventh: يَخْتَطِف, on the original form. The eighth: يَخْطِّف, with fatḥa on the yāʾ, sukūn on the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ doubled; this is poor, because it leads to the meeting of two vowelless letters. The ninth: with ḍamma on the yāʾ, fatḥa on the khāʾ, and the ṭāʾ doubled with kasra; the doubling in it is for intensification (takthīr), not for making it transitive. The tenth: يَتَخَطَّف.
الخَطْفُ is taking something quickly. This clause — I mean His words «يكاد البرق يَخْطَف» — has no grammatical position, because it is resumptive (istiʾnāf), as if it had been asked: "What is their state with that lightning?" and it was said: "It nearly snatches." It may also be in the position of the genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of the omitted «ذوي», the implied form being: «أو كذوي صيبٍ كائدٍ البرقُ يَخْطَف» (or like the people of a rainstorm whose lightning nearly snatches).
The words of the Exalted: {كُلَّمَا أَضَآءَ لَهُمْ مَّشَوْاْ فِيهِ}: «كل» is accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyya), because it is annexed to the temporal «ما»; what governs it is its apodosis, namely «مَشَوا». It was also said: «ما» is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective (nakira mawṣūfa), also meaning "time", and the referring pronoun is omitted, its implied form being «كلَّ وقتٍ أضاءَ لهم فيه» (every time it gave them light in it). So «أضاء» has no grammatical position on the first view, being a ṣila (relative clause), and its position is genitive on the second.
«أضاء» may be intransitive. Al-Mubarrad said: "It is transitive, and its object is omitted", i.e. the lightning lit the road for them. So the hāʾ in «فيه» refers to the lightning according to the majority, and to the omitted «الطريق» (road) according to al-Mubarrad.
«فيه» is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «مَشَوا», and «في» has its basic meaning, i.e. the light surrounds them. It was also said: it is in the sense of the bāʾ. On both views an omission is necessary, i.e. they walked in its light, or by its light. The clause «مَشَوا» has no grammatical position, because it is resumptive.
Know that «كُلّ» is one of the words of generality. It is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) that is necessarily annexed, though what it is annexed to may be omitted; is its tanwīn in that case the tanwīn of compensation (ʿiwaḍ) or the tanwīn of declinability (ṣarf)? There are two views. If what «كل» is annexed to is definite and is omitted, it remains definite; for this reason a ḥāl (circumstantial) can be made accusative from it, and the definite article does not enter it, even though that occurs in the wording of some. Sometimes it is made accusative as a ḥāl. Its original use is as tawkīd (emphasis), like «أجمع», and the best use of it is as a mubtadaʾ (subject). Its being a direct object is not restricted to what is heard (samāʿ), nor peculiar to poetry, contrary to whoever claimed that.
When it is annexed to an indefinite noun, or to one made definite by the lām of the genus, it may well follow verbal governing words. When annexed to an indefinite noun, that indefinite noun must be taken into account in the pronoun and so on referring to it: you say «كلُّ رجال أتَوْكَ فأكرِمْهم» (all men who come to you, honour them), and it is not permitted to take account of the wording of «كل» and say «كلُّ رجال أتاكَ فأكرمه»; and [you say] «كلُّ رجلٍ أتاك فأكرمه» (every man who comes to you, honour him), and you do not say «أَتَوْك فأكرِمْهم», taking account of the meaning. As for the poet's words:
248 - جادَتْ عليه كلُّ عَيْن ثَرَّةٍ ... فتركْنَ كلَّ حدَيقةٍ كالدرهم
(Every abundant spring [cloud] poured generously on it, and they left every garden like a silver coin.)
where he took account of the meaning, it is anomalous and not taken as a basis for analogy. When it is annexed to a definite noun there are two options, whether the annexation is in wording, as in {وَكُلُّهُمْ آتِيهِ يَوْمَ القيامة فَرْداً} [Maryam: 95], where the wording of «كل» is taken into account, or in meaning, as in {فَكُلاًّ أَخَذْنَا بِذَنبِهِ} [al-ʿAnkabūt: 40], where its wording is taken into account, and He said {وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ دَاخِرِينَ} [al-Naml: 87], where the meaning is taken into account.
As for some people's statement that «كُلَّما» conveys repetition, that is not part of its original coinage: if you say «كلما جِئْتَني أَكْرَمْتُك», the meaning is: I honour you on each and every one of your comings to me.
It was read «ضاء» as a triliteral verb, which shows that the quadriliteral [أضاء] is intransitive. It was also read «وإذا أُظْلِم», in the passive, and al-Zamakhsharī took this as showing that «أَظْلَمَ» is transitive; he also cited in support the words of Ḥabīb [Abū Tammām]:
249 - هما أَظْلما حالَيَّ ثُمَّتَ أَجْلَيَا ... ظَلامَيْهِما عن وجهِ أَمْرَدَ أَشْيَبِ
(These two darkened both my states, then cleared away their two darknesses from the face of one beardless yet grey.)
But there is no proof in the verse, since its origin may be «وإذا أَظْلم الليلُ عليهم» (when the night grew dark upon them); when it was made passive, «الليل» was omitted and «عليهم» stood in its place. As for Ḥabīb, he is a post-classical (muwallad) poet [and not cited as evidence].
As for why the first clause is introduced with «كلما» and the second with «إذا», al-Zamakhsharī said: "Because they were eager for the existence of what their concern was bound to — the possibility and feasibility of walking — so whenever they met with an opportunity for it they seized it; stopping and being held back are not like that." What he said is the apparent view, except that some grammarians held that «إذا» also conveys repetition, and recited:
250 - إذا وَجَدْتُ أُوارَ الحُبِّ في كَبْدِي ... أَقْبَلْتُ نحو سِقاءِ القومِ أَبْتَرِدُ
(Whenever I find the burning heat of love in my liver, I go to the people's water-skin to cool myself.)
He said: "Its meaning is the meaning of «كلما»."
The words of the Exalted: {وَلَوْ شَآءَ الله لَذَهَبَ بِسَمْعِهِمْ وَأَبْصَارِهِمْ}: «لو» is "a particle for what would have occurred because of the occurrence of something else"; this is Sībawayh's wording, and it is preferable to the wording of others, "a particle of impossibility for impossibility" (ḥarf imtināʿ li-mtināʿ), because the first wording is valid in cases such as the word of the Exalted {لَّوْ كَانَ البحر مِدَاداً لِّكَلِمَاتِ رَبِّي لَنَفِدَ البحر} [al-Kahf: 109], and in his words (peace be upon him): «نِعْمَ العبدُ صُهَيْبٌ لو لم يَخَفِ اللهَ لم يُعْصِه» (What an excellent servant is Ṣuhayb: had he not feared Allah, he would not have disobeyed Him), whereas the second is not valid there, as will come in detail; and because of the unsoundness [on the second wording] of a statement such as «لو كان إنساناً لكان حيواناً» (if it were a human, it would be an animal), since the impossibility of being human does not entail the impossibility of being an animal.
It does not make the verb jussive, contrary to some. As for the poet's words:
251 - لو يَشَأْ طارَ به ذو مَيْعَةٍ ... لاحِقُ الآطالِ نَهْدٌ ذو خُصَلْ
(Had he wished, a spirited steed would have flown off with him, lean-flanked, sturdy, with flowing forelocks.)
and the other's words:
252 - تامَتْ فؤادَك لو يَحْزُنْكَ مَا صَنَعَتْ ... إحدى نساءِ بني ذُهْلِ بنِ شَيْبَانا
(One of the women of Banū Dhuhl ibn Shaybān enslaved your heart — if only what she did grieved you.)
these are from making a vowelled letter vowelless out of poetic necessity.
It is mostly a conditional in the past, but it may come in the sense of «إنْ», as in the word of the Exalted: {وَلْيَخْشَ الذين لَوْ تَرَكُواْ مِنْ خَلْفِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّةً ضِعَافاً خَافُواْ عَلَيْهِمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 9], and the poet's words:
253 - ولَوْ أَنَّ ليلى الأخيليَّةَ سَلَّمَتْ ... عليَّ ودوني جَنْدَلٌ وصَفائِحُ
لسَلَّمْتُ تسليمَ البشاشةِ أَوْزَقَا ... إليها صَدَىً مِنْ جانبِ القبرِ صائحُ
