Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is resumptive and not reported by «القول»," then he allowed that in it [too].
«تُبْدُون» has the pattern tufʿūn, because its origin is «تُبْدِوُونَ», like «تُخْرِجون»; it was modified by dropping the wāw after it became quiescent. Al-ibdāʾ is making manifest, and al-katm is concealing. One says «بَدا يَبْدُو بَداءً»; he said:
354 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... بَدا لَكَ في تلك القَلوصِ بَداءُ
(… a new view occurred to you concerning that young she-camel.)
His saying: {وَمَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ}: «ما» is conjoined to the first «ما», according to whatever case it has.

semin-durr:119-119.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {بالحق}: three aspects are permissible. The first: it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), i.e. "because of establishing the truth". [Translator's note: so in the source; the gloss given is causal.] The second: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the object in «أَرْسلناك», i.e. "We sent you clothed with the truth". The third: it is a ḥāl from the agent, i.e. "[We] being clothed in the truth". His words «بَشيراً ونذيراً»: two aspects are permissible in them. The first: they are a ḥāl from the object, and this is the apparent one. The second: they are a ḥāl from «الحقّ», because it too is described with bringing glad tidings and warning. «بشير» and «نذير» are on the pattern فَعيل. As for «بشير», you say it is from بَشَر without shadda, because that is heard in it, and فَعِيل is regular from the triliteral. As for «نذير», it is from the quadriliteral [i.e. أنذر], and turning مُفْعِل into فعيل is not regular by analogy; but here it has something that makes it fine.
His words: {وَلاَ تُسْأَلُ}: the majority read «تُسْأَلُ» as passive, with the verb nominative on [the reading of] negation. It was read irregularly (shādhdh) «تَسْأَلُ» as active, also nominative. In this clause there are two aspects. The first: it is a ḥāl, and so is conjoined to the ḥāl before it, as if it were said: "a bearer of glad tidings or a warner, and not to be asked". The second: it is resumptive. Nāfiʿ read «تُسْأَلْ» as a prohibition, and this is only resumptive; it may not be a ḥāl, because a request does not occur as a ḥāl. «الجحيم» is the intense blazing of fire; from it the lion's eye is called «جَحْمة», because of its intense blazing. One says: جَحِمَتِ النارُ تَجْحَمُ (the fire blazed), and intense heat is called «جاحم». [The poet] said:
704 - والحربُ لا يَبْقى لِجَا ... حمِها التخيُّلُ والمِراحُ
(And war — before its blazing heat, neither swagger nor frolic remains.)
«الرِّضا» is the opposite of anger, and it is from roots with final wāw, because of their saying «الرُّضْوان». The maṣdar (verbal noun) is رِضا and رِضاء, with short and long [final vowel], and رِضْواناً and رُضْواناً, with kasra and ḍamma on the first radical. It may include the meaning of «عَطَفَ» (to be kindly disposed) and so be made transitive with «على». [The poet] said:
705 - إذا رَضِيَتْ عليَّ بنو قُشَيْرٍ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(When the Banū Qushayr are pleased with me…)
«المِلَّة» is originally "the way"; one says طريقٌ مُمِلٌّ, i.e. a path that walking has left its mark upon; and it is used for the religious law (sharīʿa) by likening it to the way. It has been said: rather, it is derived from «أَمْلَلْتُ» (I dictated), because in the sharīʿa there is one who dictates and one to whom it is dictated.

semin-durr:34-34.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلاَئِكَةِ اسجدوا لآدَمَ}: what governs «إذ» is omitted, indicated by His saying «فَسَجَدوا»; its implied form is — «فَسَجَدوا», its implied form is [Translator's note: the phrase is repeated thus in the printed text] — "they obeyed and submitted, so they prostrated," because prostration arises from submission. It has been said: what governs it is an implied «اذكُرْ» (remember); and it has been said: [«إذ»] is redundant (zāʾida); the weakness of these two views has preceded. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "«وإذ قلنا» is conjoined to the preceding «إذ»"; this is not valid because of the difference of the two times. It has been said: «إذ» is a badal (substitute) from the first «إذ»; this is not valid because of what has preceded, and because of the intervening conjunction. The clause «قلنا» is in the position of the genitive by the adverb. In it there is an iltifāt (shift) from the third person to the first person, for grandeur. The lām is for conveying (tablīgh), like its analogues.
The well-known [reading] is the genitive on the tāʾ of «الملائكة» by the preposition. Abū Jaʿfar read it with ḍamma, making it follow the ḍamma of the jīm, not taking account of the quiescent letter [between them]. Al-Zajjāj declared him in error and al-Fārisī declared him mistaken. Some compared it to His saying, Exalted is He: {وَقَالَتِ اخرج} [Yūsuf: 31] with ḍamma on the tāʾ of the feminine; but that is not correct, because that is a vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters, whereas this is a vowel of declension, which is not to be played with; the purpose there is achieved by any vowel whatever. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is not permissible to make the declensional vowel disappear except in a weak dialect, as in the reading {الحمد للَّهِ} [al-Fātiḥa: 1]" — meaning with kasra on the dāl. I say: this is more anomalous and weaker than that, despite the weakness in that which has preceded, because there [in this verse] there is a separating letter, even if it is quiescent. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is a very weak reading, and the best way to interpret it is that the transmitter did not record [it] precisely from the reader; that is, the reader made a slight indication (ishāra) of the ḍamma, to draw attention to the fact that the dropped hamza [of «اسجدوا»] has a ḍamma when beginning [with it], and the transmitter did not catch this indication. It has been said: he intended pausing on the tāʾ, quiescent, then moved it with ḍamma following the vowel of the jīm; and this is treating continuation like pausing. Like it is what is related of a woman who saw a man with women and said «أفي سَوْءَةَ أنْتُنَّه» (are you women in a shameful state?): she intended pausing on «سَوْءَة», so she made the tāʾ quiescent, then cast upon it the vowel of the hamza of «أنتنَّ»." I say: on this [view] this vowel is a vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters, and in that case it is like His saying {قَالَتِ اخرج} [Yūsuf: 31] and its kind. People have expended much on justifying this reading only because of the eminence of its reader, Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, the teacher of Nāfiʿ, the master [reader] of the people of Medina; the biographies of both are well known.
«اسجُدوا» is in the position of the accusative by «القول». The lām in «لآدمَ», on the apparent [view], is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «اسجُدُوا», and its meaning is causation, i.e. "for his sake." It has been said: it is in the sense of «إلى», i.e. towards him, because he was made a qibla (direction of prayer) for them, and the prostration was to Allah. It has been said: in the sense of «مع» (with), because he was their imam — so it is reported. It has been said: the lām is for clarification (bayān), so it is attached to an omitted [element]; but there is no need for that.
«فسجدوا»: the fāʾ is for immediate sequence (taʿqīb), and the implied form is "so they prostrated to him," the preposition-phrase being omitted because it is known. His saying, Exalted is He: {إِلاَّ إِبْلِيسَ}: [«إلا»] is a particle of exception, and «إبليس» is accusative as an excepted [term].
Is it made accusative by «إلاَّ» alone, or by the verb alone, or by [the verb] through the mediation of «إلا», or by an omitted verb, or by «أنَّ»? [Several] views. And is it a connected (muttaṣil) or disconnected (munqaṭiʿ) exception? A well-known disagreement; the most correct is that it is connected. As for His saying, Exalted is He: {إِلاَّ إِبْلِيسَ كَانَ مِنَ الجن} [al-Kahf: 50], this does not refute it, because the angels are sometimes called jinn because of their being hidden (ijtinān); he said:
355 - وسَخَّر مِنْ جِنِّ الملائِكِ تسعةً ... قياماً لَديْهِ يَعْمَلون بلا أَجْرِ
(And He subjected nine of the jinn of the angels, standing before him, working without wage.)
And Allah the Exalted said: {وَجَعَلُواْ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ الجنة نَسَباً} [al-Ṣāffāt: 158], meaning the angels.
Know that the excepted [term] is of four kinds: a kind in which the accusative is obligatory; a kind in which the genitive is obligatory; a kind in which both the accusative and the genitive are allowed; and a kind in which both the accusative and the badal from what precedes it are allowed, the badal being preponderant. The first kind: the excepted from an affirmative [statement]; the one placed first; the repeated one; the disconnected one, according to the Ḥijāzīs, without restriction; and the one occurring after «لا يكون», «ليس», «ما خلا» and «ما عدا» — according to other than al-Jarmī — e.g. «قام القومُ إلا زيداً» (the people stood except Zayd), «ما قَام إلا زيداً القومُ» (none of the people stood, except Zayd), «وما قام أحد إلا زيداً إلا عَمْراً» (no one stood except Zayd, except ʿAmr), «وقاموا إلا حماراً» (they stood, except a donkey), and «وقاموا لا يكون زيداً وليس زيداً وما خلا زيداً وما عدا زيداً» (they stood, Zayd not being [among them] / excepting Zayd). The second kind: the excepted by «غير», «سِوى», «سُوى» and «سَواء». The third kind: the excepted by «عدا», «خلا» and «حاشا». The fourth kind: the excepted from a non-affirmative [statement], e.g. {مَّا فَعَلُوهُ إِلاَّ قَلِيلٌ مِّنْهُمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 66].
Al-sujūd, lexically, is abasement and submission, and its utmost is placing the forehead on the ground. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "It is inclining." Zayd al-Khayl said:
356 - بجَمْعٍ تَضِلُّ البُلْقُ في حَجَراته ... ترى الأُكْمَ فيها سُجَّداً للحَوافِرِ
(With a host in whose flanks the piebald horses get lost; you see the hillocks in it prostrate to the hooves.)
[He means that the hooves tread the ground, so he makes the hillocks' yielding to the hooves a prostration.] Another said:
357 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... سُجودَ النصارى لأَِحْبارِها
(… like the prostration of the Christians to their learned men.)
Some distinguished between «سَجَد» and «أَسْجد»: «سجد» is placing one's forehead [on the ground], and «أَسْجَدَ» is inclining one's head and lowering it; the poet said:
358 - فُضُولَ أَزِمَّتِها أَسْجَدَتْ ... سُجودَ النَّصارى لأرْبابها
(… the ends of their halters, they bowed their heads, like the prostration of the Christians to their lords.)
And another said:
359 - وقُلْنَ له أسْجِدْ لِلَيْلَى فَأَسْجدا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(They [the women] said to it: "Bow your head for Laylā," and it bowed …)
meaning that the camel lowered its head for her sake. «دراهمُ الأسجاد» are dirhams bearing images to which they used to prostrate; the poet said:
360 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . وافى بها كدَراهمِ الأَسْجادِ
(… he brought it [the wine], like the dirhams of prostration.)
As for «إبليس», there is disagreement about it. It has been said: [it is] a foreign noun, a diptote because of being a proper name and foreignness; this is the correct [view]. It has been said: it is derived from «الإِبْلاس», which is despair of the mercy of Allah the Exalted and remoteness from it; he said:
361 - وفي الوُجوهِ صُفْرَةٌ وإبْلاسْ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(And in the faces were pallor and despair …)
and another said:
362 - يا صاحِ هل تَعْرِفُ رَسْماً مُكْرَسَا ... قال نَعَمْ أَعْرِفُه وأَبْلَسَا
(O my companion, do you recognise a trace caked with dung? He said: Yes, I recognise it — and it has become desolate.)
i.e. it became remote from habitation and from being frequented. Its pattern according to these [scholars] is ifʿīl. It was objected against them that it should then have been fully declined; they answered that it resembled foreign nouns because it has no counterpart among Arabic nouns. This was refuted against them by [the fact] that its like in Arabic is plentiful, e.g. «إزْميل» (chisel), «إكليل» (crown), «إغْريض» (spathe), «إخْريط» (a plant) and «إحْليل» (urethra). It has been said: since no Arab was named with it, it became as though it were a loanword in their language, so it resembled foreign [nouns]; and there is remoteness in this.
His saying: {أبى واستكبر}: the apparent [view] is that these two clauses are resumptive, as an answer to one who says: "So what did he do?", and the pause at His saying {إِلاَّ إِبْلِيسَ} is complete. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "[They are] in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «إبليس», its implied form being: he abandoned prostration, unwilling and too arrogant for it." So the pause, according to him, is at «واستكبر». He allowed regarding His saying, Exalted is He, {وَكَانَ مِنَ الكافرين} that it be resumptive and also that it be a ḥāl.
Al-ibāʾ is refusing; the poet said:
363 - وإما أَنْ يقولوا قَدْ أَبَيْنا ... وشَرُّ مواطِنِ الحَسَبِ الإِباءُ
(Or that they say: "We have refused" — and the worst of the stances of noble lineage is refusal.)
It is one of the verbs that convey negation, and for that reason the emptied exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh) occurs after it; Allah the Exalted said: {ويأبى الله إِلاَّ أَن يُتِمَّ نُورَهُ} [al-Tawba: 32]. The well-known [form] is «أبى يأبى», with fatḥa in both, whereas the analogy would be kasra on the middle radical of the imperfect; for that reason some took it into account and put kasra on the imperfect prefix, saying «تِئْبى» and «نِئْبى». It has been said: since the alif resembles the guttural letters, the middle radical of the imperfect was given fatḥa on its account. It has been said: «أَبى يأبى» with fatḥa in both, whereas the analogy would be kasra on the middle radical of the imperfect; for that reason some took it into account and put kasra on the imperfect prefix, saying «تئبى» and «نئبى». It has been said: since the alif resembles the guttural letters, the middle radical of the imperfect was given fatḥa on its account. [Translator's note: these two sentences repeat the preceding ones in the printed text, apparently a duplication.] It has been said: «أَبِيَ يأبى», with kasra in the past and fatḥa in the imperfect; this is regular. So it is possible that whoever says «أبى يأبى» with fatḥa in both made do with the imperfect of the one who says «أبِيَ» with kasra, and that it is a case of overlapping (tadākhul), like «ركَن يركَنُ» and its kind.
«استكبر» is in the sense of «تكبَّر» (was arrogant). Refusal was put before it, even though it comes after it in sequence, only because it is one of the outward acts, unlike arrogance, which is one of the acts of the heart. As for His saying «وكان», it has been said that it is in the sense of «صار» (became), as in his saying:
364 - بتَيْهاءَ قَفْرٍ والمَطِيُّ كأنَّها ... قطا الحَزْن قد كانَتْ فراخاً بيوضُها
(In a trackless waste, the mounts as though they were sandgrouse of the rugged land whose eggs had become chicks.)
i.e. had become. Ibn Fūrak rejected this, saying: "The principles refute it." The more apparent [view] is that it has its usual sense, and the meaning is: and he was of the disbelieving people who were on the earth before the creation of Adam, according to what has been related; or: and he was [so] in the knowledge of Allah.

semin-durr:120-120.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {هُوَ الهدى}: «هو» may be a separating pronoun (faṣl), or a mubtadaʾ (subject) with what follows as its khabar (predicate). It may not be a badal (substitute) from «هدى الله», because it comes in the nominative form. Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed it to be a tawkīd (emphasis) of the noun of «إنّ», but this is not permissible, for a pronoun does not emphasise an overt noun.
His words: {وَلَئِنِ اتبعت}: this is called the lām that prepares for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa li-l-qasam). Its sign is that it occurs before conditional particles; it most often comes with «إنْ», and it may come with others, as in {لَمَآ آتَيْتُكُم مِّن كِتَابٍ} [Āl ʿImrān: 81] and {لَّمَن تَبِعَكَ مِنْهُمْ} [al-Aʿrāf: 18], and its explanation will come. Since it announces the oath, its precedence was taken into account, so the oath, not the condition, was answered by His words {مَا لَكَ مِنَ الله مِن وَلِيٍّ}, and the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) was omitted. Had the condition been answered, the fāʾ would have been necessary. This lām may be omitted while its requirement is still acted upon, so that the oath is answered, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: {وَإِن لَّمْ يَنتَهُواْ عَمَّا يَقُولُونَ لَيَمَسَّنَّ} [al-Māʾida: 73]. His words «من العِلْم» are in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «جاءك», and «مِنْ» is partitive, i.e. "came to you, it being part of the knowledge".

semin-durr:41-41.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {بِمَآ أَنزَلْتُ} … «ما» may be in the sense of «الذي» (that which), with the referring pronoun omitted, i.e. "that which I sent down"; and it may be maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun), the maṣdar (verbal noun) standing in the place of the object, i.e. "in what was sent down". «مصدقاً» is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and the one it describes is the omitted referring pronoun. It has also been said: the one it describes is «ما», and what governs it is «آمنوا». Some permitted «ما» to be maṣdariyya without making the maṣdar stand in the place of a direct object, and made «لِما معكم» part of its completion, i.e. "in My sending down to what is with you", and made «مُصَدِّقاً» a ḥāl from the «ما» put in the genitive by the lām, placed before it even though the one it describes is in the genitive, because the correct view is that a ḥāl of a noun in the genitive [by a preposition] may be put before it, as in his saying:
406 - فإنْ تَكُ أَذْوادٌ أُصِبْنَ ونِسْوَةٌ ... فَلَنْ يَذْهبوا فَرْغاً بقَتْلِ حِبالِ
(If herds of camels have been seized and women, they shall not get away with the killing of Ḥibāl unavenged.)
«فَرْغا» is a ḥāl from «بقتل». Moreover, this lām is redundant (zāʾida), so it counts as discarded. «مصدقاً» is a corroborative ḥāl, because it can only be so. The apparent view is that «ما» is in the sense of «الذي», that «مصدقاً» is a ḥāl from the relative's referring pronoun, and that the lām in «لِما» strengthens the transitivity of «مصَدِّقاً» to the «ما» whose relative clause is the adverbial phrase.
His saying: {أَوَّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ}: «أولَ» is the khabar (predicate) of «كان» before it, and there are four views on it. The first, which is Sībawayh's doctrine: that it is afʿal, and that its first and second radicals are wāw, and its feminine is أُوْلى, originally وُوْلى; the wāw was obligatorily changed into hamza. It is not like «وُوْرِيَ» in which there is no change owing to the wāw after it being quiescent, because the wāw of «أُولَى» is vowelled in the plural, in their saying «أُوَل», so the singular was treated like the plural in that. No verb was formed from «أوَّل» because of its heaviness. It has also been said: it is from وَأَل, when one escapes, so its first radical is wāw and its second hamza; its origin is أَوْأَل, and it was lightened by changing the hamza into wāw and assimilating the wāw into it, giving أوَّل. [Translator's note: the printed text has «أَوْ أَل» with a space, evidently for «أَوْأَل».] This is not the analogical way of lightening it; rather the analogy is that the vowel of the hamza be cast onto the quiescent wāw and the hamza dropped; but they likened it to خَطِيَّة and برِيَّة. This is weak. The plural is أَوائل, and also أَوالي, by transposition. It has also been said: it is from آل يَؤُول, when one returns, its origin being أَأْوَل with two hamzas, the first augmentative and the second the first radical; then it was transposed, the first radical being put after the second, giving أوْأَل on the pattern aʿfal; then what was done in the previous aspect, transposition and assimilation, was done to it; and it is weaker than that. It has also been said: it is وَوَّل on the pattern fawʿal, and the first wāw was changed into hamza. This view is the weakest of them, because it would then have to be a triptote, nothing else. The plural is أوائل, originally وَواوِل; the first was changed into hamza for what has preceded, and the third too because it occurs after the alif of the plural.
Know that «أَوَّل» is an elative (afʿal al-tafḍīl), and an elative annexed to an indefinite noun is singular and masculine in all cases.
Then the indefinite noun to which afʿal is annexed is either non-derived (jāmid) or derived. If it is non-derived, it agrees with what precedes it, as in: الزيدان أفضلُ رجلَيْن (the two Zayds are the best of two men), الزيدون أفضلُ رجال, الهنداتُ أفضلُ نسوةٍ. Al-Mubarrad permitted making it singular in all cases, and the grammarians refuted him. If it is derived, the majority likewise hold that agreement is obligatory, as in: «الزيدُون أفضلُ ذاهبين وأكرمُ قادمين», while some permitted agreement and its absence. Al-Farrāʾ cited:
407 - وإذا هُمُ طَعِمُوا فَالأَمُ طاعِمٍ ... وإذا هُمُ جاعوا فَشَرُّ جِياعِ
(When they eat, they are the meanest of eaters, and when they hunger, the worst of the hungry.)
So he used the singular in the first and agreement in the second. In their view, of this kind is: {وَلاَ تكونوا أَوَّلَ كَافِرٍ بِهِ}.
This being established, on the view of the majority «كافر» ought to have been plural. They answered that in several ways. The best of them: that afʿal in the verse and in the verse of poetry is annexed to a singular noun conveying a plural sense, which was omitted, its adjective remaining in its place; so the indefinite noun to which afʿal is annexed came in the singular in consideration of that omitted qualified noun, the implied form being: "and do not be the first group or band disbelieving", and likewise: "the meanest group eating". It has also been said: because it is to be interpreted as "the first to disbelieve in it". And it has been said: because it has the meaning "let not each one of you be the first disbeliever", as in your saying: كساناً حُلَّةً (he clothed us with a garment), i.e. each one of us. This adjective has no contrary implication (mafhūm) here, so it is not meant "do not be the first disbeliever, but be the last disbeliever". When someone believed that it has a contrary implication, he needed the interpretation of making «أول» redundant; he said: its implied form is "and do not be disbelievers in it". This amounts to nothing. Someone supposed that there is an omitted conjoined item, its implied form being: "and do not be the first disbeliever in it nor the last disbeliever", and the first was stated explicitly because it is the more outrageous, since it is initiating it. It parallels his saying:
408 - مِنْ اُناسٍ ليسَ في أَخْلاقِهِمْ عاجلُ ... الفُحْشِ ولا سوءُ الجَزَعْ
(Of a people in whose characters there is no immediate obscenity, nor ugly impatience.)
He does not mean that there is deferred obscenity in them; rather he means there is no obscenity with them, neither immediate nor deferred. The hāʾ in «به» refers to «ما أَنْزَلْتُ», which is the apparent view; it has also been said: to «ما معكم»; and it has been said: to the Messenger, upon him be peace, because sending down requires someone to whom it is sent down; and it has been said: to the favour, taking it in the sense of beneficence.
His saying: {بِآيَاتِي ثَمَناً قَلِيلاً} is attached to the purchasing before it. Purchasing has been made to include the meaning of exchanging; for that reason the bāʾ entered on "the signs". Analogy would have required it to enter on what is the price, because the price in a sale is properly that with which one buys, not what one buys; but since the sense of exchanging entered the speech, that became permissible, because the meaning of exchanging is that the accusative is what is obtained and that put in the genitive by the bāʾ is what is given up. Some thought that in «بَدَّلْتُ الدرهمَ بالدينار» — and likewise «أَبْدَلْتُ» — the dinar is what is obtained and the dirham what is given up; this is an error. Of the occurrence of اشترى in the sense of استبدل is his saying:
409 - كما اشْتَرَى المسلمُ إذا تَنَصَّرا ...
(…as the Muslim made an exchange when he became a Christian.)
And another's saying:
410 - فإنْ تَزْعُمِينِي كُنْتُ أَجْهَلُ فيكم ... فإنِّي شَرَيْتُ الحِلْمَ بعدكِ بالجَهْلِ
(If you claim that I used to act foolishly among you, I have, since you, exchanged foolishness for forbearance.)
Al-Mahdawī said: "The bāʾ's entering on 'the signs' is like its entering on the price; and likewise everything in which there is no specific article of value. When there are dirhams or dinars in the speech, the bāʾ enters on the price. Al-Farrāʾ said it." End of quotation.
He means that when there is neither dirham nor dinar in the speech, each of the two countervalues may properly be price and thing priced; but [that] differs with respect to the two contracting parties: whoever ascribes the buying to himself puts the bāʾ on what went out from him and left him, and puts in the accusative what he obtained; so you say: اشتريتُ هذا الثوبَ بهذا العبدِ (I bought this garment for this slave). But when there are dirhams or dinars, they are the price and nothing else, as in اشتريْتُ الثوبَ بالدرهمِ (I bought the garment for the dirham), and you do not say: اشتريتُ الدرهمَ بالثوبِ. Some supposed [a muḍāf] and said: "for teaching My signs", because the signs themselves are not something with which one buys. There is no need for that, because its meaning is exchanging, as has preceded.
«ثَمناً» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and «قليلاً» its adjective. {وَإِيَّايَ فاتقون} is like His saying {وَإِيَّايَ فارهبون} [al-Baqara: 40]. He said here [«فاتقون» and there «فارهبون» because neglecting what was commanded there is disobedience, namely neglecting remembrance of the favour and fulfilment of the covenant, while here] neglecting faith in what was sent down and purchasing a small price with it is disbelief. So mention of fear (rahab) suited that place, because it is lighter and pardon of it is possible, since it is disobedience; and He mentioned piety (taqwā) here because it is disbelief, which cannot be pardoned, since taqwā is taking protection against what is bound to happen.

semin-durr:172-172.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {كُلُواْ مِن طَيِّبَاتِ}: the object of «كُلوا» is omitted, i.e. "eat your provision". «مِنْ» then admits two interpretations. The first: that it marks the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), and so is attached (mutaʿalliq) to «كلوا». The second: that it is partitive, and so is attached to something omitted, since it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from that implied object, i.e. "eat your provision, it being part of the good things We have provided you". According to al-Akhfash's opinion it is permissible for «مِنْ» to be redundant (zāʾida) within the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), i.e. "eat the good things We have provided you". «إنْ كُنْتُمْ» is a condition whose apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted, i.e. "then be grateful to Him". The view of those Kufans who said that it means «إذ» (since) is weak. «إياه» is an object placed first in order to convey restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), or because its governing word ends a verse; its being detached is obligatory, since whenever it comes after [the verb] it must be attached, except under poetic necessity, as in the poet's words:
815 - إليك حتى بَلَغَتْ إيَّا كا
(…to you, until she reached you [lit. "iyyāka"].)
In His words {واشكروا للَّهِ} there is iltifāt (a shift of person) from the first-person pronoun to the third person, since had it continued in the first style He would have said «واشكرونا» (and be grateful to Us).

semin-durr:173-173.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ الميتة}: The majority read «حَرَّم» with a doubled letter, active, and «الميتة» in the accusative, on the basis that «ما» is the restraining particle (kāffa) that prepares inna for entering upon this verbal clause; the fāʿil (agent) of «حَرَّم» is a pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, and «الميتةَ» is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). Ibn Abī ʿAbla read «الميتة» and what follows it in the nominative. The explanation of this reading is easy: «ما» is a relative noun and «حَرَّمَ» its ṣila (relative clause); the fāʿil is a pronoun referring to Allah the Exalted, and the referent pronoun is omitted because the conditions are fulfilled, its implied form being "ḥarramahu" (He forbade it); the relative noun and its ṣila are in the position of the accusative as the noun (ism) of «إنَّ», and «الميتةُ» is its khabar (predicate).
Abū Jaʿfar read «حُرِّم» «[Translator's note: the text vocalises it «حُرَّم».]» in the passive. In this reading «ما» admits two interpretations. The first: that «ما» is preparatory (muhayyiʾa) and «الميتةُ» is the object of a verb whose agent is not named (i.e. the nāʾib fāʿil, deputy agent). The second: that it is a relative noun, so that the object of «حَرَّمَ» standing in place of the fāʿil is a latent (mustatir) pronoun referring to the relative «ما», and «الميتةُ» is the khabar of «إنَّ».
Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read «حَرُمَ», with ḍamma on the rāʾ and without doubling, and «الميتةُ» in the nominative. Here too «ما» admits both interpretations: it may be preparatory, with «الميتةُ» the fāʿil of «حَرُم»; or relative, with the fāʿil a pronoun referring to «ما», which is the ism of «إنَّ», and «الميتةُ» its khabar.
The majority read «المَيْتَة» without doubling throughout the Quran, and Abū Jaʿfar with doubling, which is the original form. This is as stated earlier, that «المَيْت» is lightened from «الميِّت», whose original form is mayyiwit; the two are dialectal variants, and the full treatment of this will come at His words {وَتُخْرِجُ الحي مِنَ الميت} [verse 27] in Āl ʿImrān. It is reported from the early grammarians that «المَيْت» without doubling is one whose soul has left his body, and with doubling one who has seen the causes of death but has not died. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported from Abū Ḥātim that for what has already died both forms are said, while for what has not yet died the light form is not said; then he said: «No one read the light form for what has not died except what al-Bazzī related from Ibn Kathīr: {وَمَا هُوَ بِمَيِّتٍ} [Ibrāhīm: 17]». As for the poet's words:
816 - إذا ما ماتَ مَيْتٌ من تميمٍ ... فَسَرَّكَ أن يعيشَ فَجِىءْ بِزادِ
(When someone of Tamīm dies and you would be glad for him to live, then bring provisions.)
[It has been taken to refer to one on the verge of death; but taking it to refer to one actually dead is more cutting as satire.]
The original form of «مَيِّتة» is mayyiwita; it was modified by turning the wāw into yāʾ and assimilating the yāʾ into it. The Kufans said: its original form is mawīt, on the pattern faʿīl.
Al-laḥm (meat) is well known; its plural is luḥūm and luḥmān. One says laḥuma the man, with ḍamma, laḥāmatan, so he is laḥīm, i.e. he became stout; and laḥima, with kasra, yalḥamu, with fatḥa, so he is laḥim: he craved meat; and alḥama the people, so he is lāḥim, i.e. he fed them meat; and alḥama: meat became plentiful with him.
Al-khinzīr (swine) is a well-known animal. There are two views about its nūn: the sounder of them is that it is radical, and its pattern is fiʿlīl, like ghirbīb. The second: that it is augmentative; they derived it from khazar al-ʿayn, i.e. narrowness of the eye, because it looks in that way. It has also been said that al-khazar is looking with the corner of the eye; one says: he is akhzar, plainly squint-eyed.
His words: {وَمَآ أُهِلَّ بِهِ}: «ما» is a relative noun meaning alladhī (that which), and its position is either accusative or nominative, by conjunction with «الميِّتة»; the nominative being either as khabar of inna or as fāʿil, according to the readings mentioned earlier. «أُهِلَّ» is passive, and what stands in place of the fāʿil is the preposition and its genitive noun in «به»; the pronoun refers to «ما», and the bāʾ has the sense of «في» (in). A muḍāf must be supplied, i.e. "in its slaughter", because the meaning is: "and that over whose slaughter [a name] other than Allah's was valid" «[Translator's note: «صَحَّ» as written; presumably «صِيحَ», "was cried out".]». Al-ihlāl is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of ahalla, i.e. he cried out and raised his voice; from it comes al-hilāl (the crescent), because people cry out on seeing it, and istahalla al-ṣabiyy (the newborn cried out). Ibn Aḥmar said:
817 - يُهِلُّ بالغَرْقَدِ رُكْبَانُها ... كما يُهِلُّ الراكبُ المُعْتَمِرُ
(Its riders raise their voices at al-Gharqad, as the rider performing ʿumra raises his voice.)
Al-Nābigha said:
818 - أو دُرَّةٌ صَدَفِيَّةٌ غَوَّاصُها ... بَهِجٌ متى يَرَها يَهِلُّ ويَسْجُدُ
(Or a pearl from its shell, whose diver is joyful: whenever he sees it he cries out and prostrates.)
And he said:
819 - تَضْحَكُ الضَّبْعُ لقتلى هُذَيْلٍ ... وترى الذئبَ لها يَسْتَهِلُّ
(The hyena laughs over the slain of Hudhayl, and you see the wolf crying out with joy over them.)
His words: {فَمَنِ اضطر}: «مَنْ» admits two interpretations. The first: that it is conditional. The second: that it is a relative meaning alladhī (the one who). On the first, «اضطُرَّ» is in the position of the jussive (majzūm) by it.
His words {فلا إِثْمَ} are the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), and the fāʾ in it is obligatory. On the second, «اضطُّرَّ» has no grammatical position, since it occurs as a ṣila, and the fāʾ entered the khabar by likening the relative to the condition. The position of {فلا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ} is jussive on the first, and nominative on the second.
The majority read «اضْطُرَّ» with ḍamma on the ṭāʾ, which is its original vowel; Abū Jaʿfar read it with kasra, because the original form is «اضْطُرِرَ» with kasra on the first rāʾ; when the rāʾ was assimilated into the rāʾ, its vowel was transferred to the ṭāʾ after the ṭāʾ was stripped of its own vowel. Ibn Muḥayṣin read «اطُّرَّ», assimilating the ḍād into the ṭāʾ. This question has been discussed more fully than this at His words: {ثُمَّ أَضْطَرُّهُ إلى عَذَابِ النار} [al-Baqara: 126].
Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read the nūn of «مَنْ» with kasra, according to the basic rule for the meeting of two vowelless letters, and the rest gave it ḍamma, in harmony with the ḍamma of the third letter. This disagreement is not confined to this word; rather whenever two vowelless letters from two words meet and the third letter has a fixed ḍamma — as in {وَلَقَدِ استهزىء} [al-Anʿām: 10], {قُلِ ادعوا} [al-Isrāʾ: 110], «قالتِ اخْرُجْ» — the said disagreement occurs. However, Abū ʿAmr departed from his rule in {أو} [al-Muzzammil: 3] and {قل} [al-Isrāʾ: 110] and gave them ḍamma; and Ibn Dhakwān departed from his rule and gave kasra to the tanwīn in particular, as in {مَحْظُوراً انظر} [al-Isrāʾ: 20-21]; and there is disagreement in what is reported from him concerning {بِرَحْمَةٍ ادخلوا} [al-Aʿrāf: 49], and disagreement in what is reported from him concerning {خَبِيثَةٍ اجتثت} [Ibrāhīm: 26]. The explanation of the wisdom behind this will come where it is mentioned, if Allah the Exalted wills.
His words: {غَيْرَ بَاغٍ}: accusative as a ḥāl. There is disagreement about the one to whom it refers (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl). The apparent view is that it is the latent pronoun in «اضطُرَّ». Al-Qāḍī and Abū Bakr al-Rāzī made it refer to the fāʿil of an omitted verb after His words «اضطُرَّ»; they said: its implied form is "so whoever is compelled and eats, not desiring…", as though they intended thereby to make it a restriction on the eating, not on the compulsion.
The Shaykh said: «What they said is not necessarily so, since this implied element may be supplied after His words {غَيْرَ بِاغٍ وَلاَ عَادٍ}; indeed that is the apparent and preferable view, because supplying it before «غيرَ باغ» involves separating things that are apparently connected with what follows them, whereas this is not the case when supplying it after His words «غيرَ باغ»».
«عادٍ» is the active participle of ʿadā yaʿdū, when one exceeds one's limit. The original form is ʿādiwun; the wāw was turned into yāʾ because of the kasra before it, like ghāzin from al-ghazw. This is the correct view. There is a second view about it: that it is metathesised from ʿāda yaʿūdu, so ʿāʾid; the lām [third radical] was placed before the ʿayn [second radical], and the word became ʿādiw, and it was modified as described; its pattern is fāliʿ, like their saying shākin for shāʾik, from al-shawka, and hārin whose original is hāʾir, since it is from hāra yahūru. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: «Had it come outside the Quran in the accusative, conjoined to the position of «غير», it would be permissible», meaning that one would then say "wa-lā ʿādiyan".
The readers differed over the vowel used for the meeting of two vowelless letters in cases like {فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ} and its class: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and ʿĀṣim give kasra to the first of them, and the rest ḍamma, except for what is excepted for some of them. The rule defining the scope of their disagreement: any two vowelless letters from two words that meet, where the third letter of the second word has a fixed ḍamma, such as «فَمَنِ اضطُرَّ», {فَمَنِ اضطُرَّ}, {أَوِ انقص مِنْهُ قَلِيلاً} [al-Muzzammil: 3], {وَقَالَتِ اخرج عَلَيْهِنَّ} [Yūsuf: 31], {قُلِ ادعوا الله} [al-Isrāʾ: 110], {أَنِ اعبدوا} [al-Māʾida: 117], {وَلَقَدِ استهزىء} [al-Anʿām: 10], «محظوراً انظر». By my saying "two words" I exclude cases where another word separates them, as in {إِنِ الحكم} [al-Anʿām: 57]: even though it is true of this that the third letter has a fixed ḍamma, another word separates the two, namely the definite article al. And by my saying "a fixed ḍamma" I exclude cases like {أَنِ امشوا} [Ṣād: 6] «[Translator's note: the text gives the reference as «ص: 26»; the verse is Ṣād: 6.]», for the original vowel of the shīn is kasra; so whoever gives kasra does so by the basic rule for the meeting of two vowelless letters, and whoever gives ḍamma does so for harmony.
Two places are excepted for Abū ʿAmr, which he reads with ḍamma: «قُل ادْعُوا» and «أو انْقُصْ منه»; and the tanwīn is excepted for Ibn Dhakwān from Ibn ʿĀmir, which he reads with kasra, as in «محظوراً نظر» «[Translator's note: so in the text, for «محظوراً انظر».]»; and there is disagreement in what is reported from him in two words: {خَبِيثَةٍ اجتثت} [Ibrāhīm: 26] and {بِرَحْمَةٍ ادخلوا الجنة} [al-Aʿrāf: 49]. The purpose of this is to combine the two dialects.

semin-durr:135-135.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {هُوداً أَوْ نصارى}: The discussion of «أو» is like the discussion of it at His saying: «وقالوا: لن يَدْخُلَ الجنةَ إلا مَنْ كان هوداً أو نصارى», and it has preceded. And «تهتدوا» is jussive (majzūm) as the answer to the imperative, and the disagreement about it is known: I mean, is its jussive due to the clause before it, or to an implied «إنْ»?

His saying: {مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ}: The majority read «مِلَّةَ» in the accusative, and there are four aspects in it. The first: that it is the object of an implied verb, i.e.: "rather, we follow the religion of…", because the meaning of "Be Jews" is: follow Judaism or Christianity. The second: that it is accusative as the khabar of «كان», i.e.: "rather, we are the religion", i.e.: the people of the religion, like the saying of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim: "I am of a religion", i.e.: of the people of a religion; and this is the view of al-Zajjāj, and al-Zamakhsharī followed him. The third: that it is accusative by way of incitement (al-ighrāʾ), i.e.: "hold to the religion of…", and this is the view of Abū ʿUbayda; this is like the first aspect in its being a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), even though the governor differs. The fourth: that it is accusative by the dropping of the preposition, the origin being: "we follow the example of (naqtadī bi-) the religion of Abraham"; when the particle was elided it became accusative. This may be part of the speech of the believers, so the implied verb would be: "rather, we are", or "we follow", or "we take as example", as has preceded; or it may be an address to the unbelievers, so the implied form would be: "be", or "follow", or "take as example". Ibn Hurmuz and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read «مِلَّةُ» in the nominative, and there are two aspects in it. The first: it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e.: "rather, our religion is the religion of Abraham", or "we are the religion", i.e.: the people of the religion.
The second: that it is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, its implied form being: "the religion of Abraham is our religion".

His saying: {حَنِيفاً}: Concerning its accusative there are four views. The first: that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «إبراهيم», because the ḥāl comes from the muḍāf ilayhi (the noun in the genitive construct) regularly in three places, according to what some have mentioned. The first: that the muḍāf governs as a verb governs. The second: that it is a part [of the muḍāf ilayhi], as in: {وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَاناً} [al-Ḥijr: 47]. The third: that it is like a part, as in this verse; because Abraham, since he adhered to it, it came to stand to him in the status of a part. The grammarians consider weak its coming from the muḍāf ilayhi, even if the muḍāf is a part. They said: because the ḥāl must have a governor, and the governor of the ḥāl is the governor of the one it describes (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl), and the governor of its ṣāḥib does not govern as a verb governs. Those who permit that construe the governor in it as the meaning of the lām or the meaning of iḍāfa, these two being the governors of its ṣāḥib according to this speaker. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned no aspect other than this one, and likened it to your saying: "I saw Hind's face, [she] standing"; and it is the view of al-Zajjāj.
The second: its accusative by an implied verb, i.e.: "we follow, as a ḥanīf"; Abū al-Baqāʾ construed it as «أعني» ("I mean"); and this is the view of al-Akhfash the Younger, who held the ḥāl [reading] to be an error.
The third: that it is accusative by severance (al-qaṭʿ), and this is the opinion of the Kufans; the origin according to them was «إبراهيمَ الحنيفَ» ("Abraham the ḥanīf"), but when it was made indefinite it could no longer be made to follow [as an adjective]. The establishment of that has preceded.
The fourth — and it is the preferred one —: that it is a ḥāl from «ملَّة», so its governor is what we have construed as the governor of it [«ملة»], as has preceded; and it is a permanent ḥāl (ḥāl lāzima), because the religion does not change from this description; and likewise on the view of making it a ḥāl from «إبراهيم», because he did not depart from it. If it is said: The ṣāḥib al-ḥāl is feminine, so it should have agreed with it in the feminine, so that «حنيفةً» would be said — the answer is from two aspects. The first: that faʿīl is the same in masculine and feminine. The second: that «الملَّة» is in the sense of «الدِّين» (the religion), and for that reason it was made a badal (substitute) from it in His saying: {دِيناً قِيَماً مِّلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ حَنِيفاً} [al-Anʿām: 161]. Ibn al-Shajarī mentioned that in his «Amālī».

And al-ḥanaf is inclination (al-mayl); from it al-Aḥnaf was so named, because of the inclination of one of his feet, at the toes, towards the other. His mother said:
742 - واللَّهِ لولا حَنَفٌ برِجْلِه ... ما كانَ في فِتْيانكم مِنْ مثلهِ
(By Allah, were it not for a crookedness in his foot, there would be none like him among your young men.)
One says: rajul aḥnaf and imraʾa ḥanfāʾ. It has been said: it is uprightness, and the one with a crooked foot was called so as a good omen, like their saying of one stung [by a snake] "salīm" (sound), and of a place of perdition "mafāza" (place of success); Ibn Qutayba said this. It has been said: al-ḥanīf is an epithet for whoever professes Islam. ʿAmr said:
743 - حَمَدْتُ اللهَ حين هدى فؤادي ... إلى الإِسلام والدينِ الحَنيفِ
(I praised Allah when He guided my heart to Islam and the ḥanīf religion.)
Al-Qaffāl said this. It has been said: al-ḥanīf is the one who inclines away from what the generality hold to what he has adhered to; al-Zajjāj said this, and he recited:
744 - ولكنَّا خُلِقْنا إذْ خُلِقْنا ... حنيفاً دينُنا عَنْ كلِّ دِينِ
(But we were created, when we were created, with our religion inclining away from every [other] religion.)

semin-durr:102-102.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {واتبعوا مَا تَتْلُواْ الشياطين}: this clause is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to the whole of the preceding clause, from His saying «ولمَّا جاءَهم» to its end.
Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is conjoined to «أُشْرِبوا» or to «نَبَذَ فريقٌ»." This is not apparent, because conjoining it to «نَبَذَ» entails its being the response to His saying {وَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمْ رَسُولٌ}, whereas their following what the devils recited was not consequent upon the coming of the Messenger; rather their following of that was before it. So it is better that it be conjoined to a clause, not as preceded. «ما» is a relative noun and its referring pronoun is omitted, the implied form being: «تَتْلوه». It has been said: «ما» is negative; this is a gross error which the arrangement of the speech does not call for at all; Ibn al-ʿArabī transmitted it. And «يَتْلو» [Translator's note: so in the source; the Qurʾānic word is «تَتْلُوا»] is in the sense of «تَلَتْ»; it is an imperfect verb standing in the place of the past, as in the saying:
639 - وإذا مَرَرْتَ بقبرِه فاعْقِرْ بِه ... كُوَمَ الهِجانِ وكلَّ طَرْفٍ سابحِ
وانضَحْ جوانِبَ قبرِه بدِمائِها ... فَلَقَدْ يكونُ أخا دمٍ وذَبائحِ
(When you pass by his grave, hamstring there the high-humped white camels and every swift-running steed, and sprinkle the sides of his grave with their blood, for he used to be a man of blood and sacrifices.)
i.e. "for he was". The Kufans said: the original is «ما كانت تَتْلو الشياطينُ»; they do not mean by this that the ṣila (relative clause) of «ما» is omitted, namely «كانَتْ», with «تتلو» in the position of the khabar; they only intended an explanation of the meaning, and it is the counterpart of «كانَ زيدٌ يقوم», the meaning being a report of his standing in past time.
Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read: «الشياطُون», treating it like a sound plural. They said: it is an error; and some of them said: a gross solecism. Al-Aṣmaʿī related: "So-and-so's garden has basātūn (gardens) around it", and this strengthens the reading of al-Ḥasan.
His saying: {على مُلْكِ سُلَيْمَانَ}: there are two views on it. One: that it has the sense of «في», i.e. in the time of his kingship, and al-mulk here is his law. The second: that «تَتْلو» is made to include the sense of «تتقوَّل» ("fabricate"), i.e. they fabricate against the kingdom of Solomon; and «تَقَوَّل» is made transitive with «على»; the Exalted said: {وَلَوْ تَقَوَّلَ عَلَيْنَا بَعْضَ الأقاويل} [al-Ḥāqqa: 44]. This second is preferable, for figurative extension in verbs is preferable to figurative extension in particles, and it is the school of the Basrans, as has passed more than once. These two interpretations were made necessary only because when «تلا» is made transitive with «على», the noun governed by «على» is something upon which it is valid to recite, as in «تَلَوْتُ على زيدٍ القرآنَ» ("I recited the Qurʾān to Zayd"), and al-mulk is not like that.
Al-tilāwa is following, or reading, and it [reading] is close to it. Sulaymān is a foreign proper name, and for that reason it is a diptote. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "In it there are three causes: foreignness, definiteness, and the alif and nūn." This would only hold after derivation and morphological treatment entered it, so that the redundancy of those two letters became known; and it has preceded that these do not enter foreign nouns. He repeated His saying {وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيْمَانُ} by mentioning it overtly, to magnify and exalt him, as in the saying:
640 - لا أرى الموتَ يَسْبِقُ الموتَ شيءٌ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(I see nothing outstrip death — death! …)
and the precise statement of that has preceded.
His saying: {ولكن الشياطين كَفَرُواْ}: this wāw conjoins the clause of rectification (istidrāk) to what precedes it.
Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza read «لكنْ» lightened, with the nominative after it; the rest read with doubling and the accusative, and that is clear. As for the first reading, «لكنْ» is lightened from the heavy form, brought merely for rectification; and when it is lightened it does not govern according to the majority, while permissibility of that is transmitted from Yūnus and al-Akhfash. Is it then a conjunction? The majority hold that it is a conjunction when the wāw is not with it and what follows it is a single word; Yūnus held that it is not a conjunction, and this is strong, for it was not heard from their tongue: «ما قام زيدٌ لكن عمروٌ», and if that is found in the books of the grammarians it is from their own made-up examples; for that reason Sībawayh did not exemplify it except with the wāw, and this indicates its denial. As for when clauses occur after it, sometimes it is joined with the wāw and sometimes not. Zuhayr said:
641 - إنَّ ابنَ وَرْقَاءَ لا تُخْشَى بوادِرُهُ ... لكنْ وقائِعُه في الحَرْبِ تُنْتَظَرُ
(Ibn Warqāʾ — his outbursts are not feared, but his onslaughts in war are awaited.)
Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ said: "The preferred choice is to double it when there is a wāw before it, and to lighten it when there is not." This is an inclination on their part toward the view that it is a conjunction. And far-fetched is whoever claimed that it is compounded of three words: the negative lā, the kāf of address, and the affirmative an, the hamza being dropped only for lightness.
His saying: {يُعَلِّمُونَ الناس السحر}: «الناسَ» is the first object and «السحرَ» the second object. They disagreed about this clause in five views. One: that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «كفروا», i.e. they disbelieved, teaching. The second: that it is a ḥāl from «الشياطين»; Abū al-Baqāʾ rejected it on the ground that «لكنّ» does not govern a ḥāl. This is of no weight, for «لكنَّ» has the scent of a verb. The third: that it is in the position of the nominative as a second khabar of «الشياطين». The fourth: that it is a badal (substitute) from «كَفروا», the verb substituted from the verb. The fifth: that it is resumptive, informing about them thereby. This is if we refer the pronoun in «يُعَلِّمون» to the devils; if we refer it to "those who followed what the devils recited", it is a ḥāl from the agent of «اتَّبعوا», or resumptive only. Al-siḥr (sorcery) is anything subtle and fine. Saḥarahu: when he shows him something that is too fine for him and hidden. [The poet] said:
642 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... أَدَاءٌ عَراني من حُبابِكِ أَمْ سِحْرُ
(… is it a sickness that has come upon me from loving you, or sorcery?)
And one says: saḥarahu, i.e. he deceived him and distracted him. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
643 - أرانا مُوضِعِيْنَ لأمرٍ غَيْبٍ ... ونُسْحَرُ بالطَّعام وبِالشَّرابِ
(I see us hastening toward a hidden matter, and we are beguiled by food and drink.)
i.e. we are distracted. It is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun): saḥarahu siḥran; and no maṣdar of faʿala yafʿalu came on the pattern fiʿl except siḥr and fiʿl.
His saying: {وَمَآ أُنْزِلَ}: there are four views on it. The most apparent: that «ما» is a relative noun in the sense of «الذي», its position being the accusative by conjunction to «السِّحْر», the implied form being: "they teach people sorcery and what was sent down to the two angels". The second: that it is also a relative noun and its position is the accusative, but by conjunction to {مَا تَتْلُواْ الشياطين}, the implied form being: "and they followed what the devils recited and what was sent down to the two angels"; on this view, what is between them is parenthetical, and there is no need to say that there is fronting and postponement in the speech.
The third: that its position is the genitive by conjunction to «مُلْكِ سليمان», the implied form being: "fabricating against the kingdom of Solomon and fabricating against what was sent down to the two angels". Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "Its implied form is: and in the time of that which was sent down." The fourth: that «ما» is a negative particle and the clause is conjoined to the negated clause before it, namely {وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيْمَانُ}, and the meaning is: "and the permissibility of sorcery was not sent down to the two angels".
The majority read the lām of «المَلَكَيْن» with fatḥa, on the basis that they are of the angels; Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-Aswad and al-Ḥasan read it with kasra [المَلِكَيْن, "the two kings"], on the basis that they are two men from among people; the establishment of this will come.
His saying {بِبَابِلَ} is attached to «أُنْزِلَ», and the bāʾ is in the sense of «في», i.e. in Babylon. It may also be in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from «المَلَكَيْن» or from the pronoun in «أُنْزل», so it is attached to something omitted; Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned these two aspects.
Bābil is a diptote because of foreignness and being a proper name, for it is the name of a land; or, if you wish, because of femininity and being a proper name. It was so called — he said — because of the confounding (tabalbul) of the tongues of creatures there; that is, Allah the Exalted commanded a wind which gathered them in this land, and no one knew what the other was saying; then the wind scattered them in the lands, each one speaking a language. Al-balbala is dispersal. It has been said: when Noah, peace be upon him, was brought down [from the ark] he alighted and built a town and named it "Thamānīn" (Eighty), and one day he awoke and their tongues had been confounded into eighty languages. And it has been said: because of the confounding of the tongues of creation upon the fall of Nimrod's tower.
His saying: {هَارُوتَ وَمَارُوتَ}: the majority read both their tāʾs with fatḥa. The grammarians disagreed about their i'rab, and that is built on the two readings of «المَلَكَيْنِ». For those who read the lām of «المَلَكَيْنِ» with fatḥa — and they are the majority — there are four aspects in Hārūt and Mārūt. The most apparent: that they are a badal (substitute) from «الملَكَيْنِ», put in the genitive with the fatḥa because they are diptotes due to foreignness and being proper names. The second: that they are an ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition) for them. The third: that they are a badal from «الناس» in His saying {يُعَلِّمُونَ الناس}, a substitute of part for whole, or because the minimum of a plural is two. The fourth: that they are a badal from «الشياطين» in His saying «ولكنَّ الشياطينَ» in the reading of those who put it in the accusative, the justification of the substitution being as preceded. It has also been said: Hārūt and Mārūt are names of two tribes of the jinn, so it is a substitute of whole for whole. On these two views the fatḥa is for the accusative. As for those who read «الشياطين» in the nominative, «هاروت وماروت» cannot be a badal from them; rather on this view it is in the accusative by way of censure, i.e. "I censure Hārūt and Mārūt among all the devils", as in the saying:
644 - أَقَارِعُ عَوْفٍ لا أُحاولُ غيرَها ... وجوهَ قرودٍ تَبْتَغي مَنْ تُجادِعُ
(The Aqāriʿ of ʿAwf — I seek none other than them — faces of apes, seeking whom they may revile.)
i.e. "I censure faces of apes". For those who read their lām with kasra, they are a badal from them, as in the first view — except if they [the two kings] are explained as David and Solomon, as some commentators mentioned; then they cannot be a badal from them, but are connected to «الشياطين» on the two preceding aspects of the nominative and accusative of «الشياطين», or they are a badal from «الناس» as preceded.
Al-Ḥasan read: «هاروتُ وماروتُ» in the nominative; they are the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "they are Hārūt and Mārūt". They may also be a badal from the first «الشياطين», namely His saying {مَا تَتْلُواْ الشياطين}, or the second, according to the reading of those who put it in the nominative. Their plurals are hawārīt and mawārīt, and hawārita and mawārita. Whoever claimed they are derived from al-hart and al-mart, which is breaking, is not correct, because they are diptotes; had they been derived as mentioned they would have been declinable.
His saying: {وَمَا يُعَلِّمَانِ مِنْ أَحَدٍ}: this clause is conjoined to what precedes it. The majority read «يُعَلِّمان» with doubling, and there are two views on it. One: that it is in its proper sense, from teaching. The second: that it is in the sense of «يُعْلِمان», from «أَعْلم» ("to inform"), the doubling and the hamza alternating. They said: because the two angels do not teach people sorcery; they only inform them of it and forbid them from it. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif inclined to this, and he used to read: «يُعْلِمان», from informing. Among those who related «تَعَلَّمْ» in the sense of «اعلَمْ» are Ibn al-Aʿrābī and Ibn al-Anbārī, and they recited the saying of Zuhayr:
645 - تَعَلَّمَنْ هالَعَمْرُ اللهِ ذا قَسَمَاً ... فاقْدِرْ بِذَرْعِكِ وانظُرْ أينَ تَنْسَلِكُ
(Know — by the life of Allah, this is an oath — so measure by your stride and see where you are going.)
and the saying of al-Quṭāmī:
646 - تَعَلَّمْ أنَّ بعدَ الغَيِّ رُشْداً ... وأَنَّ لذلك الغَيِّ انقِشاعاً
(Know that after error comes right guidance, and that this error will clear away.)
and the saying of Kaʿb ibn Mālik:
647 - تَعَلَّمْ رسولَ اللهِ أنَّك مُدْرِكي ... وأنَّ وعيداً منكَ كالأخذِ باليدِ
(Know, O Messenger of Allah, that you will overtake me, and that a threat from you is like seizing by the hand.)
and the saying of another:
648 - تَعَلَّمْ أنه لا طيرَ إلا ... على مُتَطَيِّرٍ وهو الثُّبُورُ
(Know that there is no ill omen except upon the one who takes omens, and that is ruin.)
About the pronoun in «يُعَلِّمان» there are two views. One: that it refers to Hārūt and Mārūt. The second: that it refers to the two angels; this is supported by the reading of Ubayy with the agent made overt: «وما يُعَلَّمُ المَلَكان» [Translator's note: so vocalised in the source; presumably «يُعَلِّمُ»]. The first is the more correct; that is because reliance is on the badal, not on the one substituted for, for that is as if discarded, so regard for it [the badal] is preferable. You say «هندٌ حُسْنُها فاتِنٌ» ("Hind — her beauty is captivating"), and you do not say «فاتنةٌ» out of regard for Hind, except in a small part of speech, as in the saying:
649 - إنَّ السيوفَ غُدُوَّها ورَواحَها ... تَرَكَتْ هوازنَ مثلَ قَرْنِ الأعْضَبِ
(The swords, morning and evening, left Hawāzin like the horn of a broken-horned beast.)
and the saying of another:
650 - فكأنَّه لَهِقُ السَّراةِ كأنه ... ما حاجِبَيْهِ مُعَيَّنٌ بِسَوادِ
(As though he were a wild bull white of back, as though — his two brows — he were marked with black.)
So he had regard for the one substituted for in his saying «تَرَكَتْ» and in his saying «مُعَيَّن»; had he had regard for the badal, which is the common usage, he would have said «تَرَكا» and «مُعَيَّنان», as in the saying of another:
651 - فما كانَ قيسٌ هُلْكُهُ هُلْكَ واحدٍ ... ولكنَّه بُنْيَانُ قَوْمٍ تَهَدَّمَا
(Qays — his death was not the death of one man, but it was the edifice of a people that collapsed.)
And had he not had regard for the badal, it would entail predicating an abstract meaning of a concrete body. The Shaykh answered regarding the two verses that «رَواحَهَا وغدوَّها» is in the accusative as an adverb, and that his saying «مُعَيَّنٌ» is the khabar of «حاجِبَيْه», and that this is permissible because any pair where one cannot do without the other admits this. [The poet] said:
652 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ...
بها العَيْنانُ تَنْهَلُّ
(… with it the two eyes pour [singular verb].)
And he said:
653 - لكأنَّ في العَيْنَيْن حَبَّ قَرَنْفُلٍ ... أو سُنْبَلٍ كُحِلَتْ به فانْهَلَّتِ
(As though in the two eyes were cloves or spikenard with which they [singular verb] were anointed, so they [singular] poured forth.)
And the reverse is permissible; he said:
654 - إذا ذَكَرَتْ عيني الزمانَ الذي مضى ... بصحراء فَلْجٍ ظَلَّتا تَكِفَانِ
(When my eye [singular] remembers the time gone by in the desert of Falj, they both [dual] keep on dripping.)
And «مِنْ» is redundant (zāʾida), to emphasise comprehensiveness, not to produce comprehensiveness, because «أحداً» conveys it — unlike «ما جاءَني من رجلٍ», where it is redundant to produce comprehensiveness. «أحد» here, apparently, is the one that is bound to negation and whose hamza is original in itself.
Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted it to be in the sense of «واحد», so that its hamza is a substitute for a wāw.
His saying: {حتى يَقُولاَ إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ}: «حتى» is a particle of limit, and here it is in the sense of «إلى»; the verb after it is in the accusative by an implied «أَنْ», whose overt expression is not permissible; the sign of the accusative is the dropping of the nūn. The implied form is: "until they say", and it is attached to His saying «وما يُعَلِّمانِ»; the meaning is that their teaching, or their informing — according to the disagreement that has passed — is negated up to this limit, namely their saying: {إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ فَلاَ تَكْفُرْ}. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted [it to be in the sense of «إلا»: "except that] they say" [Translator's note: the text here appears to have a lacuna; the quoted verse and the following gloss make clear that the meaning "except" is intended]. This which he permitted is not known from most of the early scholars; it is only something said by the Shaykh Jamāl al-Dīn ibn Mālik, who recited:
655 - ليسَ العطاءُ من الفُضُولِ سَماحةً ... حتى تَجودَ وما لَدَيْكَ قليلُ
(Giving out of surplus is not generosity — unless you give when what you have is little.)
He said: "Its implied form is: except that you give."
Know that «حتى» may be a preposition in the sense of «إلى», as in this verse and as in His saying: {حتى مَطْلَعِ [الفجر]} [al-Qadr: 5]; it may be a conjunction; and it may be a particle of commencement, so that [clauses] occur after it, [as in the saying]:
656 - فما زالَتِ القَتْلَى تَمُجُّ دماءَها ... بدَجْلَةَ حتى ماءُ دَجْلَةَ أَشْكَلُ
(The slain kept spilling their blood into the Tigris, until the water of the Tigris was reddish.)
Limit is a meaning that does not leave it in these three states, [so what follows it] can only be a limit of what precedes it, whether in strength or weakness or otherwise; and it has rulings which will come, if Allah the Exalted wills. «إنَّما» is restrained by the redundant «ما», and for that reason a clause occurs after it; it has preceded that some of them permit it to govern. The clause is in the position of the accusative by the verb of saying, and likewise «فَلا تَكْفُرْ».
His saying: {فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ}: there are seven views on this clause. The most apparent: that it is conjoined to His saying «وما يُعَلِّمان», and the pronoun in «فيتعلَّمون» refers to «أحد».
It was made plural by construal according to meaning, as in His saying: {فَمَا مِنكُمْ مِّنْ أَحَدٍ عَنْهُ حَاجِزِينَ} [al-Ḥāqqa: 47]. If it is said: the thing conjoined to is negated, so «فيتعلَّمون» must also be negated by being conjoined to it, and then the meaning is reversed — the answer is what they said, namely that {وَمَا يُعَلِّمَانِ مِنْ أَحَدٍ حتى يَقُولاَ}, though negative in wording, is affirmative in meaning, because the meaning is: they teach people sorcery after their saying "we are only a trial". Al-Zajjāj and others mentioned this aspect.
The second: that it is conjoined to {يُعَلِّمُونَ الناس السحر}; al-Farrāʾ said this. Al-Zajjāj objected to this view because of the plural wording in «يُعَلِّمون» while He used the dual pronoun in «منهما» — meaning that it ought then to have been said «منهم» because of «يُعَلِّمون». Abū ʿAlī and others permitted it, and said: it is not impossible to conjoin «فيتعلَّمون» to «يُعَلِّمون» even though the teaching is from the two angels specifically, and the pronoun in «منهما» refers to them, for His saying «منهما» only came after the two angels had been mentioned earlier.
Al-Farrāʾ's view has been objected to from another angle: that it entails using a pronoun before mention; that is, the pronoun in «مِنهما» refers to the two angels, and you have supposed that «فيتعلَّمون منهما» is conjoined to «يُعَلِّمون», so the implied form would be: «يُعَلِّمون الناسَ السحرَ فيتعلَّمون منهما», which entails the pronoun in «منهما» before the mention of the two angels. This is a feeble objection, for they precede in wording, and supposing them postponed does no harm, since what is to be avoided is a pronoun referring to something not mentioned in the wording.
The third — and it is one of Sībawayh's two views: that it is conjoined to «كفروا», and «كفروا» is a verb in the position of the nominative, so a nominative verb was conjoined to it. Sībawayh said: "«فيتعلَّمون» was put in the nominative because He did not report about the two angels that they said 'Do not disbelieve, so that they learn' [in the subjunctive], so as to make his disbelief a cause of another's learning; rather it is on the basis of: they disbelieved, and they learn." The explanation of what he said is that he means that «فيتعلَّمون» is not a response to His saying «فلا تَكْفُرْ», so as to be put in the accusative in response to the prohibition, as «فَيُسْحِتَكم» was put in the accusative after His saying «لا تَفْتَرُوا»; because the disbelief of the one they forbade to disbelieve is not a cause of the learning of whoever learns. This has been objected to by what preceded, namely the entailment of a pronoun before mention, and its answer has preceded.
The fourth — and it is Sībawayh's second view: that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, the implied form being «فهم يتعلَّمون» ("so they learn"); so He conjoined a nominal clause to a verbal one.
The fifth: al-Zajjāj also said: "The best is that it be conjoined to «يُعَلِّمان فيتعلَّمون», and He dispensed with mentioning «يُعَلِّمان» because of what is in the speech indicating it." Abū ʿAlī objected to al-Zajjāj's view, saying: "There is no sense to his saying 'He dispensed with mentioning يُعَلِّمان', because it is present in the text." This objection of Abū ʿAlī is a prejudice against him, because of something that occurred between the two of them; for al-Zajjāj did not mean that «فيتعلَّمون» is conjoined to «يُعَلِّمان» negated by «ما» in His saying «وما يُعَلِّمان», so that it would be mentioned in the text; he only meant that there is an implied verb indicated by the force of the speech, namely: "they teach, so they learn".
The sixth: that it is conjoined to the sense indicated by the beginning of the speech, the implied form being: "so they come and learn"; al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj also mentioned it.
The seventh: Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "And it has been said it is resumptive." This may mean that it is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, as in Sībawayh's view, or that it stands independently, not construed with anything before it, which is the apparent sense of his words. This is the end of what is said on this question; al-Mahdawī — may Allah have mercy on him — went deeply into it and gave delight.
His saying: «مِنْهُمَا» is attached to «يُعَلِّمون» [Translator's note: so in the source; the verb in this phrase is «فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ»]. «مِنْ» is for the beginning of the extent. About the pronoun there are three views. The most apparent: its referring to the two angels, whether read with kasra on the lām or with fatḥa.
The second: that it refers to sorcery and to what was sent down to the two angels. The third: that it refers to the trial and to the disbelief understood from His saying «فَلا تَكْفُرْ»; this is the view of Abū Muslim.
His saying: {مَا يُفَرِّقُونَ بِهِ}: the apparent view about «ما» is that it is a nominal relative. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted it to be an indefinite noun described [by what follows], and this is not clear. It may not be maṣdariyya (forming a maṣdar), because the pronoun in «به» refers to it, and the maṣdariyya «ما» is a particle according to the majority of grammarians, as has preceded more than once.
«بين المرءِ» is an adverb for «يُفَرِّقون». The majority read the mīm of «المَرْء» with fatḥa, with hamza, and it is the highest dialect. Ibn Abī Isḥāq read: «المُرْء» with ḍamma on the mīm, with hamza; and al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī and al-Ḥasan read: «المِرْء» with kasra on the mīm, with hamza. As for the ḍamma, it is a recorded dialect. As for the kasra, it may be a dialect absolutely, or it may be for vowel harmony; that is, in «المَرْء» there is a dialect in which its first radical follows its last radical: if this takes ḍamma, it takes ḍamma; if fatḥa, fatḥa; if kasra, kasra. You say: «ما قام المُرْءُ» with ḍamma on the mīm, «رأيت المَرْءَ» with fatḥa, and «مررت بالمِرْءِ» with kasra. It is sometimes pluralised with wāw and nūn, and that is anomalous; al-Ḥasan said in one of his sermons: "Make your manners good, O al-marʾūn", i.e. your characters [Translator's note: al-malaʾ here glossed by the author as "characters"]. Al-Ḥasan and al-Zuhrī read: «المِرِ» with kasra on the mīm and a light kasra on the rāʾ; its justification is that he transferred the vowel of the hamza onto the rāʾ and dropped the hamza for lightness, and this is a regular analogy. Al-Zuhrī also read: «المَرِّ» with a doubled rāʾ, without hamza; its justification is that he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the rāʾ, then intended pausing on it with doubling — as «مُسْتَطرٌّ» with a doubled rāʾ is related from ʿĀṣim — then treated continuation like pause.
His saying: {وَمَا هُم بِضَآرِّينَ بِهِ مِنْ أَحَدٍ}: two aspects are permissible for «ما». One: that it is the Hijazi «ما», so «هم» is its noun and «بضارِّين» its khabar, the bāʾ being redundant; so it is in the position of the accusative. The second: that it is the Tamimi «ما», so «هم» is a mubtadaʾ and «بضارِّين» its khabar, the bāʾ also redundant; so it is in the position of the nominative. About the pronoun there are three views. One: that it refers to the sorcerers, to whom the pronoun of «فيتعلَّمون» refers. The second: it refers to the Jews, to whom the pronoun of «واتَّبَعوا» refers. The third: it refers to the devils. And the pronoun in «به» refers to «ما» in His saying {مَا يُفَرِّقُونَ بِهِ}.
The majority read «بضارِّين» with the nūn retained, and «من أحدٍ» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object). Al-Aʿmash read: «بضارِّي» without nūn, and there are two views on its justification. The more apparent of them: that he dropped the nūn for lightness, even though the active participle does not occur as the ṣila of «ال»; and like it is the poet's saying:
657 - ولَسْنا إذا تَأَبْون سِلْماً بمُذْعِني ... لكم غيرَ أنَّا إنْ نُسالَمْ نُسالِم
(When you refuse peace we are not submissive to you; but if we are offered peace, we make peace.)
i.e. «بمُذْعنين»; and its counterpart in the dual: "Qaṭā, qaṭā, your eggs are thintā, and my eggs are miʾatā", they mean thintān (two) and miʾatān (two hundred). The second — and al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya held it: that the nūn was dropped for annexation to «أحد», and the muḍāf and muḍāf ilayhi were separated by the preposition and its genitive noun, namely «به», as they were separated by it in the saying of another:
658 - هما أَخَوا في الحربِ مَنْ لا أخَاله ... إذا خافَ يَوْماً نَبْوةً فَدَعاهُما
(They are two brothers — in war — of the one who has no brother, if one day he fears a reverse and calls on them.)
and in the saying:
659 - كما خُطَّ الكتابُ بكفِّ يوماً ... يهوديٍ يقارِبُ أو يُزِيلُ
(As writing was traced, by the hand — one day — of a Jew, bringing [lines] close or spreading them.)
Then al-Zamakhsharī found this problematic and said: "If you say: how can it be annexed to «أحد» when it is governed in the genitive by «مِن»? I say: the preposition was made part of the genitive noun." The Shaykh said: "This derivation is not good, because separating the two terms of a construct by an adverb or a prepositional phrase is among the licences of poetry; and worse than that is that there is no muḍāf ilayhi there, because it is occupied by a governor of the genitive, which is what affects it, not the annexation. As for his making the preposition part of the genitive noun, it is of no weight, because this [preposition] affects it, and the part of a thing does not affect it." In the Shaykh's saying there is an objection. As for the separation being among the licences of poetry, it is not as he said, because separation by the direct object occurred in the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, so with the adverb and its like it is more fitting; the precise statement of that will come in al-Anʿām.
As for his saying "because the part of a thing does not affect it", that is only with a real part, whereas he [al-Zamakhsharī] only said: we treat it as a part. Evidence for that is the saying of the grammarians: the verb is like a part of the agent, and therefore it is made feminine for its femininity; and yet it affects it.
«مِنْ» in «مِنْ أَحَد» is redundant, to emphasise comprehensiveness, as preceded in {وَمَا يُعَلِّمَانِ مِنْ أَحَدٍ}. And Abū al-Baqāʾ's saying ought to come here, that «أَحَداً» may be in the sense of «واحد». The familiar usage is the redundancy of «مِنْ» in a direct object governed by a negated verb, as in «ما ضَربْتُ من أحدٍ»; but the nominal clause entered by the particle of negation was construed in this like the negated verbal clause, because the meaning is: "and they do not harm anyone"; except that He turned to this clause headed by a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is an active participle denoting permanence and stability, with the bāʾ of the genitive added in it, for the intended emphasis which the verbal clause would not have conveyed.
His saying: {إِلاَّ بِإِذْنِ الله}: this is an exception emptied out from the states (ḥāls); so it is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl, attached to something omitted. About the possessor of this ḥāl there are four aspects. One: that it is the latent agent in «بضارِّين». The second: that it is the object, namely «أَحَدٍ», the ḥāl coming from an indefinite because it rests on negation. The third: that it is the hāʾ in «به», i.e. by sorcery; the implied form being: "they do not harm anyone by sorcery except with the knowledge of Allah accompanying it", or "joined with the permission of Allah", and the like. The fourth: that it is the defining maṣdar, namely the harm, except that it was omitted because of what indicates it.
His saying: {وَلاَ يَنفَعُهُمْ}: there are two aspects for this clause. One — and it is the apparent one: that it is conjoined to «يَضُرُّهم», so it too is part of the ṣila of «ما», and so it has no grammatical position. The second — Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted it: that it is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, its implied form being "and it does not benefit them"; on this view the wāw is circumstantial and the clause of mubtadaʾ and khabar is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl; and this ḥāl is emphatic, because from His saying «ما يَضُرُّهم» the absence of benefit is understood. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "And it is not valid to conjoin it to «ما», because a verb is not conjoined to a noun." This is one of the cases where stating its prohibition is unnecessary because of its clarity; one only states the prohibition of something whose permissibility might be imagined. He used «لا» here because by it the present and the future are negated, even though some restricted it to the future. Al-ḍurr (harm) and al-nafʿ (benefit) are known. One says: ḍarrahu yaḍurruhu with ḍamma on the ḍād, which is the analogy of the transitive doubled verb; the maṣdar is al-ḍurr and al-ḍarr, with ḍamma and fatḥa, and also al-ḍarar with the doubling undone. One also says: ḍārahu yaḍīruhu ḍayran in the same sense; the poet said:
660 - تقولُ أُناسٌ لا يَضِيرُك نَأْيُها ... بلى كلُّ ما شَفَّ النفوسَ يَضِيرُها
(People say: her distance does not harm you. Yes it does — all that wastes souls harms them.)
The weak letter is not a substitute for the doubling. Some transmitted that no passive participle is formed from «نفع», so that one would say manfūʿ; but analogy does not refuse it.
His saying: {وَلَقَدْ عَلِمُواْ}: it has preceded that this lām is the response of an omitted oath. And «عَلِمَ» may take two objects or one; on both suppositions it is suspended from governing what follows because of the lām, so the clause after it is in the position of the accusative, either standing in place of two objects or of one object, according to what preceded. The effect of that appears in conjoining to it: if we hold that it takes two objects, we conjoin two objects to the clause after it; otherwise we conjoin one object. Its counterpart in speech is: «عَلِمْتُ لزيدٌ قائمٌ وعمراً ذاهباً» or «عَلِمْتُ لزَيدٌ قائمٌ وذهابَ عمروٍ». What shows that the suspended clause after «عَلِم» is in the position of the accusative, and that an accusative may be conjoined to its position, is the poet's saying:
661 - وما كنْتُ أدري قبلَ عَزَّةَ ما الهَوى ... ولا موجعاتِ القَلْبِ حتى تَوَلَّتِ
(Before ʿAzza I did not know what love was, nor the heart's torments, until she turned away.)
It is related with «مُوجعات» in the accusative, as conjoined to the position of «ما الهوى». In the verse there is discussion, since «ما» may be redundant and «الهوى» a direct object, so «موجعات» is conjoined to it; or «لا» may be the lā of generic negation, «موجعاتِ» its noun and the khabar omitted, as if he said: "and there were no heart's torments with me until she turned away".
About the pronoun in «عَلِموا» there are five views: the pronoun of the Jews in the presence of Muhammad, upon him be peace; or the pronoun of those in Solomon's presence; or the pronoun of all the Jews; or the pronoun of the devils; or the pronoun of the two angels, according to those who hold that two is a plural.
His saying: {لَمَنِ اشتراه}: about this lām there are two views. One — and it is the apparent one according to the grammarians: that it is the lām of commencement which suspends «عَلِم» from governing, as preceded; «مَنْ» is a relative noun in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and «اشتراهُ» is its ṣila with its referring pronoun. And {مَا لَهُ فِي الآخرة مِنْ خَلاَقٍ} is a clause of mubtadaʾ and khabar, with «مِن» redundant in the mubtadaʾ, the implied form being: "he has no share in the Hereafter". This clause is in the position of the nominative as the khabar of the relative «مَنْ». So the clause «ولقد عَلِموا» is what is sworn to, as preceded, and «لَمَن اشتراه» is not sworn to. This is the school of Sībawayh and the majority. The second — the view of al-Farrāʾ, followed by Abū al-Baqāʾ: that this lām is the one paving the way for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa), «مَنْ» is conditional in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and {مَا لَهُ فِي الآخرة مِنْ خَلاَقٍ} is the response of the oath. So «اشتراه» on the first view is a ṣila, and on this second is the khabar of the conditional noun; and the apodosis of the condition is omitted, because when a condition and an oath come together without something requiring a khabar preceding them, the earlier of them is usually answered; though the condition is sometimes answered absolutely, as in the saying:
662 - لَئِنْ كان ما حُدِّثْتُه اليومَ صادِقاً ... أَصُمْ في نهارِ القَيْظِ للشمسِ باديا
(If what I was told today is true, I will fast in the day of summer heat, exposed to the sun.)
The apodosis of the condition is only omitted when its verb is past, though it is sometimes imperfect, as in the saying:
663 - لَئِنْ تَكُ قَدْ ضاقَتْ عليكم بيوتُكُمْ ... لَيَعْلَمُ ربِّي أنَّ بيتيَ واسِعُ
(If your houses have become narrow for you, my Lord knows that my house is wide.)
So on al-Farrāʾ's view both clauses of His saying {وَلَقَدْ عَلِمُواْ لَمَنِ اشتراه} are sworn to. Al-Zajjāj is reported to have rejected al-Farrāʾ's view, for he said: "This is not a place for a condition", without explaining the reason for rejecting it.
