Here He said «ولن يَتَمَنَّوْه», negating with «لن», while in [Sūrat] al-Jumuʿa [He negated] with «لا». The author of «al-Muntakhab» said: "Because their claim here is greater than their claim there, since the ultimate felicity is above the rank of sainthood (wilāya), for the latter is sought for the sake of attaining the former; and negation with «لن» is more emphatic than negation with «لا»."
His saying: {بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ} is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «يتمنَّوْه», and the bāʾ is causal, i.e. because of their committing enormities. Three views are permissible regarding «ما». The most apparent: that it is a relative noun meaning «الذي». The second: an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective; on both views the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e. «بما قَدَّمَتْه» ("because of what [their hands] sent forth"), so the clause has no grammatical position on the first and its position is genitive on the second. The third: that it is maṣdariyya, i.e. "because of their hands' sending forth." The object of «قَدَّمَتْ» is omitted, i.e. "because of what their hands sent forth of evil, or of alteration [of scripture], and the like."

semin-durr:140-140.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {أَمْ تَقُولُونَ}: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with the tāʾ of address, and the rest with the yāʾ. As for the reading of address, «أم» in it admits two aspects. The first: that it is the conjunctive (muttaṣila) one, the balancing being between this clause and His saying «أتحاجُّوننا»; so the question is about the occurrence of one of these two matters: arguing about Allah, or claiming Judaism and Christianity for Abraham and those mentioned with him. It is a question of disapproval and rebuke, as has preceded, for both matters are false. The second: that it is the disjunctive (munqaṭiʿa) one, so it is construed as «بل» plus the hamza, according to what has been established about the disjunctive one on the soundest of the doctrines; the implied form is: "rather, do you say?", the question being also for disapproval and rebuke. So He will have moved away from His saying "Do you argue with us" and begun asking about another matter, the meaning being disapproval of attributing Judaism and Christianity to Abraham and those mentioned with him.

As for the reading with the third person, the apparent [view] is that «أم» in it is disjunctive, in the meaning given above. Al-Ṭabarī reported from some grammarians that it is conjunctive, because when you say "Will you stand, or will ʿAmr stand?" [it means]: will this be or that? «[Translator's note: the source prints «يقولم», evidently a misprint for «يقوم».]» Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejected this aspect, saying: "This example is not good, because the speaker in it is one and the one addressed is one, whereas the speech in the verse is from two, and the ones addressed are two different [parties]. The balancing of «أم» with the alif is valid only on the semantic judgement, as if the meaning of 'Say: Do you argue with us' were: 'Do they argue, O Muḥammad, or do they say?'" End quote. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "For whoever reads with the yāʾ, it can only be disjunctive." The Shaykh said: "Conjunction is possible with the yāʾ reading too, that being by way of iltifāt (a shift of person), since there is in it [a departure] from address to the third person, the pronoun being for particular people." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "«أم يقولونَ» is read with the yāʾ, referring back to His saying «فَسَيَكْفيكُهُم الله»"; so he made this clause connected with His saying «فسيكفيكَهم», and in that case it can only be disjunctive, because you know that a condition of the conjunctive one is the preceding of an interrogative hamza or a hamza of equalisation (taswiya); besides, the meaning is not that the transition is from His saying «فَسَيَكْفيكهم» to His saying «أم يقولون», such that he should make it refer back to it — and it is remote from it in wording and meaning.

The Shaykh said: "The best [view] in the two readings is that «أم» is disjunctive, as though He disapproved of their arguing about Allah and their attributing His prophets to Judaism and Christianity, while what He disapproved of had actually occurred from them. Do you not see His saying: {قُلْ ياأهل الكتاب لِمَ تُحَآجُّونَ في إِبْرَاهِيمَ} [Āl ʿImrān: 65] and the following verses? If we make it conjunctive, that does not include the occurrence of both clauses, but only one of them, and the question becomes about specifying one of them; and the matter is not so when both occurred together." «[Translator's note: the Qurʾānic text of Āl ʿImrān 65 begins «يَا أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ», without «قُلْ»; the source quotes it with «قُلْ».]» What the Shaykh said is very good. And «أو» in His saying «هوداً أو نصارى» is like it in His saying {لَن يَدْخُلَ الجنة إِلاَّ مَن كَانَ هُوداً أَوْ نصارى} [al-Baqara: 111], and its verification has preceded.

His saying: {أَمِ الله}: «أم» is conjunctive, and the Name of Majesty is conjoined to «أنتم»; but He separated between the two conjoined elements with what is asked about, and this is the best of the three usages. That is because in such a construction three aspects are permissible: putting what is asked about first, as in «أأعلم أنتم أم اللهُ»; putting it in the middle, as in «أأنتم أعلمُ أم اللهُ»; and putting it last, as in «أأنتم أم الله أعلمُ». Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "«أم الله» is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and the khabar (predicate) is omitted, i.e.: «أم الله أعلمُ»; and «أم» here is the conjunctive one, i.e.: which of you is more knowing?" There is a reservation about what he said, because if he implies for it a technical khabar, it becomes a clause, and the conjunctive «أم» does not conjoin a clause, but rather a single word and what is in its meaning. And Abū al-Baqāʾ's statement is not an explanation of meaning, such that this could be overlooked for him, but an explanation of iʿrāb. The preference in His saying «أعلمُ» is by way of mockery, and on the assumption that knowledge is supposed of them by the ignorant; otherwise there is no sharing. Its parallel is the saying of Ḥassān:
751 - أتَهْجوه ولَسْتَ له بكُفْءٍ ... فَشَرُّكما لخيرِ كما الفِداءُ
(Do you lampoon him when you are no match for him? May the worse of you two be a ransom for the better of you two.)
And it is known that the Messenger is good entirely.

His saying: {مِنَ الله}: In «مِنْ» there are four aspects. The first: that it is attached to «كَتَم», and that is on the omission of a muḍāf (annexed noun), i.e.: he concealed from the servants of Allah a testimony that he has. The second: that it is attached to something omitted, as a naʿt (adjective) for «شهادة» after another naʿt, because «عنده» is a naʿt of «شهادة». This is the apparent sense of al-Zamakhsharī's statement, for he said: "And «مِنْ» in His saying {شَهَادَةً عِندَهُ مِنَ الله} is like it in your saying 'This is a testimony from me for so-and-so', when you testify for him; and similar to it is {بَرَآءَةٌ مِّنَ الله وَرَسُولِهِ} [Barāʾa: 1]." The third: that it is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun latent in «عنده», meaning the pronoun made nominative by the adverb because it falls as a naʿt; Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned it. The fourth: that it is attached to that omitted element to which the adverb «عنده» is attached, because it falls as a naʿt. The difference between this and the second aspect is that the latter has an independent governor other than the governor of the adverb.

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is not permissible for «مِنْ» to be attached to «شهادة», lest the relative and its ṣila be separated by the naʿt" — meaning that «شهادة» is a maṣdar interpretable as a maṣdar-forming particle plus a verb, so had you attached «مِنْ» to it you would have separated, between what is in the sense of the relative and the parts of the ṣila, by something extraneous, namely the adverb falling as a naʿt of «شهادة». There is a reservation about this from two aspects. The first: we do not concede that «شهادة» resolves into a relative and its ṣila, for not every maṣdar resolves into them. The second: we concede that, but we do not concede, in that case, that the adverb is a naʿt; rather it is governed by it, so it is part of the ṣila, not extraneous, such that separation between the relative and its ṣila would follow from it. The way to forbid this is only by something other than what he mentioned, namely that the meaning rejects it.

«كَتَمَ» is transitive to two objects; the first of them in the noble verse is omitted, its implied form being: he concealed from people a testimony. The best of these aspects is that «من الله» is a naʿt for «شهادة», or attached to the governor of the adverb, not attached to «كتم»; that is because concealing the testimony while it is something deposited with him from Allah is more extreme in wrongdoing than concealing a testimony absolutely from the servants of Allah.

He said in «Riyy al-Ẓamʾān»: "In the verse there is a putting forward and putting back (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr), the implied form being: 'And who is more unjust than Allah, among those who conceal a testimony obtained by them?' — like your saying 'And who is more unjust than Zayd, among the totality of the two words of testimony?' «[Translator's note: so in the source; the comparison sentence is obscure as printed.]» The meaning is: had Abraham and his sons been Jews or Christians, and then Allah concealed this testimony, no one among those who conceal testimony would be more unjust than He; but since that is impossible, given His justice and His being far above lying, we know that the matter is not so." The Shaykh said: "This is extremely forced, both in respect of construction and in respect of what is signified. As for the construction, putting forward and putting back is among the poetic licences (ḍarāʾir) according to the majority. Further, His saying «مِمَّن كتم» then remains attached either to «أظلم», so that it would be by way of badal (substitute), and it would then be the substitution of a general from a particular, which is not established — even if some have claimed it occurs, the majority interpreted it as putting the general in place of the particular; or «مِنْ» is attached to something omitted, so it is in the position of a ḥāl, i.e.: being among those who conceal. As for what is signified, the establishment of being most unjust for the one made genitive by «مِنْ» would be on an assumption, i.e.: if He concealed it, then no one is more unjust than He; and all this is a meaning that does not befit Him, Exalted is He, and His Book is far above it."

semin-durr:62-62.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {مَنْ آمَنَ بالله}. Two options are possible for «مَنْ». The first: that it is conditional, in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), «آمَن» being jussive (majzūm) by it in implied form and being the khabar (predicate) according to the correct view, in accordance with the disagreement mentioned before about it. His saying «فلهم» is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), and this conditional clause is in the position of the nominative as the khabar of «إنَّ» in His saying «إنَّ الذين آمنُوا»; the returning pronoun is omitted, its implied form being "whoever of them believes", as is stated explicitly in another place. The second: that it is a relative in the sense of «الذي», its position then being the accusative as a badal (substitute) from the noun of «إنَّ», namely «الذين» — a substitute of part for whole; the returning pronoun is also omitted, as preceded, and «آمن» is its ṣila (relative clause), so it then has no grammatical position.
His saying: {فَلَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ} is the khabar of «إنَّ الذين»; the fāʾ entered because the relative resembles the condition. This is according to those other than al-Akhfash; as for al-Akhfash, it is transmitted from him that when the mubtadaʾ is abrogated by «إنَّ», that is not allowed in it. [Translator's note: the attribution here to al-Akhfash is as in the source; this restriction is more usually ascribed to Sībawayh, al-Akhfash being reported as permitting it.] So the position of His saying {فَلَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ} is the nominative on this view, and the jussive on the first view. «لهمْ» is a fronted khabar attached to something omitted, and «أجرُهُمْ» is the mubtadaʾ. According to al-Akhfash it may be a fāʿil (agent) of the preposition [phrase] before it, even though it is not supported [by a preceding element]; the disagreement about that has been mentioned before.
His saying: {عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ}: «عند» is an adverb of place that is necessarily annexed, in wording and in meaning. What governs it is the [notion of] being settled (al-istiqrār) contained in «لهم». It may also be in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «أجرُهم», and so be attached to something omitted, its implied form being: "then they have their reward, established with their Lord". The "with-ness" (ʿindiyya) is figurative, because He is exalted above direction. It may pass into [being] an adverb of time when what it contains is an abstract notion; from it is his saying, peace be upon him: «إنما الصبرُ عند الصَّدمةِ الأولى» ("patience is only at the first blow"). The well-known [vocalization] is a kasra on its ʿayn; it may also take a fatḥa and a ḍamma.
«والذين هادُوا» are the Jews. There are two views about the alif of «هادُوا». The first is that it is from a wāw, the original being هاد يهودُ, i.e. "he repented". The poet said:
512 - إنِّي امرؤٌ من حُبِّه هائِدُ
(I am a man repentant of [excessive] love for him.)
i.e. repentant. From it the Jews were named, because they repented of worshipping the calf. And the Exalted said: {إِنَّا هُدْنَآ إِلَيْكَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 156], i.e. we have repented. It has also been said: it is from al-tahwīd, which is speaking with calm and gravity, and they recited:
513 - وخُودٌ من اللائي تَسَمَّعْنَ بالضُّحى ... قَريضَ الرُّدافَى بالغِناءِ المُهَوَّد
(And a soft young woman, of those who in the forenoon listen to the poetry of the riders behind, sung in gentle song.)
It has also been said: it is from al-hawāda, which is submission. The second: that it is from a yāʾ, the original being هاد يَهِيد, i.e. "to move"; from it the Jews were named, because of their moving [their bodies] in their study. It has also been said: they were named Yahūd by attribution to Yahūdhā, with the dotted dhāl, who was the son of Jacob, peace be upon him; the Arabs changed it from the dotted dhāl to the undotted [dāl], following their custom of playing with foreign names.
Al-naṣārā ("Christians") is a plural; its singular is naṣrān and naṣrāna, like nadmān, nadmāna and nadāmā. Sībawayh said this, and recited:
514 - فَكِلْتاهما خَرَّتْ وأَسْجَدَ رأسُها ... كما أَسْجَدَتْ نَصْرانَةٌ لم تَحَنَّفِ
(Both of them fell down and bowed their heads, as a Christian woman bows who has not become a ḥanīf.)
Al-Ṭabarī recited for naṣrān his saying:
515 - يَظَلُّ إذا دارَ العِشَا مُتَحَنِّفاً ... ويُضْحي لَدَيْه وهو نَصرْانُ شامِسُ
(When evening comes round he becomes a ḥanīf, and by forenoon he is with him a Christian worshipping the sun.)
Sībawayh said: "Except that it is not used in speech except with the yāʾ of relation." Al-Khalīl said: "The singular of al-naṣārā is naṣriyy, like mahriyy and mahārā." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The yāʾ in naṣrāniyy is for intensiveness, like the one in aḥmariyy." Naṣārā is indefinite, and for that reason al is added to it and it is qualified by an indefinite [adjective] in the poet's saying:
516 - صَدَّتْ كما صَدَّ عما لا يَحِلُّ له ... ساقي نصارى قُبَيْل الفِصْحِ صُوَّامِ
(She turned away, as the cupbearer of fasting Christians turns away, shortly before Easter, from what is not lawful for him.)
They were named thus by attribution to a village called Nāṣira (Nazareth), where Jesus, peace be upon him, used to stay; or because they used to help one another (yatanāṣarūn). The poet said:
517 - لَمَّا رأيتُ نَبَطاً أَنْصارا ... شَمَّرْتُ عن رُكْبَتيَ الإِزارا
كُنْتُ لهم من النَّصارى جَارا
(When I saw Nabataeans as helpers, I tucked my waist-wrapper up from my knees; I was to them a protector among the helpers.)
Al-ṣābiʾūn are a people who worshipped the angels; it has also been said: the stars. The majority pronounce it with hamza, and Nāfiʿ read it without hamza. Those who pronounce the hamza make it from صَبَأَ نابُ البعير, i.e. the camel's tooth came out, and صَبَأَتِ النجومُ, "the stars rose". Abū ʿAlī said: "صَبَأْتُ على القومِ means 'I came upon the people unexpectedly'; so the ṣābiʾ is the one who leaves his religion, like the ṣābiʾ who comes upon a people unexpectedly, for he has left his land and moved from it." Those who do not pronounce the hamza: two possibilities exist. The first: that it is taken from the hamzated [form], the hamza being replaced by a weak letter, either yāʾ or wāw, so it became of the category of the defective noun (manqūṣ) like qāḍin or ghāzin, the original being ṣābin; then it was pluralized as al-qāḍī or al-ghāzī is pluralized — except that Sībawayh does not consider changing this hamza [permissible] except in poetry, while al-Akhfash and Abū Zayd consider it [permissible] without restriction. The second: that it is from صَبَا يَصْبو, when one inclines; so al-ṣābī is like al-ghāzī, its original being ṣābiwun, and it underwent weak-letter change like ghāzin. Abū ʿUbayd related with a chain to Ibn ʿAbbās: "What is al-ṣābūn? It is only al-ṣābiʾūn. What is al-khāṭūn? It is only al-khāṭiʾūn." So the reading of Nāfiʿ combines pronouncing the hamza in al-nabiyyīn and omitting the hamza in al-ṣābiʾīn, and you have learned that the reverse is more eloquent in both.
He construed the pronoun in His saying {مَنْ آمَنَ وَعَمِلَ} according to the wording of «مَنْ», so He made it singular; and according to the meaning in His saying {فَلَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ}, so He made it plural, as in his saying:
518 - أَلِمَّا بسَلْمى عنكما إنْ عَرَضْتُما ... وقولا لها عُوجِي على مَنْ تَخَلَّفوا
(Visit Salmā briefly on my behalf if you pass by, and say to her: turn aside toward those who have stayed behind.)
So he observed the meaning. The verification of that has preceded at His saying: {وَمِنَ الناس مَن يَقُولُ آمَنَّا} [al-Baqara: 8].
Al-ajr is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun): one says أَجَرَهُ الله يأجِرُهُ أَجْراً. It may express the very thing with which one is recompensed, and the noble verse admits both meanings.
Abū al-Sammāl read {والذين هَادَوْا} with a fatḥa on the dāl, as though in his view it were from the mufāʿala [form], the original being «هادَيُوا», and it underwent weak-letter change like its counterparts.

semin-durr:63-63.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {فَوْقَكُمُ} is an adverb of place made accusative by «رَفعْنا». The rule of «فوق» is like the rule of «تحت», whose discussion has preceded. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is weak for it to be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «الطور», because the implied meaning would become: We raised the Mount high, and [this] is already understood from «رَفَعْنا»." This is open to question, because what is meant by it is a specific height, namely its being high above them, not height in general, such that it would become "We raised it high" as he supposed. He said: "And because the mountain was not above them at the time of raising; it only came to be above them by the raising." Someone might say: why can it not be an anticipated ḥāl (ḥāl muqaddara)? For he himself said of His saying «بقوة» that it is an anticipated ḥāl, as will come.
Al-ṭūr is a name for every mountain; it has also been said: for those that grow vegetation specifically, not those that do not. Is it Arabic or Syriac? There are two views. It has also been said: it was named after Ṭūr son of Ismāʿīl, peace be upon him. Al-ʿAjjāj said:
519 - داني جَنَاحَيْهِ من الطُّور فَمَرّْ ... تَقَضِّيَ البازي إذا البازي كَسَرْ
(Bringing his wings close, [he came] from the mountain and swept by, swooping as the falcon swoops when the falcon folds [its wings].)
His saying: «خُذُوا» is in the position of the accusative governed by an implied "saying", i.e. "and We said to them: take". This implied saying may be in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the fāʿil (agent) of «رَفَعْنا», the implied form being: "and We raised the Mount, saying to you: take". It has preceded, at His saying {وَكُلاَ مِنْهَا رَغَداً} [al-Baqara: 35], that «خُذْ» has its first radical (fāʾ) omitted and that the original is uʾkhudh.
His saying: {مَآ آتَيْنَاكُم} is the object of «خُذوا»; «ما» is a relative in the sense of «الذي», not an indefinite qualified noun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e. ما آتيناكموه.
His saying: «بقوةٍ» is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl. There are two views about the one it qualifies (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl). The first: that it is the agent of «خُذوا», and it is an anticipated ḥāl, the meaning being: take what We have given you while you are resolved on earnestness in acting upon it. The second: that it is that omitted returning pronoun, the implied form being: take what We have given you while it is held firmly, i.e. in acting upon it and striving to know it. In His saying «ما فيه» the pronoun refers to «ما آتيناكم». Al-tawallī ("turning away") is tafaʿʿul from al-waly; its basic meaning is turning away from a thing with the body, then it was used for turning away from matters and beliefs, by extension and figuratively. «ذلك» points to what preceded of the raising of the Mount and the giving of the Torah.

semin-durr:48-48.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {واتقوا يَوْماً}: «يوماً» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and an omitted muḍāf must be supposed, i.e. "the punishment of a day" or "the terror of a day". It has also been permitted to be accusative as an adverb (ẓarf), with the object omitted, its implied form being: "and guard against the punishment on a day whose description is such-and-such". Abū al-Baqāʾ forbade its being an adverb; he said: "because the command to guard (taqwā) does not take place on the Day of Resurrection." The answer to what he said is that the command is to beware of the causes leading to punishment on the Day of Resurrection. The origin of اتَّقُوا is اوْتَقُوا, and what was mentioned before at {تَتَّقُونَ} [al-Baqara: 22] was done to it.
His saying: {لاَّ تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍ}: the indefiniteness in «نفسٌ» and «شيئاً» means that no soul among souls will avail a soul like it in anything whatsoever; likewise in «شفاعةٌ» and «عدلٌ». The clause is in the position of the accusative as an adjective of «يوماً», and the referring pronoun is omitted, the implied form being: "in which (a soul) will not avail" (لا تَجْزي فيه); then the preposition and its genitive noun were omitted, because with adverbs a latitude is allowed that is not allowed with others. This is the doctrine of Sībawayh. It has also been said: rather it was omitted after the preposition [was dropped] and the verb reached it directly, giving «لا تَجْزيه», as in his saying:
435 - ويومٍ شَهِدْناه سُلَيْماً وعامِراً ... قليلٌ سوى الطَّعْنِ النِّهالِ نوافِلُهْ
(Many a day in which we witnessed Sulaym and ʿĀmir, whose spoils were few apart from thirst-quenching spear-thrusts.)
This is ascribed to al-Akhfash; however, al-Mahdawī transmitted that both of the aforementioned aspects are permissible according to Sībawayh, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj. The omission of the pronoun referring to the qualified noun when it is accusative is indicated by his saying:
436 - وما أَدْري: أَغَيَّرَهُمْ تَنَاءِ ... وطولُ العهدِ أم مالٌ أصابوا
(I do not know: has distance and long separation changed them, or wealth that they have acquired?)
i.e. "acquired it". According to the Kufans the implied form may be: "a day, the day when no soul will avail" (يوماً يومَ لا تَجْزي نفسٌ), so it becomes like His saying, Exalted is He: {يَوْمَ لاَ تَمْلِكُ نَفْسٌ} [al-Infiṭār: 19], the second "day" being a badal (substitute) of the first «يوماً»; then the muḍāf was omitted and the muḍāf ilayhi was put in its place, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {وَسْئَلِ القرية} [Yūsuf: 82]. On this view there is no need to suppose a referring pronoun, because when an adverb is annexed to the clause after it, no pronoun referring to it is brought in that clause except under poetic licence (ḍarūra), as in his saying:
437 - مَضَتْ مِئَةٌ لِعامَ وُلِدْتُ فيه ... وعَشْرٌ بعدَ ذاكَ وحِجَّتانِ
(A hundred years have passed since the year I was born in, and ten after that, and two years more.)
{عَن نَّفْسٍ} is attached to تَجْزي, so it is in the position of the accusative by it. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It may also be accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial)."
Al-jazāʾ: settling a debt and requiting. The poet said:
438 - يَجْزِيه ربُّ العرشِ عَنِّي إذْ جَزَى ... جناتِ عَدْنٍ في العَلالِيِّ العُلَى
(May the Lord of the Throne requite him on my behalf, when He requites, with the Gardens of Eden in the highest lofty chambers.)
Al-ijzāʾ: sufficing and being enough; أَجْزَأَني كذا: it sufficed me. He said:
439 - وأجْزَأْتَ أمرَ العالمينَ ولم يكُنْ ... لِيُجْزَأَ إلا كاملٌ وابنُ كاملِ
(You sufficed for the affairs of all people, and none could suffice for them but a perfect man, son of a perfect man.)
It has been said: أَجْزَأْتُ and جَزَأْتُ are close in meaning. And it has been said: al-jazāʾ and al-ijzāʾ have one meaning; you say from it: جَزَيْتُه and أَجْزَيْته. It has been read «تُجْزِئُ» with a ḍamma on the imperfect prefix, from أَجْزَأ. And جَزَأْتُ بكذا, i.e. I was content with it. The poet said:
440 - فإنَّ الغَدْرَ في الأقوام عارٌ ... وإنَّ الحُرَّ يَجْزَأُ بالكُراعِ
(Treachery among peoples is a disgrace, and the free man is content with a trotter.)
i.e. he is content with it.
His saying: «شيئاً» is accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun), i.e. "anything of requital", because requital is a thing; the general was put in place of the particular. It may also be a direct object on the basis that «تَجْزِي» is in the sense of «تَقْضي» (pays), i.e. "[a soul] will not pay on behalf of another anything of the dues". The first is more apparent.
His saying: {وَلاَ يُقْبَلُ مِنْهَا شَفَاعَةٌ}: this clause is conjoined to what precedes it, so it too is an adjective of «يوماً», and the pronoun referring from it to it is omitted, as has preceded, i.e. "and no intercession will be accepted from it on it". «شفاعةٌ» is an object whose agent is not named (i.e. a nāʾib fāʿil, deputy agent), and for that reason it is nominative. «يُقْبَل» has been read with the masculine and the feminine: the feminine for the wording, and the masculine because it is a figurative feminine, made good by the separation. It has also been read «ولا يَقْبل», active, the agent being Allah the Exalted, with «شفاعةً» in the accusative as a direct object. {لاَ يُؤْخَذُ مِنْهَا عَدْلٌ} is likewise an adjective, and the discussion of it is clear. «منها» is attached to «يُقْبل» and «يُؤْخذ». Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted it to be accusative as a ḥāl, because it is originally an adjective of شفاعة and عدل, and when it was put before them it became accusative as a ḥāl, being then attached to an omitted element. This is not clear, for the meaning is directed towards its being attached to the verb. The pronoun in «منها» refers to the second «نفس», because it is the nearest thing mentioned; it may refer to the first, because it is the one being spoken about; and the first pronoun may refer to the first, which is the soul that avails, and the second to the second, which is the one on whose behalf it would avail; and this is fitting.
Al-shafāʿa is derived from al-shafʿ, which is the pair; of it is al-shufʿa (pre-emption), because it is joining one property to another; and the intercessor and the one interceded for, because each of them pairs himself with the other. A shafūʿ she-camel is one that fills two milking-vessels in a single milking; and a shāfiʿ she-camel is one that has both a foetus and a young one following her. Al-ʿadl with fatḥa is ransom, and with kasra it is the like; one says ʿadl and ʿadīl. It has also been said: ʿadl with fatḥa is what equals a thing in value and amount, even if not of its kind, and with kasra what equals it in its kind and its bulk. Al-Ṭabarī related that some of the Arabs pronounce with kasra the one meaning ransom; the first is better known. As for ʿidl, the singular of al-aʿdāl (pack-loads), it is with kasra only.
His saying: {وَلاَ هُمْ يُنْصَرُونَ} is a clause of mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar (predicate), conjoined to what precedes it. The clause here was brought headed by the mubtadaʾ, with an imperfect verb as its predicate, only to draw attention to the intensity and emphasis in the absence of help. The pronoun in His saying «ولا هُمْ» refers to «النفس», because what is meant by it is the genus of souls; the pronoun refers to it in the masculine, even though «النفس» is feminine, only because what is meant by it is servants and human beings. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "as you say: three souls (ثلاثةُ أنفسٍ)", meaning when males are intended, as in his saying:
441 - ثلاثةُ أَنْفُسٍ وثلاثُ ذَوْدٍ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Three souls and three camels…)
But the grammarians stated explicitly that this is poetic licence; so it is preferable that it refer to the disbelievers whom the verse implies, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said.
Al-naṣr: help; al-anṣār: helpers; of this is: {مَنْ أنصاري إِلَى الله} [Āl ʿImrān: 52]. Al-naṣr is also taking revenge: انتصر زيد, i.e. he took revenge. Al-naṣr is also coming: نَصَرْتُ أرضَ بني فلان: I came to it. The poet said:
442 - إذا دَخَلَ الشهرُ الحرامُ فودِّعي ... بلاد تميمٍ وانصُري أرضَ عامرِ
(When the sacred month comes, bid farewell to the land of Tamīm and go to the land of ʿĀmir.)
It is also giving. The rajaz poet said:
443 - إني وأسطارٍ سُطِرْنَ سَطْراً ... لَقائِلٌ يا نصرُ نَصْرٌ نَصْرا
(By lines that have been written line by line, I say: O Naṣr, a gift, a gift!)
It is made transitive by «على»; He said: {فانصرنا عَلَى القوم الكافرين} [al-Baqara: 286]. As for His saying: {وَنَصَرْنَاهُ مِنَ القوم} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 77], it may be transitivity by «مِنْ», or it may be by implication of another meaning (taḍmīn), i.e. "We helped him by taking revenge for him on them".

semin-durr:106-106.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {مَا نَنسَخْ} . .: about «ما» there are two views. One — and it is the apparent one: that it is the fronted object of «نَنْسَخْ», and it is conditional, putting it in the jussive (majzūm); the implied form is: "whatever thing We abrogate", like His saying {أَيّاً مَّا تَدْعُواْ} [al-Isrāʾ: 110]. The second: that it is also conditional, putting «نَنْسَخْ» in the jussive, but it stands in the place of the maṣdar (verbal noun), and «مِنْ آيةٍ» is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), the implied form being: "whatever abrogation We abrogate a verse with"; Abū al-Baqāʾ and others said this. They said: the occurrence of «ما» as a maṣdar is permissible, and they recited:
671 - نَعَبَ الغرابُ فقلتُ: بَيْنٌ عاجِلُ ... ما شِئْتَ إذ ظَعَنُوا لِبَيْنٍ فانْعَبِ
(The crow croaked, and I said: a swift parting! Since they have set off for separation, croak as much as you like.)
Some rejected this view on two grounds. One: that it entails the apodosis clause being devoid of a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun, which is not permissible; the precise discussion of that has preceded at His saying: {مَن كَانَ عَدُوّاً لِّجِبْرِيلَ} [al-Baqara: 97]. The second: that «مِنْ» is not added in an affirmative context, and the condition is affirmative. On this there is the disagreement of some Basrans, who permitted its addition in a condition because it resembles negation; but it is a weak disagreement.
Ibn ʿĀmir read: «نُنْسِخْ» with ḍamma on the nūn and kasra on the sīn, from ansakha. Abū Ḥātim said: "It is an error" — and this is audacity on his part, as is his habit. Abū ʿAlī said: it is not a dialect form, because one does not say nasakha and ansakha in one sense; nor is it for transitivity, because the meaning would then come out [differently]; so it only remains that the meaning is: "whatever We find abrogated", as one says aḥmadtuhu and abkhaltuhu, i.e. I found him so. Then he said: "And We do not find it abrogated except by abrogating it, so the two readings agree in meaning even though they differ in wording." So according to him the hamza is not for transitivity. Al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya made the hamza for transitivity, but they differed in supposing the omitted first object and in the meaning of al-insākh. Al-Zamakhsharī made the omitted object Gabriel, peace be upon him, and al-insākh the command to abrogate it, i.e. informing of it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya made the object the pronoun of the Prophet, upon him be peace, and al-insākh the permitting of abrogation to His Prophet — as though, when He abrogated it, He permitted him to abandon it, and He called that permission insākh.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya derived the reading, with the hamza for transitivity, from another angle: from naskh al-kitāb, which is copying it without removing it. He said: "The meaning is: whatever We write and send down from the Preserved Tablet, or whatever We postpone in it and leave, not sending it down — whichever of that We do, We only bring something better than the postponed, left one, or something like it. So the two pronouns in «منها» and «بمثلها» come referring to the pronoun in «نَنْسَأْها»." The Shaykh said: "He overlooked the rule that there must be a pronoun referring from the apodosis to the conditional noun; and «ما» in His saying «ما نَنْسَخْ» is conditional, and His saying «أو نَنْسَأْها» refers to the verse, though in meaning it does not refer to it in both wording and meaning, but only in wording, as in «عندي درهمٌ ونصفُه» ("I have a dirham and half of it"); so it is really on the supposition of the conditional «ما», the implied form being: "or whatever verse We postpone", necessarily, since the abrogated is other than the postponed. But then His saying «مَا نَنْسَخْ من آيةٍ» remains cut loose from the apodosis, since there is no linking element referring from it to it; so this meaning which he stated is invalid."
His saying: {مِنْ آيَةٍ}: «مِنْ» is partitive, so it is attached to something omitted, because it is a naʿt (adjective) of the conditional noun; making it a ḥāl (circumstantial) is weak. The meaning is: "whatever thing of the verses We abrogate", so «آية» is a singular standing in the place of the plural. Likewise is the derivation of everything that comes in this construction: {مَّا يَفْتَحِ الله لِلنَّاسِ مِن رَّحْمَةٍ} [Fāṭir: 2], {وَمَا بِكُم مِّن نِّعْمَةٍ فَمِنَ الله}. This genitive noun is what specifies and explains the conditional noun; that is because there is vagueness in it on account of its generality. Do you not see that if you said «مَنْ يُكْرِمْ أُكْرِمْ» ("whoever honours, I honour") [Translator's note: the source has the typo «يُكْرشمْ»], it would cover women and men, and if you said «مِن الرجالِ» ("of the men"), you would explain and specify what the conditional noun covers?
Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted two other aspects for it. One: that it is in the position of the accusative as a tamyīz (specification), the thing specified being «ما», the implied form being "whatever thing We abrogate". He said: "It is not good to suppose 'whatever verse We abrogate', because you do not combine «آية» and what is specified by «آية»; you do not say: 'whatever verse We abrogate, of verse'" — meaning that if you supposed that, you would dispense with the tamyīz. The second: that it is redundant (zāʾida) and «آية» is a ḥāl, the meaning being "whatever thing We abrogate, little or much"; «آية» has come as a ḥāl in His saying: {هذه نَاقَةُ الله لَكُمْ آيَةً} [al-Aʿrāf: 73], i.e. "as a sign". This is corrupt, because a ḥāl is not put in the genitive by «مِنْ». It has preceded that it is a direct object with «مِنْ» redundant, on the view that makes «ما» stand in the place of the maṣdar. So these are four aspects.
His saying: {أَوْ نُنسِهَا}: «أو» here is for division, and «نُنْسِها» is jussive, conjoined (maʿṭūf) to the verb of the condition before it. There are thirteen readings of it. [First:] «نَنْسَأها» with fatḥa on the imperfect prefix, sukūn on the nūn and fatḥa on the sīn, with hamza; Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read with it. The second: the same but without hamza; Abū ʿUbayd al-Bakrī mentioned it from Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "I think he erred." The third: «تَنْسَها» with fatḥa on the tāʾ of address, followed by a vowelless nūn and a sīn with fatḥa, without hamza; it is the reading of al-Ḥasan and is related from Ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. It was said to Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ: "Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab reads it with a first nūn with ḍamma and a sīn with kasra", and he said: "The Qurʾān was not sent down upon al-Musayyab nor upon Ibn al-Musayyab", and he recited: {سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلاَ تنسى} [al-Aʿlā: 6], {واذكر رَّبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ} [al-Kahf: 24] — Saʿd meaning by that that the attribution of forgetting to him, upon him be peace, is present in the Book of Allah, so this is like it.
The fourth: the same but with hamza. The fifth: the same but with ḍamma on the tāʾ; it is the reading of Abū Ḥaywa. The sixth: the same but without hamza; it is the reading of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab. The seventh: «نُنْسِها» with ḍamma on the imperfect prefix, sukūn on the nūn and kasra on the sīn, without hamza; it is the reading of the rest of the Seven. The eighth: the same but with hamza. The ninth: «نُنَسِّها» with ḍamma on the imperfect prefix, fatḥa on the nūn and a doubled sīn with kasra; it is the reading of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Abū Rajāʾ. The tenth: «نُنْسِكَ» with ḍamma on the imperfect prefix, sukūn on the nūn, kasra on the sīn and a kāf of address after it. The eleventh: the same but with fatḥa on the second nūn and a doubled sīn with kasra [نُنَسِّكَ]; it is also related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Abū Rajāʾ. The twelfth: the same but with the pronoun of the verse added after the kāf: «نُنَسِّكَها»; it is the reading of Ḥudhayfa, and so it is in the codex of Sālim, his client. The thirteenth: «ما نُنْسِكَ من آيةٍ أو نَنْسَخْها نَجِىءْ بمثلِها»; it is the reading of al-Aʿmash, and so it is established in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh.
As for the reading with hamza, in its various forms, its meaning is deferment, from their saying: nasaʾa Allāhu and ansaʾa Allāhu fī ajalika, i.e. He deferred it; and biʿtuhu nasīʾatan, i.e. deferred [on credit]. The Arabs say: nasaʾtu al-ibila ʿan al-ḥawḍ, ansaʾuhā nasʾan; and ansaʾa al-ibila: when he defers them from coming to water for two days or more. So on this view there are three views on the meaning of the verse. One: We defer its abrogation and its descent; this is the view of ʿAṭāʾ. The second: We erase it in wording and ruling; this is the view of Ibn Zayd. The third: We let it stand and do not abrogate it; this is the view of Abū ʿUbayd, and it is weak because of His saying «نَأْتِ بخيرٍ منها», since of what is let stand and confirmed one does not say: "We bring something better than it".
As for the reading without hamza, also in its various forms, it bears two possibilities. The more apparent: that it is from forgetting; then what is meant by it may, in some readings, be the opposite of remembering, and in some, abandoning. The second: that its origin is with hamza, from al-nasʾ, which is deferment, except that the hamza was replaced by an alif; then the two readings become one. Then, those of the readers who read «نَنْساها» from the triliteral — that is clear. As for those of them who read from afʿala — Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and the Kufans — its meaning according to them is: «نُنْسِكَها», i.e. We make you forget it; or the meaning is: We command its abandonment; one says: ansaytuhu al-shayʾa, i.e. I commanded him to abandon it, and nasītuhu: I abandoned it. They recited:
672 - إنَّ عليَّ عُقْبَةً أَقْضِيها ... لستُ بِناسِيها ولا مُنْسِيها
(I owe a turn which I shall pay off; I neither abandon it nor bid it be abandoned.)
i.e. neither abandoning it nor commanding its abandonment. Al-Zajjāj spoke about this reading and said: "In this reading the meaning of abandoning is not tenable; one does not say ansā in the sense of taraka (abandoned)." Al-Fārisī and others said: "That is tenable, because it is in the sense of: We make you abandon it." Al-Zajjāj also judged weak taking the verse in the sense of forgetting as the opposite of remembering, and said: "This did not happen to him, upon him be peace, nor did he forget any Qurʾān", and he adduced His saying, Exalted is He: {وَلَئِن شِئْنَا لَنَذْهَبَنَّ بالذي أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ} [al-Isrāʾ: 86], i.e. We did not do any of that. Al-Fārisī answered him that its meaning is: We did not take away all of it. This is the furthest of what I have come upon in people's discussion.
His saying: «نَأْت» is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) of the condition. The verb of the condition and of the apodosis came as two imperfects, and this construction is the most eloquent of constructions — I mean their coming as two imperfects. His saying «بخيرٍ منها» is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «نَأْتِ». About «خير» here there are two views. The apparent one of them: that it is in its proper sense, as an elative; that is, if what is brought is lighter than the abrogated or the deferred, its being better is in relation to the dropping of the burdens of obligation; and if it is heavier, its being better is in relation to the increase of reward. And His saying «أو مثلِها», i.e. in obligation and reward; this is clear. The second: that «خيراً» here is a maṣdar and has nothing to do with the elative; it is only a good among goods, like «خير» in His saying {أَن يُنَزَّلَ عَلَيْكُمْ مِّنْ خَيْرٍ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ} [al-Baqara: 105]; «مِنْ» is for the beginning of the extent, and the preposition and its genitive noun are a naʿt of His saying «خير», i.e. "a good issuing from its side". The meaning according to these is: whatever verse We abrogate or defer, We bring a good among goods from the side of the abrogated or deferred. This is very far-fetched because of His saying after that «أو مثلِها», for its conjunction to «بخير» is not valid on this meaning — unless by "good" is intended the absence of obligation, so that the meaning would be: We bring a good among goods, namely the absence of obligation, or We bring the like of the abrogated or deferred. As for conjoining «مثلِها» to the pronoun in «منها», it is not permissible except according to the Kufans, because the genitive governor is not repeated. His saying «ما نَنْسَخْ» contains a shift (iltifāt) from the third person to the first person; do you not see that before it is «واللهُ يَخْتَصُّ» and {والله ذُو الفضل}?
Al-naskh lexically is removal without a substitute that follows it — the wind effaced (nasakhat) the trace, and the sun the shade — or transferring a thing without removal, [as in:] nasakhtu al-kitāb (I copied the book). One of them said: "Al-naskh is removal, and it is lexically of two kinds: a kind in which there is removal of a thing and the setting up of another in its place, as in 'the sun effaced the shade', for it removed it and stood in its place, and from this is {مَا نَنسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ}; and the second, that it removes it and nothing stands in its place, as in 'the wind effaced the trace', and from this is «فَيَنْسَخُ اللهُ ما يُلْقي الشيطانُ»." Al-nasīʾa is deferment, as preceded; and also letting go forward [driving on]; [the poet] said:
673 - أَمُونٍ كأَلْواحِ الإرانِ نَسَأْتُها ... على لاحِبٍ كأنَّه ظَهْرُ بُرْجُدٍ
(A trusty she-camel, like the planks of a bier, which I drove on along a beaten track like the back of a striped cloak.)

semin-durr:126-126.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {اجعل هذا بَلَداً آمِناً}: «الجَعْل» here means "rendering", so it is transitive to two objects: «هذا» is the first object and «بلداً» the second. The meaning is: make this town, or this place [secure]. «آمناً» is an adjective, i.e. "possessing security", as in «عيشةٌ راضيةٌ» (a pleasing life), or "secure are those in it", as in «ليلةٌ نائمٌ» (a night that sleeps, i.e. in which one sleeps). «البلد» is well known, and concerning its naming there are two views. The first: it is taken from «البَلْد», and «البَلْد» is originally the chest; one says وضَعَتِ الناقةُ بَلْدَتها, when the she-camel kneels, i.e. [puts down] her chest; and the town (al-balad) is the chest of the settlements, so it was named thus. The second: «البلد» is originally a trace (athar); from it is «رجلٌ بَليد» (a dull man), because of the trace ignorance leaves in him; and the camel's kneeling-place is called «بَلْدَة» because of the trace it leaves in the ground when it kneels. [The poet] said:
719 - أُنِيخَتْ فأَلْقَتْ بَلْدَةً فوق بلْدةٍ ... قليلٌ بها الأصواتُ إلاَّ بُغامُها
(She was made to kneel, and laid her chest upon a [desolate] land where voices are few, save her own soft grunting.)
His words: {مَنْ آمَنَ}: a badal (substitute) of part from whole, namely from «أهلَه»; for that reason a pronoun in it refers back to that from which it is substituted. «مِنْ» in «مِن الثمرات» is partitive. It has been said: it is explicative (bayān); this is worthless, since nothing vague has preceded to be explained by it.
His words: {وَمَن كَفَرَ فَأُمَتِّعُهُ}: three aspects are permissible in «مَنْ». The first: it is relative, and in that case there are two aspects regarding its position. The first: it is in the position of the accusative by an omitted verb, the implied form being: "Allah said: and I will provide for whoever disbelieves", and «فأمتِّعُه» is conjoined to this implied verb. The second of the two aspects: it is in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and «فأمتِّعُه» is the khabar (predicate); the fāʾ entered the khabar by likening it to the condition. It will come that Abū al-Baqāʾ forbids this, and the reply to him. The second of the three aspects: it is an indefinite qualified noun (nakira mawṣūfa); Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned it, and its ruling is what has been said about its being in the position of the accusative or the nominative. The third: it is conditional, and its position is only the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, with «فأمتِّعُه» as the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ).
In none of its aspects may «مَنْ» be accusative by preoccupation (ishtighāl). When it is conditional, that is clear, because what explains the governor of a conditional noun is the verb of the condition, not the consequence, and the verb of the condition here does not put its pronoun in the accusative but rather in the nominative. When it is relative, [it is not permissible] because the khabar, «فأمتِّعه», resembles the consequence, which is why the fāʾ entered it; and just as the consequence does not explain a governor, what resembles it is all the more so. Likewise when it is a qualified indefinite, for the adjective does not explain [a governor]. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "«مَنْ» may not be a mubtadaʾ with «فأمتِّعُه» as the khabar, because the fāʾ does not enter the khabar of «الذي» unless the khabar is merited by the ṣila (relative clause), as in «الذي يأتيني فله درهمٌ» (whoever comes to me shall have a dirham); and enjoyment is not merited by disbelief. If you make the fāʾ redundant, on the view of al-Akhfash, it is permissible; or if [you make] the khabar omitted with «فأمتِّعُه» as evidence for it, it is permissible, the implied form being: 'and whoever disbelieves, I will provide for him, and I will let him enjoy'.
«مَنْ» may be conditional with the fāʾ as its apodosis. It has been said: the apodosis is omitted, the implied form being: 'and whoever disbelieves, I will provide [for him]'; on this «مَنْ» is nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and it may not be accusative, because a conditional particle is not governed by its apodosis but by the verb of the condition." End of quote.
As for his saying "because enjoyment is not merited by disbelief", it is not conceded; rather, the brief enjoyment and the destination of the Fire are both merited by disbelief. Also, even if we concede that enjoyment is not merited by disbelief, something merited by it has been conjoined to it, namely the destination of the Fire, so it was fitting that both occur together as the khabar. Also, he contradicted his own words, since he allowed it to be conditional — and is the consequence anything but merited by the condition and following from it? So likewise the khabar that is likened to it. As for his allowing the fāʾ to be redundant and the omission of the khabar or of the apodosis, these are far-fetched aspects with no need for them. It was read «أُمْتِعُه» without shadda, from أَمْتَع يُمْتِعُ, and this is the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir; and «فَأُمْتِعْه» with the final radical quiescent [Translator's note: the source prints «فَأُمْتِعُّه», which appears corrupt], and there are two aspects in it. The first: it is a lightening, as in the poet's saying:
720 - فاليومَ أشربْ غيرَ مُسْتَحْقِبٍ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(So today I drink, not burdening myself [with sin]…)
The second: the fāʾ is redundant and it is the apodosis, so it is made jussive with sukūn. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid read {فَأُمَتِّعُهُ قَلِيلاً ثُمَّ أَضْطَرُّهُ} in the imperative form in both [Translator's note: i.e. فأمْتِعْه … ثم اضْطَرَّه, as an address by Abraham; the source prints the verse in the majority wording], and its justification is that the pronoun in «قال» is for Abraham, i.e. he asked his Lord for that. On this reading «مَنْ» may be a mubtadaʾ, or accusative by preoccupation with an implied verb, whether you make it relative or conditional; except that if you make it conditional, you imply the verb that puts it in the accusative after it, because a conditional particle has the head of the sentence.
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "{وَمَن كَفَرَ} is conjoined to «مَنْ آمَنَ», just as «ومِنْ ذريتي» was conjoined to the kāf in «جاعِلُك»." The Shaykh said: "As for conjoining «مَنْ كَفَر» to «من آمَنَ», it is not sound, because it conflicts with the construction of the speech, since the meaning would become: 'Abraham said: and provide for whoever disbelieves', because it is not conjoined to it unless it shares its governor, and what governs «من آمن» is the imperative verb, and it is what governs «ومَنْ كفر». If you take it as an imperative, it conflicts with His words «فَأُمَتِّعه», because the apparent sense of this is a statement from Allah ascribing the enjoyment and compelling them to Himself the Exalted, and each of the two verbs includes a pronoun. That is not permissible except far-fetchedly, by there being after the fāʾ an omitted saying containing the pronoun of Allah the Exalted, i.e. 'Abraham said: and provide for whoever disbelieves; and Allah said: I will let him enjoy a little, then compel him'. Then al-Zamakhsharī contradicted this saying of his — that it is conjoined to «مَنْ» just as «ومِنْ ذرِّيتي» was conjoined to the kāf in «جاعِلك» — by saying: 'If you say: why did Abraham single out the believers, so that He corrected him? I say: he drew an analogy between provision and leadership, so He made known to him the difference between them, in that leadership does not belong to the wrongdoer, whereas provision may be a gradual luring [to ruin]; and the meaning is: He said: and I will provide for whoever disbelieves, and I will let him enjoy.' The apparent sense of his saying 'and the meaning is: He said' is that the pronoun in «قال» is for Allah the Exalted, and that «مَنْ كَفَرَ» is accusative by the imperfect verb ascribed to the pronoun of the speaker."
«قليلاً» is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun) or [adverb of] time; its parallels and Sībawayh's preference concerning it have been given.
The majority read «أضطَرُّه» as a statement. Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read «إضطرُّه» with kasra on the hamza; its justification is giving kasra to the prefix of the imperfect, as in their saying إخالُ for أخال. Ibn Muḥayṣin read «أطَّرُّه», assimilating the ḍād into the ṭāʾ, as in اطّجع for اضطجع; this is rejected, because the ḍād is one of the five letters into which [others] are assimilated but which are not themselves assimilated into others, namely the letters «ضم شغر», as in اطَّجع for اضطجع. [Translator's note: the source repeats this sentence verbatim twice; it is translated once.] [Al-Zamakhsharī said this, and it is open to question, for these letters have been assimilated into others: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī [Translator's note: so in the source; the reader who assimilates in these places is Abū ʿAmr (ibn al-ʿAlāʾ), not al-Dānī] assimilated the lām in {يَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ} [Nūḥ: 4] [Translator's note: the assimilated letter there is the rāʾ into the lām], the ḍād into the shīn in {لِبَعْضِ شَأْنِهِمْ} [al-Nūr: 62], and the shīn into the sīn in {العرش سَبِيلاً} [al-Isrāʾ: 42]; al-Kisāʾī assimilated the fāʾ into the bāʾ in {نَخْسِفْ بِهِمُ الأرض} [Sabaʾ: 9]; and Sībawayh related that «مُضَّجعاً» is more frequent, which shows that «مُطَّجعاً» is frequent [too].] Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb read «أضطُّرُّه» with ḍamma on the ṭāʾ, as though for vowel harmony (itbāʿ). Ubayy read «فَنُمَتِّعُه ثم نَضَطَرُه» with nūn.
«اضْطَرَّ» is افتعَل from الضُرّ (harm); its origin is اضْتَرَّ, and the tāʾ was replaced with ṭāʾ, because the tāʾ of iftiʿāl is replaced with ṭāʾ after the emphatic (iṭbāq) letters. It is transitive, and the Revelation came accordingly. [The poet] said:
721 - اضطَرَّكَ الحِرْرُ مِنْ سَلْمى إِلى أَجَأٍ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Vigilance [for your safety] drove you from Salmā to Ajaʾ…) [Translator's note: the source prints «الحِرْرُ»; the word is usually «الحِرْزُ» (refuge, safekeeping).]
«الاضطرار» is compelling and forcing toward a disliked matter.
His words: «وبئس المصيرُ»: «المصير» is the fāʿil (agent), and what is specified for blame (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, i.e. the Fire. «مصير» is مَفْعِل from صار يصير; it is fit for time and place. As for the maṣdar, its regular form is with fatḥa, because for a verb whose imperfect has kasra on the middle radical, the regular form of its adverbs [of time and place] is kasra and of its maṣdar fatḥa. But the grammarians differed concerning verbs whose middle radical is yāʾ, on three positions. The first: it is like the sound verb, as has been said. The second: there is a choice in it. The third: [Translator's note: the source repeats the words "positions. The first: it is like the sound verb, as has been said. The second: there is a choice in it. The third:" a second time here] what is heard is followed, so what was heard with kasra or fatḥa is not extended. If «المصير» in the verse is a noun of place, it is regular by agreement, and the implied form is "and wretched is the destination: the Fire", as has been said; if it is a maṣdar, on the view of whoever allows that, the implied form is "and wretched is the becoming: their becoming [destined] to the Fire".

semin-durr:164-164.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {الليل والنهار}: as for «الليل», it is said that it is a generic noun (ism jins), its singular and collective being distinguished by the feminine tāʾ, so one says «ليلة» and «ليل», like «تمرة» and «تمر». The correct view is that it is singular and no plural of it is recorded; for that reason people judged wrong whoever claimed that «الليالي» is the plural of «ليل». Rather «الليالي» is the plural of «لَيْلة», and it is an unusual plural; for that reason they said it is the plural of a supposed «ليلاة», and this singular has been stated explicitly in the poet's saying:
785 - في كلِّ يوم وبكلِّ ليلاهْ ...
(On every day and in every night…)
This is also indicated by their diminutive of it as «لُيَيْلَة». A parallel to «ليلة» and «ليال» is «كَيْكة» and «كَيَاك», as though they imagined it was originally «كَيْكات»; «الكيكة» is the egg.

As for «النهار», al-Rāghib said: "In the Sharīʿa it is for what lies between the rising of the dawn and the setting of the sun," while the apparent sense in the language is that it begins from the time of the brightening of morning. Thaʿlab and al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "It is from the rising of the sun"; al-Naḍr added: "and nothing before that is counted as part of the day." Al-Zajjāj said: "The beginning of the day is the shining forth of the sun." It is pluralised as «نُهُر» and «أَنْهِرَة», like «قَذَال», «قُذُل» and «أَقْذِلة». It is also said: "It is not pluralised, because it is on a par with the maṣdar (verbal noun)"; but the correct view is that it is pluralised as given above. [The poet] said:
786 - لولا الثَّريدان لَمُتْنا بالضُّمُرْ ... ثريدُ ليلٍ وثريدٌ بالنُّهُرْ
(Were it not for the two tharīds we would have died of leanness: a tharīd by night and a tharīd by the days.)
The derivation of this root has already been given, and that it indicates breadth — «النهار» comes from it because of the breadth of its light — at His saying {مِن تَحْتِهَا الأنهار} [al-Baqara: 25].

«الاختلاف» is a maṣdar annexed to its agent. What is meant by their alternation is that each one succeeds [the other]; from this is: {جَعَلَ الليل والنهار خِلْفَةً} [al-Furqān: 62]. Zuhayr said:
787 - بِها العِيْنُ والآرامُ يَمْشِيْنَ خِلْفَةً ... وأَطْلاؤُها يَنْهَضْنَ مِنْ كلِّ مَجْثَمِ
(In it the wild cows and white gazelles walk one after another, and their young rise from every resting place.)
And another said:
788 - ولها بالماطِرُون إذا ... أَكَلَ النملُ الذي جَمَعا
خِلْفَةٌ حتى إذا ارتَبَعَتْ ... سَكَنَتْ من جِلَّقٍ بِيَعَا
(She has, at al-Māṭirūn, when the ants eat what they have gathered, an alternating abode; then when she enters spring she dwells among the churches of Jilliq [Damascus].)

He put the night before the day because it precedes it. The Exalted said: {وَآيَةٌ لَّهُمُ الليل نَسْلَخُ مِنْهُ النهار} [Yā Sīn: 37]. This is the more correct of two views; it is also said that light precedes darkness. A useful consequence rests on this disagreement: does the night belong to the day before it or to the day after it? On the correct view the night belongs to the day after it, so the day is subordinate to it. On the second view it belongs to the day before it, so the night is subordinate to it. The Day of ʿArafa, on the first view, is an exception to the rule, since it is followed by the night after it; on the second it comes according to the rule.

His saying: {والفلك}: conjoined (maʿṭūf) to «خَلْقِ», which is put in the genitive by «في», not to «السماواتِ», which is genitive by annexation. «الفُلْك» [may be singular, as in His saying: {فِي الفلك المشحون} [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 119], or plural], as in His saying: {فِي الفلك وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم} [Yūnus: 22]. When the plural is meant by it, there are several views. One of them is the view of Sībawayh — and it is the correct one — "that it is a broken plural (jamʿ taksīr)". If it is said: a broken plural must involve some change, the answer is that its change is implied: the ḍamma when it is plural is like the ḍamma in «حُمُر» and «نُدُب», and when it is singular it is like the ḍamma in «قُفْل». What led Sībawayh to this, rather than making it shared between singular and plural like «جُنُب» and «شُلُل», is that had they intended sharing they would not have put it in the dual, just as they do not put «جُنُب» and «شُلُل» in the dual; when they put it in the dual and said «فُلْكان», we knew that they did not intend the sharing they intended in «جُنُب» and «شُلُل». Its parallel is «ناقةٌ هِجان» and «نوقٌ هِجان» (a pure-white she-camel / pure-white she-camels), and «دِرْع دِلاص» and «دُروع دِلاص» (a smooth coat of mail / smooth coats of mail): the kasra in the singular is like the kasra in «كتاب», and in the plural like the kasra in «رجال», because they said in the dual «هِجانان» and «دِلاصان».

The second: the doctrine of al-Akhfash, that it is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) like «صَحْب» and «رَكْب». The third: that it is the plural of «فَلَك» with two fatḥas, like «أَسَد» and «أُسْد». The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] chose that it is shared between singular and plural; he is refuted by the dual mentioned above, and he gave no reason for his choice.

When «فُلْك» is singular it is masculine; the Exalted said: {فِي الفلك المشحون}. They said — Abū al-Baqāʾ among them —: it may also be feminine, adducing His saying: {والفلك التي تَجْرِي}, where He described it with a feminine attribute. There is no proof in that, since the plural may be meant by it, and then it is described with what a single feminine noun is described with. Its origin is from turning round; from it are «فَلَك السماء» (the celestial sphere), because the stars revolve in it, «فَلْكَة المِغْزَل» (the whorl of the spindle), and «فَلَكَتِ الجاريةُ», [said when] the girl's breast became rounded. He gave the ṣila (relative clause) of «التي» as an imperfect verb to indicate renewal and occurrence. Attributing running to them [the ships] is figurative (majāz). His saying «في البحر» is emphasis, since it is known that they do not run anywhere else; it is like His saying: {يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيْهِ} [al-Anʿām: 38].

His saying: «بما يَنْفَعُ»: there are two views on «ما». One: that it is a nominal relative; on this the bāʾ is for the ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e.: they run accompanied by the goods that benefit people. The second: that it is a particle [maṣdariyya]; on this the bāʾ is causal, i.e.: they run because of people's benefit in trade and other things.

His saying: {مِنَ السمآء مِن مَّآءٍ}: the first «مِنْ» means the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), i.e.: He sent down from the direction of the sky. As for the second, it admits three views. The first: that it is for explaining the genus (bayān al-jins), for what is sent down from the sky is water and other things. The second: that it is partitive, for what is sent down of it is a part, not the whole. The third: that it and what follows it are a badal (substitute) from His saying «من السماء», a badal of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) with the governor repeated. Both of them — I mean the first «مِنْ» and the second — are attached to «أَنْزَلَ». If it is said: how can two identical particles be attached to a single governor? The answer is that what is disallowed is for them to be identical in meaning without conjunction or badal; you do not say «أخذت من الدراهم من الدنانير». As for the verse, the objection does not apply to it: if you make the second «مِنْ» explicative or partitive, it is clear, because their meanings differ, the first being for the beginning; and if you make it for the beginning of the extent, it and what follows it are a badal, and that is permissible [in] the badal, as stated. It is also possible for the first «مِنْ» to be attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl: either from the relative noun itself, namely «ما», or from its pronoun made accusative by «أنزل», i.e.: and what Allah sent down while it is from the sky.

His saying: {فَأَحْيَا بِهِ}: He conjoined «أحيا» to «أنزل», which is the ṣila, with the fāʾ of immediate sequence, to indicate the speed of growth. «به» is attached to «أحيا»; the bāʾ may be causal or the bāʾ of the instrument, and all of this is figurative, for He is exalted above that. The pronoun in «به» refers back to the relative noun.

His saying: {وَبَثَّ فِيهَا}: «بَثَّ» admits two views. The more evident of them: that it is conjoined to «أنزل», falling under the scope of the ṣila, because His saying «فَأَحْيا» is conjoined to «أنزل» and so joined to it, and the two together became like a single thing; it is as though it were said: "and what He sent down in the earth of water and spread in it of every creature", because they grow through fertility and live through the rain. This is the text of al-Zamakhsharī. The second: that it is conjoined to «أحيا».

The Shaykh found its conjunction to that problematic, because it is part of the ṣila of the relative noun, so there must be a pronoun returning from this clause, and there is no pronoun in the wording, since «فيها» refers back to the earth; it remains that it be omitted, its implied form being «وبث به فيها». But a pronoun put in the genitive by a preposition may not be omitted except under conditions: that the relative noun be put in the genitive by the same preposition, that what they are attached to be the same, that the pronoun not be restricted, that it be the only possible link, and that the prepositional phrase not stand in place of a nominative; and the relative noun here is not in the genitive at all. When he found this problematic for the reason he mentioned, he explained the verse as involving the omission of a nominal relative. He said: "That is permissible and widespread in their speech, though the Basrans do not permit it." He cited as evidence for it:
789 - ما الذي دأبُه احتياطَ وحَزْمٌ ... وهواه أطاع يَسْتويانِ
(He whose habit is caution and resolve, and [he who] obeyed his whim, are not equal.)
i.e. "and he who obeyed"; and his saying:
790 - أَمَنْ يهجو رسولَ الله منكم ... ويمدَحُه ويَنْصُره سَواءُ
(Is he among you who satirises the Messenger of Allah, and [he who] praises and supports him, equal?)
i.e. "and he who supports him"; and his saying:
791 - فواللهِ ما نِلْتُمْ وما نِيلَ منكمُ ... بمعتدلٍ وَفْقٍ ولا متقاربِ
(By Allah, what you obtained and what was obtained from you are not balanced and even, nor close.)
i.e. "what is it that you obtained"; and His saying, the Exalted: {وقولوا آمَنَّا بالذي أُنزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَأُنزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ} [al-ʿAnkabūt: 46], i.e. "and in what was sent down to you", so that it matches His saying: {والكتاب الذي نَزَّلَ على رَسُولِهِ والكتاب الذي أَنَزلَ مِن قَبْلُ} [al-Nisāʾ: 136]. Then the Shaykh said: "The first assumption may also work" — meaning the permissibility of the omission even though its condition is not met. He said: "That has occurred in their poetry", and he recited:
792 - وإنَّ لساني شُهْدَةٌ يُشْتَفَى بها ... وهُوَّ على مَنْ صَبَّه اللهُ عَلْقَمُ
(My tongue is a honeycomb by which one is healed, but it is colocynth to the one upon whom Allah pours it.)
i.e. colocynth to him; and his saying:
793 - لعلَّ الذي أَصْعَدْتِني أَنْ يَرُدَّني ... إلى الأرض إن لم يَقْدِرِ الخيرَ قِادرُه
(Perhaps that by which you raised me up will bring me back down to the earth, if the One who decrees does not decree good.)
i.e. "you raised me up by it".

His saying: {مِن كُلِّ دَآبَّةٍ}: «كل» admits three views. One: that it is in the position of the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of «بثَّ», with «مِنْ» partitive. The second: that «مِنْ» is redundant (zāʾida) according to the doctrine of al-Akhfash, and «كلَّ دابة» is likewise the mafʿūl bihi of «بَثَّ». The third: that it is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the omitted object of «بَثَّ», if we say that there is an omitted relative noun there, its implied form being: and what He spread, being of every creature. «مِنْ» then admits two views: one, that it is explicative; the second, that it is partitive. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "The object of «بَثَّ» is omitted, its implied form being: and He spread in it creatures, every creature." The apparent sense of this is that {مِن كُلِّ دَآبَّةٍ} is a naʿt (adjective) of that omitted [noun], and it is an assumption that yields nothing.

«البَثُّ» is spreading and scattering. [The poet] said:
794 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وفي الأرضِ مَبْثُوثاً شجاعٌ وعَقْربُ
(…and in the earth, spread about, are serpent and scorpion.)
Its imperfect is «يَبُثُّ» with ḍamma on the middle radical, which is the analogical rule for transitive doubled verbs; the kasra has occurred in a few words: they said «نَمَّ الحديثَ يَنِمُّه» (he carried tales) with both [vowels].

«الدابَّة» is a name for every animal. Some claimed that birds are excluded from it, and this was rejected by the saying of ʿAlqama:
795 - كأنَّهم صابَتْ عليهم سَحابةٌ ... صواعِقُها لطيرِهِنَّ دَبيبُ
(As though a cloud had poured upon them, whose thunderbolts make their birds creep.)
and by the saying of al-Aʿshā:
796 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... دبيبَ قَطا البَطْحَاءِ في كلِّ مَنْهَلِ
(…like the creeping of the sandgrouse of the valley-bed to every watering place.)
and by His saying: {والله خَلَقَ كُلَّ دَآبَّةٍ} [al-Nūr: 45], after which He detailed [them] with those that walk on two legs, which are humans and birds.

His saying: {وَتَصْرِيفِ الرياح}: «تصريف» is the maṣdar of «صَرَّف», which is turning back and turning about. It may be annexed to its agent, with the object omitted, its implied form being: and the winds' driving of the clouds, for they drive the clouds; or annexed to its object, with the agent omitted, i.e.: and Allah's directing of the wind. «الرياح» is the broken plural of «ريح». The yāʾ of «الريح» and «الرياح» derives from a wāw; the original is «رِوْح», because it is from «راح يروح». It was changed in «ريح» because it is quiescent and what precedes it has kasra, and in «رياح» because it is a middle radical in a plural after a kasra, followed by an alif, and it is quiescent in the singular; this is a regular substitution. For that reason, when the cause of its change was removed, it returned to its origin, and they said «أَرْواح». [The poet] said:
797 - أَرَبَّتْ بها الأرواحُ كلَّ عَشِيَّةٍ ... فلم يَبْقَ إلاَّ آلُ خَيْمٍ مُنَضَّدِ
(The winds kept at it every evening, until nothing remained but the poles of tents piled up.)
And similar to it:
798 - لَبَيْتٌ تَخْفُقُ الأرواحُ فيه ... أَحَبُّ إليَّ من قصرٍ مُنيفِ
(A tent in which the winds flutter is dearer to me than a lofty palace.)
ʿUmāra ibn ʿAqīl ibn Bilāl committed a solecism by saying «الأرياح» in his poetry. Abū Ḥātim said to him: "«الأرياح» is not permissible." ʿUmāra said to him: "Do you not hear their saying «رياح»?" Abū Ḥātim said: "That is different from this." He said: "You are right", and retracted. The Shaykh said: "In what I memorised long ago, «الأرياح» occurred in the poetry of one of the eloquent Arabs whose speech is cited as evidence, as though they built it on the singular even though the cause of the change is absent in the plural, just as they said «عيد» and «أعياد», the original being «أَعْواد» because it is from «عاد يَعُود»; but when the substitution was kept it was treated like a radical letter." I say: what the Shaykh said is supported by [the fact] that their keeping the yāʾ in «الأرياح» is because of confusion between it and «أَرْواح», the plural of «رُوح» (spirit), just as they said: the yāʾ was kept in «أعياد» to distinguish it from «أَعْواد», the plural of «عُود» (stick of firewood); for that reason they said in the diminutive «عُيَيْد», not «عُوَيْد», and explained it by the said confusion.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "In the Qur'an it has come in the plural with mercy and in the singular with punishment, except in His saying: {وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم بِرِيحٍ طَيِّبَةٍ} [Yūnus: 22]. This is its predominant occurrence in speech. In the ḥadīth: '«الله [Translator's note: so in the source, for «اللهمّ»] اجعلها رياحاً ولا تَجْعَلْها ريحاً»' (O Allah, make it winds and do not make it a wind), because the wind of punishment is violent, its parts cohering as though it were a single body, while the wind of mercy is gentle and broken up. It was put in the singular with the ships — meaning in Yūnus — only because it is for making ships sail, and that is a single continuous [wind]; then it was described as good, so the overlap between it and the wind of punishment was removed." End of quotation. What he said is refuted by the readers' disagreement in eleven places, whose details will come. What should rather be said is that the plural never came with punishment at all, while the singular came with both; for that reason he [the Prophet], peace be upon him, specified the plural form in his supplication.

Here Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read «الريح» in the singular, and the rest in the plural. The plural is because of the diversity of their kinds — south wind, west wind, east wind and others — and the singular is meant as the genus.

«السحاب» is a generic noun whose singular is «سَحابة»; it was so called because of its being drawn along (insiḥāb), just as it was called «حَبِيّ» because it crawls (yaḥbū) — Abū ʿAlī [al-Fārisī] mentioned that. Considering it a generic noun, He described it with the attribute of a masculine singular in His saying «المُسَخَّر», as in His saying: {أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ مُّنقَعِرٍ} [al-Qamar: 20]; and when He considered its meaning on another occasion, He described it with what a plural is described with, in His saying: {سَحَاباً ثِقَالاً} [al-Aʿrāf: 57]. It may also be described with what a single feminine noun is described with, as in His saying: {أَعْجَازُ نَخْلٍ خَاوِيَةٍ} [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. So it is with every generic noun: it has two usages, the masculine in consideration of the wording and the feminine in consideration of the meaning.

«التسخير» is subjugation and making a thing come under obedience. Al-Rāghib said: "It is compulsion to act, and it is stronger than coercion."

His saying: {بَيْنَ السمآء}: there are two views on «بين». One: that it is accusative by His saying «المُسخَّرِ», and so is an adverb of the subjugation. The second: that it is a ḥāl from the pronoun latent (mustatir) in the passive participle, and so is attached to an omitted element, i.e.: being between the sky [and the earth]. «لآياتٍ» is the noun of «إنَّ», and the prepositional phrase is its fronted khabar (predicate). The lām entered the noun because it comes after the khabar; had it been in its [normal] place, that would not have been permissible in it.

And His saying: {لِّقَوْمٍ} is in the position of the accusative because it is a naʿt of «آيات», and so is attached to an omitted element. And His saying «يَعْقِلون»: the clause is in the position of the genitive [Translator's note: the source reads «في محلذ شجرٍ», a misprint for «في محلّ جرٍّ»] because it is a naʿt of «قوم».

semin-durr:178-178.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {القصاص فِي القتلى}: i.e. because of the slain; «في» can be causal, as in his words (upon him be peace): «A woman entered the Fire in [the matter of] a cat», i.e. because of it. The pattern «فَعْلَى» is regularly a plural of faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl (passive); something of this has preceded at His words: {وَإِن يَأتُوكُمْ أسارى} [al-Baqara: 85].
His words: {الحر بِالْحُرِّ}: a mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar (predicate); the implied form is: "the free man is taken for the free man", or "is killed for the free man". So you supply a specific verb of being (kawn khāṣṣ), omitted because the context indicates it, since the bāʾ in it is causal. It is not permissible to supply a general verb of being (kawn muṭlaq), since there would be no benefit if you said "the free man is [existing] for the free man" — unless you supply a muḍāf, i.e. "the killing of the free man is for the free man". The Shaykh allowed «الحُرُّ» to be nominative by an omitted verb, its implied form being "the free man is killed for the free man", indicated by His words {القصاص فِي القتلى}, since «القصاص» suggests this implied verb; but this is far-fetched.
Al-qiṣāṣ is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of qāṣṣahu yuqāṣṣuhu qiṣāṣan and muqāṣṣatan, like qātaltuhu qitālan and muqātalatan. Its origin is from qaṣaṣtu al-shayʾ, [meaning] you followed its trace, because it is a following up of the blood of the slain.
Al-ḥurr (free) is an adjective, and the plural of an adjective of the pattern «فُعْل» on afʿāl is not regular; they said ḥurr and aḥrār, murr and amrār. The feminine is ḥurra, and its plural ḥarāʾir is likewise a matter of attested usage. One says: ḥarra the boy, yaḥarru, ḥurriyyatan (he became free).
His words: {فَمَنْ عُفِيَ}: two interpretations are permissible for «مَنْ». The first: that it is conditional. The second: that it is relative. On both, its position is nominative as mubtadaʾ. On the first, «عُفِي» is in the position of the jussive (majzūm) by the condition; on the second it has no position. The fāʾ in His words «فاتِّباع» is obligatory on the first, and its position together with what follows is jussive; and it is permissible on the second, and its position with what follows is nominative as khabar. The apparent view is that «مَنْ» is the killer, and that the pronoun in «له» and «أخيه» refers to «مَنْ»; «شيءٌ» is what stands in place of the fāʿil (i.e. nāʾib fāʿil, deputy agent), and by it the maṣdar is meant. «عُفِي» is made passive even though it is intransitive, because an intransitive verb passes over to the maṣdar, as in His words: {فَإِذَا نُفِخَ فِي الصور نَفْخَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ} [al-Muʾminūn: 101] «[Translator's note: the wording quoted combines al-Muʾminūn: 101 and al-Ḥāqqa: 13.]». The brother is the slain man or the next of kin of the blood; He called him a brother of the killer to incline him to compassion toward him. This maṣdar standing in place of the fāʿil means the blood that is pardoned. ʿAfā passes over to the offender and to the offence by «عن»: you say "I pardoned Zayd (ʿafawtu ʿan Zaydin)" and "I pardoned Zayd's sin (ʿafawtu ʿan dhanbi Zaydin)"; when it passes over to both together, it passes over to the offender with lām and to the offence with ʿan: you say "ʿafawtu li-Zaydin ʿan dhanbihi" (I pardoned Zayd his sin). The verse belongs to this class, i.e. "whoever is pardoned for his offence". It has also been said that «مَنْ» is the next of kin of the blood, i.e. whoever is granted, out of his brother's blood, a substitute for the blood, namely retaliation or blood-money; «شيء» then means that due right, and the brother means the slain. On this view the killer may also be meant by it, with «الشيء» meaning the blood-money. On these two views «عُفِي» means "was made easy"; it has also been said that it means "was left".
Al-Zamakhsharī denounced those who explained «عُفِيَ» as meaning «تُرِكَ» (was left). He said: If you say: why did you not explain «عُفي» as meaning «تُركَ», so that «شيء» would have the sense of a mafʿūl bihi (direct object)? I say: because ʿafā al-shayʾa meaning "he left it" is not established; rather [what is established is] «أعفاه», and from it «وَأَعْفوا اللَّحى» (and leave the beards to grow). If you say: their saying "ʿafā atharahu" when one effaces and removes it is established, so why not make its meaning: "whoever has something of his brother['s offence] effaced for him"? I say: it is an expression ill-suited to its place; whereas pardon (al-ʿafw) in the domain of offences is a current and well-known expression in the Book, the Sunna and people's usage, so one does not turn away from it to another expression that is ill-suited and out of place. You see many of those who engage in this science, when explaining a difficult passage of Allah's speech defeats them, venture to invent a usage and to impute to the Arabs what they did not know; and this is an audacity from which refuge is sought with Allah.
The Shaykh said: «If it is established that «عَفَا» means "effaced", it is not far-fetched to take the verse in that sense, and the attribution of «عَفَا» to its nominative would be a literal attribution, because it would then be an explicit mafʿūl bihi; whereas when it is intransitive, its attribution to its nominative is figurative, because it is a maṣdar likened to a mafʿūl bihi. So the two interpretations may balance each other: I mean intransitive ʿafā, because of its currency in [the domain of] offences, and transitive «عفا» meaning «مَحَا», because of its literal connection with its nominative». If it is said: «عَفَا» is made to include the meaning of «ترك» — the answer is that such inclusion (taḍmīn) is not a regular rule; yet Ibn ʿAṭiyya allowed ʿafā to mean taraka. It has also been said that «عُفِيَ» means "was in excess", the meaning being: whoever of the two parties has something of those blood-monies in excess over the other — from their saying ʿafā al-shayʾu when a thing became abundant. The most apparent of these views is the first.
His words: {فاتباع بالمعروف}: there are three interpretations of the nominative of «اتباع». The first: that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gave its implied form as "then the ruling, or the obligation, is following up", and al-Zamakhsharī as "then the matter is a following up".
